#1457. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

#1456. Exiled Jack Grealish RETURNS to Everton training after being dropped following boozy nights at pubs and karaoke: Ex-England star could be back in team after international break

Published: 12:34 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EDT, 6 November 2026

Jack Grealish will return to Everton training after being dropped and exiled by David Moyes.

The 31-year-old was axed for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and is not part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin when they host Coventry tonight.

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since re-joining Everton for a second season-long loan spell from Man City in the summer, had been banished since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

Grealish will now be reintegrated on a tailored training programme to regain match fitness and could be included in first-team sessions during the international break from next week.

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

Grealish was reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

Jack Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

David Moyes could start Grealish against Brentford after the international break

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London.

According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Moyes had been coy on the situation when asked about it on Thursday. He said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision (for him to be punished). It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

After the Coventry clash, Everton are next in Premier League action at Gtech Community Stadium against Brentford on November 23.

Grealish will be targeting a return in that fixture and hope he can begin to rebuild his relationship with Moyes over the next three weeks.

He has played for England 39 times and turned out for Everton on 22 occasions, scoring twice and providing six assists, with a nasty foot injury cut short his campaign last term.

#1455. A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC–VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

The photoreceptor PhyC functions as an upstream flowering regulator in grass species, promoting the expression of the photoperiodic responser PHOTOPERIODIC 1 (PPD1) and the flowering inducer FT1 (VERNALIZATION 3)21,22,23. The ancient haplotype PhyC-l, in combination with the winter-type vrn-H1 allele that requires vernalization, delays the transition from vegetative to reproductive growth, thereby preventing flowering (2nd panel, blue). In contrast, the spring-type Vrn-H1 variant, which carries a truncation in the first intron of VRN-H1 and eliminates the need of vernalization, enable flowering without cold exposure (1st panel, yellow). This allele in conjugation with PhyC-l is commonly adapted to spring-sown regimes in high-latitude or high-altitude regions. The East Asian-specific PhyC-e variant, which carries an F380S substitution at the PhyC locus and is consistently associated with winter-type vrn-H1 allele, promotes early flowering and supports adequate biomass accumulation (3rd panel, pink). The PhyC-e + vrn-H1 module allows barley to escape terminal heat stress, safeguard final yield, and fit to double-season cropping systems by leaving sufficient time for subsequent crops. This module has been widely selected in China’s Yangtze River basin. Notably, the haplotype combination PhyC-e + Vrn-H1 was not detected in barley natural germplasm (4th panel, dashed line). In this study, this novel module was generated either by base editing or by linkage breaking in the near-isogenic lines (NILs). It resulted in extremely early flowering and maturity, significantly reduced biomass, and undetected grain yield. This module holds potential for application in regions with extremely short growing seasons, such as those at very high latitudes or altitudes and at subtropical zones.

#1454. Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals

Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be important, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

“We are trying to improve the squad,” Arteta, the Arsenal head coach, said. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it [my energy] now.”

Asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really big when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”

This was an Aston Villa team there for the taking after being gutted by their Premier League rivals and still waiting for new signings to be ready to play and gel.

But Arsenal made hard work of their victory and one senses there will be more games like this if Arteta has to rely on what he has already got until at least January.

Chelsea are showing they can score goals for fun having spent £117m on Rogers. Manchester City are strengthening their firepower with the signing of Iliman Ndiaye and Bradley Barcola has joined Liverpool. Arsenal have the defence and the midfield, but not necessarily the depth of quality in forward positions of their rivals.

0.52 - Arsenal faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (1) and allowed their opponents the lowest xG (0.52) across the first two matchdays of the Premier League season.🔒 Locked. pic.twitter.com/blSUAeqoLb

Christos Tzolis is the lone attacking signing to date and there was evidence at Villa Park that it will be a risk to rely too heavily on the Greek winger.

Tzolis had made an exciting start to his Arsenal career in the Community Shield and the first Premier League victory over Coventry City, but he had to be taken off at half-time on Monday night.

The former Club Brugge winger not only lost out to Matty Cash, but was also at the centre of Villa appeals for him to be sent off.

Tzolis had already been booked for a foul on Cash, when, in the 36th minute, he appeared to foul John McGinn as Villa broke from the edge of their own penalty area.

McGinn appealed that Tzolis should have been shown a second yellow card, but referee Jarred Gillett let the Arsenal man off the hook.

Arteta was wise to take Tzolis off at the break and his replacement, Eberechi Eze, had a hand in what proved to be Arsenal’s 59th-minute winner.

Eze slipped in Riccardo Calafiori and Saka got in front of Ian Maatsen to poke the Arsenal full-back’s low cross into the net. Saka’s goal had been the first shot on target in the game.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Just before the goal, Arsenal thought they had been awarded a penalty. Ross Barkley lost possession with a sloppy pass, allowing Declan Rice to advance towards the Villa penalty area. He played the ball through for Saka and Maatsen barged into the back of the winger.

Gillett paused before pointing to the spot, but a VAR check showed that Maatsen’s foul had taken place outside the penalty area and Martin Odegaard fired the resulting free-kick wide.

The goal and the overturned penalty were pretty much it for Arsenal in terms of threatening the hosts, for whom goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made his debut. Suzuki did not have much to do with his hands, but impressed with his distribution.

It was Villa who went closest to scoring in the first half, through one of the club’s five surviving members of last season’s Europa League-winning team.

Emiliano Buendia scored Villa’s second goal in the final against Freiburg and the Argentine rattled the Arsenal crossbar with a 20-yard shot that had beaten visiting goalkeeper David Raya.

Before then, McGinn had sent a shot over Raya’s bar and into the building site where Villa are redeveloping the club’s old North Stand.

Buendia, McGinn, Cash, Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof are the only Villa players to have started the Europa League final who have not left this summer.

Defender Ezri Konsa is one of Villa’s Europa League winners to have departed and he made his Arsenal debut as a late substitute. The defender received a mixed reception, as he was first booed by some home fans but was then applauded.

Other than hitting the bar in the opening 45 minutes, Villa squandered a chance for a quick reply to Arsenal’s opener when McGinn hesitated instead of shooting after being played in by Nicolas Jackson.

Jackson lasted 71 minutes for Villa in what proved to be a promising debut. In the first half, he raced away down the right before sending the ball across the six-yard box. But there was no team-mate on hand to convert.

One of Villa’s other summer signings, Alejandro Garnacho, is yet to make an impact for his new club. The Argentine got an earful from manager Unai Emery for not being ready to go on. He eventually replaced Ross Barkley, but could not help conjure an equaliser.

This is the start Arteta wanted. But, in attacking positions, Arsenal will finish the transfer window weaker than they started it if the club are not active in the final hours of the transfer window. And that could prove costly.

We lost. We competed well. They won the league last year. We are trying to build a team but a lot of positive things [beyond] the result. How we competed. How it was progressively better. We didn’t create clear chances. Some players made fantastic debuts. Suzuki and Jackson did very good work. I think it’s the first step forward and positive for the next matches.

Accepting this result, I think we had chances to draw the match but we are in our rebuild. It is the way [ahead for us] making these changes and I say to the supporters and players that the message is there in the way we played.

To lose one match is painful but after the pain we must try to get positive things, This is the reason I am optimistic. There are 38 matches we played two. We haven’t one point but we can get better hopefully. And we will get players [Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis].

We can feel confidence because how we want to build the team again is true, to compete like today.

I think the squad we have now is how we planned with the  players we wanted.

[Are you confident you have replaced the quality that has gone?] Yes.

I’m really happy. It’s a big win. It’s a tough place to come and earn the three points but I think we deserved it.

It was a game where 11 was not enough and the finishers came in and did a magnificent job to win it. I know how tough it is to win here.

Every big team struggles against them for the past four years because they are so good. They are well coached, have great players. Great in transition. The moment you lose the ball and let them run inside they are really dangerous but I love a lot of the things I saw from my team.

Ebs [Eze] creates the action that sees us win the game, Bruno with Mikel [Merino] in midfield changed the dynamic of it, Ezri [Konsa] really composed and calm with every decision he made and then Zubi… I’m really happy with all of them.

Every game in the Premier League it’s like [you’re saying] we have to win this game. We know the level. We know how difficult it is in this league.

[Can you sign Julian Alvarez tomorrow?] I don’t know. That’s for the people upstairs.

It was a very tough match. Aston Villa’s defensive setup made things difficult for us, constantly catching us offside. We couldn’t attack as comfortably as we did last week. But as you know, sometimes one goal is enough for us. We have a very strong defence.

Today, we were great out of possession too and didn’t allow transition attacks.

I keep my targets for myself. Every week I want to be there and try decide the game as that’s what I’m in the team to do. That’s my mentality.

[Have you seen Chelsea?] I’ve seen them. [What do you think?] We’ll see on Sunday.

Jamie Carragher explains how Arsenal broke Aston Villa down for their winning goal 🔎 pic.twitter.com/CAI8zhznrJ

Arsenal host Chelsea on Sunday at 4.30pm while Villa go to Hull City at 5.30pm on Saturday. It’s too early for a must-win game for Villa who showed some positive signs tonight but they could certainly do with one.

Arsenal win with a performance of efficiency and patience that emphasises their superiority when asked to grind out a result.

John McGinnis arguing the toss with the referee about his belief that he was fouled in the box in the dying seconds. It was outside the box and if Maatsen’s ‘tackle’ wasn’t a foul, neither was Gabriel’s.

Not sure the way of refereeing that lets a lot of calls go and waits for VAR is going to enhance the game.

Maatsen tackles Bruno Guimaraes in the Villa box with an ugly lunge in which he appears to scissor him, kicking his heel with one leg before knocking the ball away with the other but the referee deems it fair and VAR lets it pass, too.

Arsenal’s game management is working well as usual until Raya goes too long and the ball bounces through to Suzuki. But when he starts a counter-attack Alysson ends it with a dive and back come Arsenal.

Maatsen slides in late on Saka down the right, bypasses the ball and crashes into his shin. Yellow card.

Aston Villa probe but Arsenal hold them 30 yards from goal and when they do slide pass down the side of a defender for Buendia to chase, Bruno is ideally positioned to cover and make the block which he celebrates as if he were Leonardo Bonucci.

Eight minutes of stoppage time are signalled by the fourth official.

Suzuki races 15 yards outside his box to head a long pass away from Havertz to McGinn. Back come Arsenal after McGinn is squeezed off the ball but Wan-Bisska wins it back with a fine tackle. He is among the best one-on-one pure defenders in the league.

Zubimendi rattles Buendia’s bones in a crunching but legal tackle.

That was Rice’s last contribution as he limps off. He is probably OK but wise to withdraw him if he has had a twinge.

Maatsen drives down the left and cuts into the box. White leans into him, Rice guides him with a rigid left arm and the rampaging left-back loses his feet. Maatsen acknowledges Rice’s fine defending when he gets back up.

Quite a few outside observers questioned why Arsenal signed Konsa. This apparent injury to Mosquera is the reason. With Saliba out for months and Timber still struggling to regain his fitness, Mosquera was the only right-sided centre-back in the squad (unless they repurposed White, who is needed at right back).

Garnacho faces up Saka after being played down the left by Buendia but his cross is blocked by the goalscorer. Raya catches the resulting corner.

McGinn wipes out Merino from behind and is deservedly booked. Moments earlier Alysson was also booked for leaving one on Gabriel after the centre-half had cleared the ball, choosing not to put on the brakes and bodychecking him instead.

Unai Emery has just gone ballistic at substitute Alejandro Garnacho.

Emery clearly wasn’t happy with Garnacho not being ready to come on and let the Chelsea loanee know about it.

And Mosquera cannot continue having overstretched so it’s a debut for the former Villa stalwart who is greeted warmly.

Suzuki saves in a one-on-one with Havertz running through from 40 yards, waiting and refusing to go down and make things easy for Havertz, sticking up a right arm to block the shot. But he may have been offside which may mitiagte it in terms of not costing Arsenal anything but he really should have beaten the keeper.

Nice pass from Merino to set the hare running.

Barkley plays a diagonal pass across the turf out to Alysson on the right and he hares round Calafiori to cross from the byline but could not get the ball past Gabriel at the near post.

Now Maatsen goes flying but this time in the Arsenal box under a challenge from White that was a duplicate of the one 30 seconds before. ‘Premier League corrupt as f---,’ sing the Villa fans, ignoring the similarities between the two incidents. The defenders’ arms made contact with the attacking players but without the force to send them sprawling.

Havertz hits the deck in the Villa penalty area when challenged by Kamara as they fought for Odegaard’s scooped dink from the right.

Bruno Guimaraes and Mikel Merino are stripped and ready to come on.

Once again, it’s Riccardo Calafiori who opens up the opposition’s defence with his off-the-ball running. He is the one player in this Arsenal team who makes genuinely unpredictable and unexpected movements.

McGinn’s combination with Jackson looks promising and the centre-forward invites him to bullock forward down the inside-right channel with a clever pass but the Villa captain is soon swamped by yellow shirts and the ball gets stuck beneath his feet.

Gary Neville makes the fair point that one of Arsenal’s most unheralded qualities is their patience. Their confidence in their rock-solid defence does not make them reckless but they are always confident of finding a way. They trust the method implicitly.

Aston Villa 0 Arsenal 1 (Saka) Mosquera has the ball 25 yards out, left of centre, he strokes it to Eze who angles a pass to Calafiori running between Cash and Lindelof. He makes it to the byline and cuts back a low cross that Saka and Maatsen both lunge at and the Arsenal winger gets there first to turn it in.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Rice, Eze and Odegaard stand over it. Rive walks away and Odegaard approaches the ball with a semi-circular run-up. He whips it over the wall and about a foot wide of the left post. Suzuki was stranded but no matter.

It was outside the box. Not all that sure it was a foul either. But Arsenal will have a free-kick.

Maatsen and Saka collide as they chase a Rice pass that Saka would never reach. Seemed to be outside the box.

It has been fairly dull fare so far as two systems and structures that cede little space clash.

Lindelof rises high to meet Rice;s dipping cross from the right as Havertz, on his shoulder, was poised to pounce. He heads it straight up and Suzuki leaps to catch it.

Now Barkley picks out a diagonal to send Jackson down the left. The centre-forward reaches the 18-yard line, cuts inside and works it over to McGinn who lofts a cross over Villa’s back-post runners and out of play.

Eze did his best work from the left last season. Villa start with Barkley scoop-chipping a pass from the middle out to the left, 40 yards upfield. Maatsen runs on to it and drives past White to ram a shot into the side-netting.

Arsenal were too slow to move the ball forward in that first half, and too loose with it when they did get into promising positions. There’s a lack of urgency in their passing. I wonder if we’ll see Bruno Guimarães soon… one of the reasons they signed him was to add more quick forward passing to their play.

Signs of encouragement for Villa without creating much while Arsenal have been stymied so far by Villa’s neutering of Tzolis and the left wing. Arsenal’s right-sided trio – White, Odegaard and Saka – look the most likely to create something.

Only a minute of added time to be played. Arsenal still lacking a spark, largely because there’s a lack of precision in their forward, line-breaking passing.

Villa will be very happy with this half. Much more like their old selves in terms of structure and organisation.

Calafiori’s throw to Gabriel is picked off by Jackson down the right and he dribbles down the right. He is forced to slow down to wait for a midfield runner. When Hemmings catches up, so have three Arsenal defenders and though Jackson bends in a low, cross to the edge of the six-yard box it is about 18 inches away from Hemmings’ reach.

Calafiori goes down in the Villa box when Pau Torres uses his arm to lever him away as they tracked the flight of a cross. The referee sees nothing wring in it and neither does VAR.

Gillett takes an age to stop the play when Cash uses his body to shove Tzolis over after the winger had played a pass. Cash obviously thinks he has rattled the new signing and is keen to rough him up some more. The ref does award a free-kick but only after that daft delay.

Tzolis loses the ball on the edge of the Villa penalty area, tackled by McGinn. The captain slots a straight pass up to Buendia who tries to bend a pass into Jackson’s stride as he sprinted down the inside right channel but Gabriel read the trajectory and got there first.

Suzuki picks out McGinn with a long pass. He feeds it to Buendia who gives Hemmings a chance to chase it down the left. Arsenal shuffle over in defence so he doubles back and returns the ball to Buendia. The No 10 whips over a dipping cross looking for Barkley and Jackson but Calafiori and Raya make sure the goalkeeper wins it.

We’ve not seen much from Christos Tzolis on Arsenal’s left wing so far. He’s been excellent since joining the club this summer but he’s hardly seen the ball in this opening half an hour and he’s just been booked after losing a battle with Matty Cash.

Arsenal free-kick 30 yards out, left of centre, for a foul on Lewis-Skelly who was artfully shielding the ball. Odegaard chips to the right post but Havertz heads it back across the box rather than going for goal and Villa clear.

Cash gets the better of Tzolis again in the tackle and then Suzuki sprays a perfect 60-yard pass out to Hemmings that Gary Neville, likening it to something Ederson was capable of delivering for Man City, one of the best goalkeeper passes he has ever seen. Tzolis was booked for stopping Cash running off with the ball.

Maatsen, who could never dislodge Digne for long, has a chance now to make the position his won. He strides down the left, exploiting Rice’s positioning error but his right-foot isn’t half as good as his left and his bending effort is scuffed far too straight and easily cleared.

Saka drives down the right after a neat Odegaard, Saka, White triangle. Pau Torres races over to toe the ball behind for a corner. Saka takes and Rice flicks it on at the near post and Suzuki tips it over. No corner, though, as Gabriel had rag-dolled McGinn at the back post after the Villa captain had backed in to him and tried to stop him making a run into the middle.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that.” Villa fans poke the wound.

Arsenal are finding it difficult to play through the middle of the pitch but have found Saka in space on the right wing on a few occasions already. Villa are congesting the central areas, where Odegaard does his best work.

Calafiori picks off Kamara’s pass looking, for the third or fourth time, to play someone, usually Jackson, in behind the left-back. A minute later Calafiori challenges McGinn for a bouncing, loose ball and stoops to use his head. colliding with McGinn’s boot. Was the head low or the boot high? Arsenal think the latter but the ref sides, rightly, with McGinn.

Arsenal corner on the left. The threat inherent every time Rice is in a quadrant diminished on this occasion because Mosquera barged Cash just after Rice struck the ball. Free-kick to Villa.

Timber may be preferred by Arteta at right-back but Saka prefers White. The two have a well-grooved partnership in tersm of who underlaps and who overlaps. They never seem to get in each other’s way.

Bukayo Saka does seem to be getting a lot of time and space on the right flank.

It’s looking a risky tactic by Villa at the moment as the England international is being invited to cut in towards the penalty area.

Havertz is played down the inside-right channel in the penalty area by a cute Odegaard pass bur he blazes his shot across goal and wide of the left post. A replay shows he was offside but even so it was a lazy finish.

Kamara grabs Tzolis round the waist from behind and when the winger hits the deck, rounds him and passus to Buendia who crashes a right-foot diagonal shot on to the bar from 20 yards. The ref did not see it as a foul despite Arsenal’s protestations but had it gone in it would have given VAR a dilemma.

Worth keeping an eye on Aston Villa midfielder George Hemmings tonight.

He is only a teenager and has emerged from Villa’s academy, but Unai Emery is already a huge fan.

Hemmings produced a highly promising performance in the Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

Suzuki misjudges the flight of Rice’s typically menacing corner and flaps at it but his defenders and an offside flag leave him without egg on his face.

McGinn stops Calafiori down the left then gives the ball straight to Tzolis. The Greece winger opens his body and passes to Lewis-Skelly who shoots with his right foot from the left of the 18-yard line. Cash slides in to block the shot and it loops over the bar for a corner.

Hemmings uses his strength to hold off Ben White and shift the ball inside to McGinn who wraps his left instep around a shot and wafts it into building site behind Raya’s goal.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis are in the directors’ box watching the game. Villa don’t look like a hastily assembled team.

Suzuki knocks the ball long with his left foot, looking for Jackson but the ball spins away from him to Raya who boots it back upfield. McGinn pounces on it, turns past Rice and plays Cash in down the right. He crosses towards the near post and Mosquera hooks it clear.

Arsenal kick off with Odegaard spinning and trying to play Saka in down the right as they defend the empty North Stand end. The ball skids off the turf and Saka can’t trap it. The ball goes out for a Villa throw-in.

Who dies in the summer and played for both clubs.

Arsenal are in fact in yellow and navy. My mistake.

Villa in claret and blue with a twist, the shorts are blue for the first time since, I think 2001. Arsenal are in yellow and black. Leeds, like Arsenal, have traditionally worn yellow and blue as their away strip but have been shunted into yellow and black as well by Adidas this season.

There are a few guys standing in the North Stand with hard hats on, and it appears they are on ball retrieval duty.

They will be on red alert for any wayward shots that land in the empty stand.

Warm reception for Ezri Konsa from Villa’s fans as he walked back to the tunnel with Arsenal’s substitutes.

Konsa joined Arsenal last week for £51m, ending a spell of seven years at Villa Park.

Wonder if the likes of Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez will get a similar reception when they return here with Chelsea.

Aston Villa  Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Barkley; McGinn, Buendía, Hemmings; Jackson. Substitutes  Bizot, Mings, Ruggeri, Garnacho, Abraham, Bogarde, Wan-Bissaka, Edward, Lynch.

Arsenal  Raya; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Rice; Saka, Odegaard, Tzolis; Havertz. Substitutes  Arrizabalaga, Hincapié, Eze, Gyokeres, Konsa, Madueke, Merino, Zubimendi, Guimaraes.

Zion Suzuki is one of two debuts for Aston Villa tonight and there is a genuine buzz of excitement around the Japan international.

Suzuki was signed from Parma for £30m as the replacement for Emiliano Martinez and arrives with a stellar reputation.

He’s got big boots – and gloves – to fill, but Unai Emery is convinced he will become a future star at Villa Park.

The other debutant is record £65m signing Nicolas Jackson, who joined last week from Chelsea.

Good evening. Yes, the first match was not as planned but we must keep going forward. Today we are playing our first home match and I am looking forward. We need to try as soon as possible to get our best individuals fit for a good performance. And today is a good match for us. Ir is difficult but always with our supporters here we feel comfortable and confident. Hopefully we can transmit our positive energy to our supporters.

We lost the first game but it is not a [team full of rookies]. We have experienced players. They play with energy and know how we want to play. We have to adapt with Suzuki but we have confidence [in him]. Jackson, the striker, and other players, George Hemmings, he is young but played fantastically in pre-season. He knows how we want to play.

Today is a challenge but I’m really looking forward to how the players will respond collectively, individually. We know we are changing things but no excuses. We have to perform today, we have to try to adapt the new players, to build our team to get their best today.

I am positive and I am optimistic. The players are ready.

Aston Villa are in a transition period and rebuilding on and off the field.

Unai Emery’s 2.0 have been under construction all summer and there could be 10 new signings in by tomorrow morning.

Villa have of course lost six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final, with Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Emiliano Martinez and Lucas Digne all departing this summer.

The North Stand at Villa Park, which faces the iconic Holte End, is also under renovation and closed down for tonight’s game.

It could be a bit quieter tonight but there is still a mood of optimism among Villa fans, despite such a summer of change.

We have had a real block of training sessions to work on things and prepare for this game in the right way.

We will have time to make changes throughout the game [on why he has picked an unchanged team]. They did really well [against Coventry] and for the game we expect [tonight] they have the right qualities to hurt them and that’s how we start.

They have that [upheaval in personnel] but they have been with Unai for a long time, they are a super well-coached team and we know how tough it is always to come here. We are very conscious of that but also very ambitious.

That’s the way we want to play [with aggression] constantly from the first minute, to suffocate the opponent and be better than them.

[Does it being your 250th Arsenal Premier League game add something special to it?] Just to win [makes it special].

She wore… she wore… she wore a yellow ribbon …

Two changes – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson make debuts. Joao Gomes misses the match as the first of his three-game suspension and Marco Bizot drops to the bench.

Arteta names unchanged starting XI but Bruno Guimaraes is fit for the bench. Ezri Konsa joins him there.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Aston Villa and Arsenal from Villa Park. The champions travel to the team that finished fourth last season in buoyant mood and form despite some misgivings within their fanbase about their recruitment this summer.

It amounts so far to making Pier Hincapié‘s loan into a proper transfer, revamping the left wing with Christos Tzolis replacing Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, upgrading options in central midfield by buying Bruno Guimarães and selling Cristian Norgaard – and signing Ezri Konsa from today’s opponents to give them the greatest elite defensive depth that I can recall at club since Manchester City’s Treble winners had Kyle Walker, Ruben Dias, John Stones, Nathan Aké, João Cancelo, Aymeric Laporte, Manuel Akanji, Rico Lewis and Sergio Gómez on the books at the same time.

Villa, by contrast, have endured a turbulent summer of trading with the departures of Europa League winners Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, the aforementioned Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emi Martínez, raising, along with other departures, more than £315m. They have spent about £180m to remodel the team though Johan Manzambi, who is injured, and João Gomes, who is suspended after his red card in the 4-0 defeat by Brighton, are absent tonight.

We can expect to see Zion Suzuki, Matteo Ruggeri and hopefully Nicolas Jackson and Leon Goretzka who have been registered in time to play, plus the loan signings Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho. Still to come are the pending purchases of Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye in a process that emphasises how profoundly Villa are invested in and dependent upon their manager, Unai Emery.

After so much upheaval, it would be foolish to set much store on Villa’s 2-1 victory last season, sealed by Emi Buendía’s winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Arsenal barely broke sweat in blowing Man City away in the Community Shield and cakewalked to victory over Coventry in the league’s opening fixture. His past work suggests Emery will be able to forge another formidable side from his talented new squad but this match feels two months too soon for him against his old club.

#1453. Celtic's Europa League win over Besiktas a welcome boost ... but Mika Baur says belief has always been there

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:32 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:41 EDT, 6 November 2026

It's fair to say that the way in which Martin O’Neill got Celtic off the mark in the Europa League against Besiktas divided public opinion.

For many of those viewing a starting line-up including Jordan Lotomba, Seb Tounekti and James Forrest, the veteran lucked out.

The opposing take was that O’Neill executed a managerial masterclass. That the belated introductions of Callum Osmand, Camilo Duran and Colby Donovan constituted a textbook rope-a-dope approach.

Whatever the truth of the matter, and only O’Neill truly knows what it is, you could not possibly argue with the outcome.

Second best in the contest for an hour, Celtic improved markedly in the final 30 minutes and refused to accept a share of the spoils when it seemed destined to be their lot.

How you finish a match is, indeed, just as important as how you start it. And it helps, of course, when those who belatedly enter the fray bring not only goals but pace, panache and a positive attitude.

Midfielder Mika Baur has been a standout performer in an up-and-down season for Celtic

‘That’s what you want from the subs — to make an impact from the bench,’ said midfielder Mika Baur.

‘It says a lot for Camilo to accept the situation of starting on the bench. But to come on and make such an impact, producing in the big moments to score those two goals to win us the game was huge.

‘Ossie [Osmand] as well, he came on with a goal and assist. He won the ball as well and was working hard. I’m really glad for them.’

In every respect, Celtic needed a night like that. O’Neill walked off the team coach before the game knowing a loss would see him become the first manager in the club’s history to oversee five straight European defeats.

With the wider picture of just three wins in ten matches, the scatter gun had been trained on everyone at the club in recent days – the hierarchy, the players, the manager and his coaching staff.

‘The win was important after some tough weeks,’ Baur reflected. ‘But the belief and the way we work together as a team has always been good. There was never any problem with that because we always believed in ourselves.

‘We showed how we can leave our hearts on the field and put in a shift. It was important to get those three points and we deserved it.

‘Hopefully, we can go forward with the confidence from this game.’

Given the air of gloom which has hung over the club lately, the Turks’ opener, stemming from a ludicrous tackle by Lotomba, felt for all the world like an extension of so much which had gone before.

From the minute Osmand levelled with his first touch, however, the entire dynamic of the evening changed.

Celtic found something deep within themselves that just hadn’t been there up until that point. The positivity on the field was mirrored by the buoyant mood in the stands.

The introductions of Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran turned Thursday's clash on its head

‘The fans helped a lot. You could feel the energy,’ said Baur. ‘It was not just us players on the field who deserved the win — it was also everyone around the stadium and they brought the energy as well.

‘It’s an unbelievable feeling as a player to have everyone pushing you and being there for you. It gives you that last percentage of energy you need at the end.’

Technically impressive and tactically astute, Baur caught the eye on Thursday, just as he has done in most of his matches since moving to Glasgow from Paderborn for £4.5million in the summer.

Whatever criticisms can justifiably be made of the club’s recruitment across a number of years, the German has already justified the faith shown in him.

It’s easy to forget that he’s still only 22. The level of scrutiny he’s being subjected to in Glasgow is a new thing. So far, however, he’s shown up well.

‘Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t,’ he shrugged. ‘But I hope people understand that as a young player it can be tough to be comfortable in a new country, a new culture and new club.

‘I have felt good in my first few months but it is a bit of a rollercoaster. Playing in this unbelievable stadium in front of these fans — you feel the pressure with some of the games we have lost, but I am getting used to it.’

Having earned his first full cap in September after being called up by new Germany boss Jurgen Klopp, Baur has dropped back down to the Under-21s in the coming fortnight but takes only positives from his experience of the last international camp.

‘I can understand,’ he said. ‘There are so many unbelievable players in the squad, especially in my position.

‘We’re talking about guys from Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund. I just do my best and hopefully they can see I am developing and improving.

‘I’m still with the Under-21s for the games against Belgium and Croatia, so that will be good.

‘European matches like Thursday can only help and I have to hope they see. I’m still young but I’ll keep doing my best and we’ll see what happens next time.’

#1452. Thomas Tuchel admits his relationship with Jude Bellingham is 'up and down' - but on the mend - as he reveals he's apologised to Kobbie Mainoo who is struggling at 'off a cliff' Man United

Published: 14:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 15:27 EDT, 6 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel says his rocky relationship with Jude Bellingham is on the mend after revealing he called his brother Jobe in to the England squad after some cajoling from the Real Madrid star.

Tuchel and Bellingham Snr have not always seen eye to eye during the German's time as England boss.

But Tuchel said today he hopes those days are behind him after he called 21-year-old Borussia Dortmund midfielder Jobe into this squad for next week's Nations League games against Croatia and Spain.

'It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place,' said Tuchel.

'I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable he would not perform on that level.

'In the moment you see he's happy to come into camp, he's happy with the role he has, he's fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them is just the next step.

Thomas Tuchel has admitted he has an up and down relationship with Jude Bellingham

'I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!'

With injury to Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for Thursday's Croatia game at Wembley, Tuchel sprung a surprise by elevating Jobe Bellingham from the Under 21s to the senior squad.

'Yeah Jude and I have spoken about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream to play with Jobe for England,' explained Tuchel.

'Jude was always saying: "Watch him, watch him he's good, he can make it". 'I would say: "Yeah we are watching him".

'I think he actually watched training very early in my reign. He came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and said it would be nice if one day he was with him.

'He was very kind and very polite and I'm glad to have him in camp. Everyone will compare them and he has to live with this.

Now Tuchel says he 'loves' to be Bellingham's coach after his brilliant World Cup campaign

Jude had a hand in brother Jobe being called up to the England squad for the first time

'They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. Jobe is more defensive. I think they are also different characters, at least that's what I heard.

'He couldn't stop smiling when I called to tell him the news. He has the same beautiful smile like Jude so it's nice to have him.'

Tuchel's squad for what he insists are two important games was once again full of messages and insights into this thinking.

There was no room for Cole Palmer and Kobbie Mainoo after both players withdrew from the October campo with injuries. There was also no call up once again for Manchester City's Phil Foden.

Asked about Palmer, fit and ready now and in decent form at Chelsea, Tuchel said: 'It's not personal and we will never assume that he is not desperate to come and play.

'But the competition is on. It's about the ones who walk the walk and come to camp.

'Someone more intelligent once said to me: 'You cannot not communicate. You cannot not send a message.'

'So yeah. A nomination is always a message, yes.'

Tuchel revealed that he almost picked Foden – who hasn't played for England since March – after an upturn in his form but had second thoughts when he saw him relegated back to the bench at the Etihad Stadium.

'He is close and he will always be close,' said Tuchel.

'There were glimpses of the Phil Foden that we would love to see. He had these two matches with four or five goal involvements and assists and being so clinical.

Cole Palmer continues to be left out by Tuchel - while Phil Foden was close to a recall

'I got excited and thought: "That's it, that's, he found his mojo, he is getting back there". Then he dropped again and played again from the bench.

'I'm in love with him as a player. What is not to love?

'If you see the boy train it's just the highest, highest quality.

'But we're talking about numbers in an England shirt which are not in proportion to his talent and to his potential.

'If we can align this and become a regular City starter and be decisive, I think he has to be always an option.

'It was very close and it's also close for Eberechi Eze to keep his place with us. He's not starting for Arsenal.

'But the advantage was maybe that Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze come again into camp. The advantage was that they have been in camp last time.'

Thomas Tuchel has told how he apologised in front of the whole England squad to Kobbie Mainoo for not giving him a single minute during the summer's World Cup in America.

Mainoo cut a lost and frustrated figure during England's campaign after a succession of players were picked ahead of him in his central midfield position.

The Manchester United star has not made Tuchel's squad for the forthcoming Nations League games with Croatia and Spain after withdrawing from the last camp with injury.

Tuchel revealed: 'He was hugely disappointed from the World Cup, and deservedly so.

'I said it in front of the team, in front of the staff.

'I said: "Sorry that I didn't pick you, you did nothing wrong, that is on me".

'He was disappointed and I think it cost him a bit of confidence.

Tuchel has noted how Man United 'fell off a cliff' - causing issues for Kobbie Mainoo

'He was excellent in training and in the way he presented himself through the tournament.

'So he was never a problem, the way he carried himself.

'Then he pulled out of last camp. I was desperate to give him the minutes. Desperate to include him in this new start, in the Nations League.

'But he then missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

'He was injured then Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he suffers from that.'

#1451. Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4,5,6.

About 50 gigatons of carbon are fixed annually by marine phototrophs, feeding the entire microbial food web7,8,9. A substantial portion of this carbon fixation occurs during large-scale algal blooms1,10. Therefore, microbial processes that control cell fate in these blooms can have profound effects on marine carbon cycling11. Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse interactions and metabolic exchange with grazers, bacteria, fungi and viruses12,13. Marine viruses, the most abundant biological entities in the ocean, are major mortality agents, driving nutrient cycling globally and significantly impacting algal bloom demise2,14,15.

Viruses regulate the fate of carbon and other nutrients16 through two distinct ecosystem processes: the viral shunt4,5, which fuels the microbial food web by catalysing nutrient recycling in the surface ocean; and the viral shuttle5,6, which facilitates carbon export through enhanced aggregation of lysed cells and sinking of particulate organic matter in the oligotrophic ocean17 and during algal blooms18. Viral lysis of algal populations creates a distinct metabolic footprint19,20,21, which can promote the growth of adapted heterotrophs22, thereby altering microbial biodiversity23,24. Yet, how virus-induced shifts in microbial community composition influence algal cell fate—and thus global carbon cycling—remains poorly understood.

We selected G. huxleyi (previously known as Emiliania huxleyi) to study algae–virus–bacteria interactions owing to its ecological significance in marine ecosystems. This cosmopolitan unicellular eukaryotic alga forms extensive blooms, covering thousands of square kilometers25. It has a crucial role in global carbon and sulfur biogeochemical cycles due to its carbon fixation, its calcite exoskeleton production, and the release of sulfur volatiles such as dimethyl sulfide25,26,27. These blooms are often terminated following infection by a giant double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus, the Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV)28. Despite the observed synchronized collapse of entire blooms29, quantification of active viral infection using single-cell approaches revealed a discrepancy: fewer than 30% of algal cells were infected by the virus during the bloom’s demise3,30. This suggests that additional mortality agents may act together with viral infection. Inspired by findings from the biomedical field demonstrating that viral–bacterial co-infections synergistically increase mortality31,32, we investigated the interplay between bacteria and viruses during algal bloom demise. Using a bacterial consortium isolated from natural algal blooms (Extended Data Fig. 1), we showed that bacteria can exacerbate virus-induced algal mortality, revealing a previously unrecognized tripartite interaction with potentially important implications for global biogeochemical cycles.

We sought to determine the role of bacteria as additional mortality agents during virus-induced algal bloom demise. We hypothesized that if bacteria that are naturally associated with an alga contribute to its mortality, then an antibiotic treatment would reduce the overall death rate during viral infection. To test this idea, we cultured a xenic strain of G. huxleyi isolated from a bloom induced during a mesocosm experiment near Bergen, Norway24. In the absence of viral infection, the xenic cultures subjected to the antibiotic treatment showed up to 1.2-fold higher algal growth (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that under normal growth conditions, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi maintain a competitive relationship. Infection with EhV induced algal population decline from day 1 (Fig. 1a). However, when antibiotics were administered to reduce the abundance of the algal microbiome (Extended Data Fig. 2a), we observed reduced algal mortality, up to 19-fold, compared with cultures that were not treated with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 0.05 from day 2; Fig. 1a). This difference suggests that the bacterial community may contribute significantly to algal mortality during viral infection, indicating a potential synergistic pathogenic interaction between viruses and bacteria. Analysis of bacterial abundance revealed that bacteria grew to 1.5-fold higher abundance in the virus-infected cultures compared with the uninfected condition (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 4; Fig. 1b). The differences in viral production between antibiotic-treated and untreated algal cultures were significant during the days of viral release, but the abundances leveled off resulting in similar total abundances (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05 on day 4 and day 6; Fig. 1c).

Dynamics of xenic alga–virus interactions for G. huxleyi (Gh) (a–c), P. globosa (Pg) (d), M. commoda (Mc) (e) and O. tauri (Ot) (f). a,d–f, Growth curves of uninfected and virus-infected xenic algal cultures with or without antibiotic (Ab) treatment. b, Bacterial abundances in uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi cultures. c, Viral abundances in antibiotics-treated and untreated G. huxleyi cultures. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures for G. huxleyi and n = 3 for all other species). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001; NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05). Exact P values are provided in the Source data.

To determine the generality of our findings, we assessed whether such synergistic pathogenic interactions occur for other marine microalgae whose bloom demise is controlled by viral infections, namely Phaeocystis globosa, Micromonas commoda and Ostreococcus tauri33,34,35. The mortality of all three algae was significantly attenuated when treating virus-infected, xenic algal cultures with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1d–f). These results demonstrate that viral–bacterial synergy leading to algal mortality is a widespread phenomenon among key marine algal species. Notably, antibiotic treatment did not reduce the mortality of O. tauri upon infection with a specialist virus (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 2e), possibly owing to the rapid recovery of a resistant population. This exemplifies that the extent of viral–bacterial synergy may depend on various factors such as host susceptibility, viral infectivity and microbiome composition. We propose that bacteria and viruses kill synergistically, whereby viral infection creates favourable conditions for bacterial pathogenicity, accelerating algal mortality and fuelling bacterial growth. Thus, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi and other cosmopolitan microalgae can expedite their bloom demise during viral infection.

We sought to disentangle the interactions between algae, viruses and bacteria during algal bloom demise. To this end, we developed a tripartite laboratory model system using algal, viral and bacterial strains that were isolated from an algal bloom (Extended Data Fig. 1). We isolated the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the demise phase and determined its effect on G. huxleyi during viral infection.

We next reconstituted the tripartite system by exposing axenic G. huxleyi cultures to EhV with and without the BAM community, and observed an enhancement of algal mortality in the presence of bacteria (Fig. 2a). Although viral infection alone significantly reduced algal abundance compared with uninfected cultures, the addition of the BAM accelerated this decline, resulting in approximately fourfold lower algal cell densities after 7 days (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 2a). This recapitulated our observations in xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1a), confirming that bacterial presence synergistically enhances virus-induced algal mortality.

a, Growth curves of axenic G. huxleyi under four conditions: uninfected, with BAM only, with EhV only and with both BAM and EhV. b, Bacterial abundances in cultures with and without viral infection. c, Viral production in axenic and BAM-inoculated cultures. d, Bacterial community composition of the inoculum (In.) and over time in uninfected (bottom blue line) and EhV-infected (bottom yellow line) cultures. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 5 independent cultures). Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per day.

Bacterial population dynamics revealed significant proliferation in the tripartite system compared with the bacteria-only treatment (Fig. 2b). Similar to xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1b), bacterial abundances in the virus-infected cultures were more than threefold higher than in the uninfected cultures 7 days post-infection (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 2), suggesting that bacterial communities exploit metabolites that are released during viral infection.

By contrast, viral production remained similar between axenic and BAM-supplemented cultures (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 2c). Additionally, we quantified the effect of BAM supplementation on the fraction of virus-infected algal cells (Extended Data Fig. 3), enumerated at the single-cell level using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH)3, based on the expression of the viral major capsid protein (mcp) gene. During the lytic phase, up to 70% of algal cells were virus-infected independent of the presence or absence of BAM (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 3d), proportions consistent with previous work with infected G. huxleyi cultures3. These findings suggest that the bacterial consortium augments algal death without affecting viral infection.

To identify whether specific bacteria are driving the synergy of this tripartite interaction, we characterized changes in microbial community composition during viral infection using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. 2d). The bacterial community changed reproducibly in all replicates during viral infection. Whereas the uninfected cultures maintained a stable community dominated by Marinomonas, a pronounced shift occurred in the virus-infected cultures by day 4, coinciding with algal decline. Notably, the relative abundances of Alteromonas and Olleya increased in the infected cultures, from approximately 2.1 ± 0.3% and 0.01 ± 0.01%, respectively, at the beginning of the experiment (day 1), to 20.2 ± 2.7% and 32.9 ± 4.4% by day 7, thereby dominating the bacterial community (Fig. 2d). Concurrently, Pseudoalteromonas and Yoonia-Loktanella increased in their relative abundances, whereas Marinomonas declined. These findings suggest that viral infection creates a distinct metabolic niche that selectively promotes specific bacterial taxa that are capable of exploiting virus-induced changes in algal metabolism or cell lysis products, as previously shown24,36.

To disentangle the microbial dynamics governing algal bloom demise, we developed two quantitative metrics that assess the contribution of individual bacterial taxa to virus-induced algal mortality, and the effect of viral infection of algal cells on bacterial fitness. The synergy index (SI) quantifies the decrease in the algal population during viral infection in the presence of bacteria compared to viral infection alone. The benefit index (BI) measures the growth advantage that bacteria gain during viral infection compared to their growth with uninfected algae.

To calculate the SI, we use the area under the algal growth curve during viral infection alone (AUCvirus) and during viral–bacterial co-infection (AUCtripartite). We selected area under the curve (AUC) as our metric because it provides a biologically meaningful measure of cumulative biomass change that captures complete temporal dynamics rather than single time points and offers robustness through multiple daily measurements. We calculated the difference between AUCvirus and AUCtripartite and normalized this value using AUCvirus, which is represented mathematically as SI (%) = (AUCvirus − AUCtripartite)/AUCvirus × 100% (Fig. 3a and Methods). Normalizing the differences in the AUC creates a dimensionless metric, enabling direct comparison across bacterial strains and experimental conditions regardless of baseline differences. A positive SI indicates that the bacterial presence reduces algal populations beyond the reduction caused by viruses alone, with higher values reflecting stronger effects (for example, SI = 10.0% means a 10% increase in tripartite-induced algal decline compared to mortality induced by viruses alone). The BAM had an SI of 22.2 ± 2.3%, which confirms the substantial effect of this bacterial community on the virus-induced demise of G. huxleyi (Fig. 3b).

A. stellipolaris (Ast) MB63 exhibits high (SI = 20.2 ± 2.7%) (c) whereas S. pontiacus (Sp) MB3 exhibits low (SI = 7.8 ± 2.7%) (d) synergistic killing. e, Illustration of the BI calculation, comparing bacterial growth curves in the presence of virus-infected or uninfected alga. f, Application of BI to the entire BAM community (BI = 259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating a substantial growth advantage during viral infection of G. huxleyi. g,h, Bacterial growth curves showing contrasting BI values. A. stellipolaris MB63 derives large benefit (BI = 112.4 ± 1.0%) from co-infection (g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 shows no advantage (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%) (h). Dashed lines mark limits for the area integration, excluding the first day which is below detection levels. i, SI and BI values for bacteria isolated directly from the BAM community (black outline) or a G. huxleyi bloom (no outline), revealing diverse ecological strategies. Asp, Alteromonas sp.; Hs, Hyphomonas sp.; Ms, Marinomonas sp.; Os, Olleya sp.; Rm, Roseovarius mucosus; Ss, Sulfitobacter sp. j, Classification of bacterial ecological strategies based on SI and BI values, identifying opportunistic pathogens, killers, consumers and agnostic bacteria (log10(BI) > 0). Asterisks indicate P values for differences in the growth dynamics as obtained by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA (b–d,f–h); exact P values are provided in the Source data.

The BI quantifies the growth advantage bacteria derive from viral infection, calculated as BI (%) = (AUCtripartite − AUCbacteria)/AUCbacteria × 100%, where AUCbacteria represents the area under the bacterial growth curve with uninfected algae (Fig. 3e). The BAM community exhibited a high BI (259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating that viral infection of G. huxleyi creates a metabolically accessible niche that enhances bacterial proliferation almost fourfold (Fig. 3f).

To identify key contributors to this synergistic interaction, we examined the SI and BI for individual bacteria isolated from the BAM (Supplementary Data 1). Alteromonas stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high SI (20.2 ± 2.7%), indicating that this species enhanced virus-induced algal population decline by about 20% (Fig. 3c). By contrast, Sulfitobacter pontiacus MB3 had a low, non-significant SI (7.8 ± 2.7%), suggesting that this species is not affecting algal death during viral infection (Fig. 3d). Correspondingly, A. stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high BI (112.4 ± 1.0%), reflecting more than twofold growth enhancement during viral infection (Fig. 3g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 showed a slight growth deficit during virus infection (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%; Fig. 3h).

To expand the taxonomic range of our analysis, we tested a total of 12 bacteria isolated either directly from the BAM community or from the G. huxleyi bloom (Supplementary Data 1), and observed high variability in both metrics (SI range from 5.4% to 23.2% and BI range from −17.2% to 451.0%; Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The three Alteromonas strains tested (MB63, MB67 and MB68) consistently exhibited a large effect on algal population decline (SI range from 18.6% to 21.7%; Fig. 3i), while simultaneously deriving growth benefits from viral infection (BI range from 18.5% to 112.4%; Fig. 3i).

By mapping all bacterial isolates onto a coordinate system defined by their SI and BI values (the SI–BI phase space), we observed distinct phenotypes (Fig. 3j) and propose a framework comprising four ecological strategies: ‘opportunistic pathogens’ (high SI, high BI), exemplified by Alteromonas species, which both accelerate algal mortality and efficiently exploit the resulting metabolic niche; ‘consumers’ (low SI, high BI), such as Olleya sp. MB6, which derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection without contributing significantly to algal mortality; ‘killers’ (high SI, low BI), including Sulfitobacter sp. MB51, which enhance algal mortality but gain no growth advantage; and ‘agnostics’ (low SI, low BI), such as S. pontiacus MB3, which neither increase algal mortality nor derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection.

To determine whether synergistic bacteria directly affect the mortality of algal cells, we quantified the fraction of dying algal cells during tripartite interaction (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Dying algal cells were identified as cells with compromised membranes using the DNA stain SYTOX Green (Fig. 4a), and were further differentiated by their chlorophyll autofluorescence as metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or metabolically impaired (low chlorophyll autofluorescence) cells (Fig. 4b). During viral infection, there was an accumulation of dying (SYTOX+) cells reaching up to 76.9 ± 2.4% of the algal population (on day 4; Fig. 4a). The addition of bacteria significantly reduced the percentage of dying algal cells (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4) reaching 21.0 ± 1.5% (on day 3; Fig. 4a), suggesting that bacteria selectively remove dying algae during viral infection. Bacteria selectively cleared low-chlorophyll cells versus high-chlorophyll cells. In the presence of bacteria, the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among all low-chlorophyll cells decreased from 54.0 ± 4.1% to 30.3 ± 3.0% on day 2 (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 4b), whereas the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among high-chlorophyll cells remained similar (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 4b). These findings show that bacteria preferentially remove metabolically impaired dying cells during virus-induced algal demise.

a, Total abundance (grey) and fraction (yellow or red) of membrane-compromised (SYTOX+) algal cells in axenic G. huxleyi cultures inoculated with EhV only (light grey, red) and with both EhV and the BAM community (dark grey, yellow). b, Fraction of SYTOX+ cells that are still metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or dead (low chlorophyll autofluorescence). Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures).

We sought to determine the metabolic basis for viral–bacterial synergy in algal killing. We focused on lipid metabolism since EhV infection profoundly remodels the lipidome of G. huxleyi, inducing triacylglycerol (TAG) production and accumulation of intracellular lipid bodies37. We thus sequenced and annotated the genomes of all bacterial isolates and correlated the SI of each one with the completeness (per cent of genes encoded in the KEGG pathway) of its fatty acid degradation (FAD) pathway. We found a significant positive correlation between SI and the FAD pathway completeness (Spearman’s ρ = 0.669, P = 0.017; Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 2). Detailed examination revealed that within the BAM consortium, the species with the highest SI values, all belonging to the genus Alteromonas, also encode the complete enzymatic machinery for TAG hydrolysis and subsequent fatty acid transmembranal transport and β-oxidation, including TAG lipase, fadL, fadD, fadE, fadB and fadA and their homologues (Extended Data Fig. 6b). By contrast, species with low SI values (for example, S. pontiacus MB3) showed several missing enzymes in the FAD pathway. Among bloom-associated bacterial isolates, only Alteromonas and Marinobacter strains encode these metabolic genes (Supplementary Data 2). Although this may be a phylogenetic trait that is not causally related to SI or BI, these genera were recently shown to selectively degrade algal lipids38. Most importantly, Alteromonas encodes a TAG lipase, an enzyme that releases free fatty acids from TAGs for cellular metabolism. This feature may be particularly advantageous during viral infection of G. huxleyi as EhV infection induces the release of extracellular vesicles that are enriched in TAGs39.

Having identified Alteromonas as having key roles in the viral–bacterial synergy during algal demise, we investigated the ecological importance of this genus during natural bloom succession. To this end, we tracked algal, viral and bacterial dynamics in a natural environment, measured daily during G. huxleyi bloom succession in a mesocosm experiment24. Following six days at low abundance (less than 5 × 105 cells per ml; pre-bloom phase), G. huxleyi showed a steady increase in cell numbers (days 7–14; bloom phase) and, upon viral infection (days 15–23; infection phase), its population collapsed (Fig. 5a).
