#1436. Maitland-Niles’ last-gasp debut goal salvages Everton’s miserable week

At the final whistle, the first song the stadium DJ played was Spirit of the Blues and how those relieved Evertonians lapped it up after a week of angst.

Their team had been on the precipice of a defeat that would have exacerbated all the frustrations that bubbled away following the chaotic conclusion to the transfer window. Indeed, it was 10 seconds over the allotted five minutes of added time when the ball fell to Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

It had been three years since the former Arsenal full-back had played in the Premier League – his last goal in England was on October 30, 2019, in an EFL Cup tie with Liverpool at Anfield that ended 5-5 – and he would not have joined Everton if their attempt to sign Kenny Tete from Fulham had not failed.

But here he was 30 yards from goal, with no need to break his stride as Manchester United’s backtracking defenders presented him with an invitation to shoot. So that’s what he did. With one perfectly timed swish of his right foot, an unlikely hero transformed the mood of a club.

"That is something SPECIAL!"Ainsley Maitland-Niles earns a draw for Everton on his debut with an unbelievable 96th minute strike! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/HNdx9PxrUP

“Brilliant technique,” said David Moyes, Everton’s manager, who had only introduced Maitland-Niles in the 77th minute after James Garner had succumbed to cramp and could run no more. “We are still getting to know Ainsley but that was a brilliant goal.”

Only those with the coldest hearts would begrudge Everton this point, which was especially hard-earned given they had conceded an 88th-minute header to Benjamin Sesko. But there is no chance a disbelieving Michael Carrick will feel that way.

Benajmin Sesko puts Manchester United back in front! 👊 pic.twitter.com/MF3A9LyaY8

United should, really, have won this game comfortably. Everton were there to be exploited and when Bryan Mbuemo put them ahead early in the second half, they should have powered away into the distance. Everton’s effort was good but they were in danger of losing hope.

Yet, incredibly, United gave Everton two helping hands. They had not been in a position to assist last Tuesday evening, when phone calls from Merseyside to Old Trafford to take Joshua Zirkzee on loan were met with rejection. But the second half display more than made up for that.

“We’re bitterly disappointed,” said Carrick, who was one step removed from having steam puffing from his ears. “All the work that went into putting us in that position at different stages to then come away like that… it’s not a great feeling. It feels like a defeat. It’s a bit of a cliché to say.”

But clichés are true. First United were passive when Tyrique George crashed in a brilliant right-footed drive in the 83rd minute and then, after Sesko profited from Jordan Pickford’s weak hands, they were passive again in allowing Everton to build the move that ended up with Maitland-Niles’ howitzer.

How had it come to this? It was beautiful bedlam, the kind of joy that only football delivers, but for long periods it felt like it was an opportunity for United. There was anticipation that Everton’s fans would create a furnace but there was also the fear it would be dispiritingly quiet.

Had this fixture been at Goodison Park, with its steep stands, tight confines and acoustics that split your ears, United would have been aware of the siege mentality as soon as their bus rolled up outside the stadium but their new sparkling home is rather more hospitable.

This is no criticism of the home crowd – it is anything but. Why should it always fall to them to bail out the failings of those in charge when those in charge, specifically the executives and recruitment department, have given them scant reason to have hope?

The route to victory for United, then, was relatively straightforward: for all Everton’s initial huff and puff, it always appeared that it would be a case of the away team repeating the simple things, retaining their concentration and waiting for a breakthrough.

It could have come as early as the eighth minute. Luke Shaw’s deep cross to the back post picked out Mbuemo, whose cushioned header invited Bruno Fernandes to take aim but the Portuguese’s volley clipped the crossbar with Pickford stranded.

United dominated and Marcus Rashford was central to it all, a scampering presence down the left who gave Merlin Röhl, playing as an auxiliary right-back, all kinds of problems. The only thing missing from his opening 45 minutes was a goal.

When Mbuemo scored so early after the break, it felt as if this was going to be one puncture too many for Everton to withstand and the anticipation was United would get the job done. In all fairness to Moyes, however, he was not in the mood to accept excuses.

His substitutions were all positive, with Jack Grealish changing the mood and Hayden Hackney providing dynamism. But it was the former Middlesbrough man who drove forward to give George, whose loan move from Chelsea was made permanent in June, the opportunity to smash an 83rd-minute bullet past Senne Lammens.

"That was unanswerable!"What a way for Tyrique George to open his account for Everton! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/c0HPRjWUia

“I told the players there would be no excuses and the players all agreed,” Moyes said. “They have hugely bought into it. And, you know, sometimes when you have [fewer] players it means everybody has to be ready. Sometimes when you have a small squad you have to find a way of making it work.”

They did just that. Pickford should have saved the header from Sesko that looked as though it had given United the lift, but Everton, with their manager belligerent and their fans sensing all was not lost, had other ideas. The noise they generated as Maitland-Niles’s goal went in was unique to this stadium.

As Moyes celebrated, shaking his fists and revelling in the positive turn of events, Carrick put his hand across his face and shook his head repeatedly. All the while, Everton’s fans sang I guess that’s why they call it the Blues. United’s head coach certainly had them. Everton, simply, had relief.

2 - For just the second time in the last 50 years, Manchester United have conceded 2+ goals in each of their first three games of a league season, along with 2020-21.Leaky. pic.twitter.com/B2Dk6Ioxkq

It felt like a win. The crowd was with us, we fight to the end and that’s how you get that type of result.

It’s amazing. Everyone wants to start like that and fortunately I did. I put my foot through it and it ended up in the top corner which I’m happy about.

I came here to work hard. It’s a team full of hard workers and I fit right in. I’m going to show I can pull my weight and give as much as everyone else, if not a little bit more.

Even I have a lump in my throat to see him do that after his original move to Everton in August 2021 was stymied by a late change of heart by Mikel Arteta. Don’t normally approve of badge kissers but he has waited such a long time for that and must have thought his chance had gone.

Just time to kick off before the whistle goes. Probably a fair result and that goal from Maitland-Niles was good enough to win a game never mind save it.

Everton 2 Manchester United 2 (Maitland-Niles) Stunning strike! Mazraoui had tackled Dewsbury-Hall in the box after more good work between Grealish and Hackney down the left. But the tackle diverted the ball to Maitland-Niles 25 yards out. And he wrapped his instep around a shot on debut that bent into the top left corner. What a goal!

"That is something SPECIAL!"Ainsley Maitland-Niles earns a draw for Everton on his debut with an unbelievable 96th minute strike! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/HNdx9PxrUP

Grealish’s beguiling feet dazzle Mazraoui down the Everton left as he tricks him to reach the byline. He cuts back a pass to Barry who tees up Hackney for a shot that he wafts miles over the bar. Grealish gives him a look as if to say, “Really?”

George finds himself in a near identical spot from which he scored and tries again with a thumping shot that flies into the side-netting via Lammens’ finger tips. He was offside on this occasion, though.

Five minutes of added time for Everton to level again.

Everton 1 Manchester United 2 (Sesko) Sesko wins the ball in the middle and works it out to Bruno Fernandes running down the left. He stops, faces up Maitland-Niles and waits for Shaw to gallop past him before rolling it into the left-back’s stride. Shaw fizzes over a cross that parts Tarkowski’s luxuriant barnet and Sesko, lurking on his shoulder, buries it from eight yards.

Benajmin Sesko puts Manchester United back in front! 👊 pic.twitter.com/MF3A9LyaY8

As Dominic says, below, Manchester United have been asking for this. They have been toothless since Mbeumo’s goal and the only significant threat, Rashford, was taken off for a left-back.

Everton 1 Man Utd 1 (George) A rasping, rising shot that beats Lammens at his near post. He absolutely larruped it after good work by Hackney to put him in space down the right of the box.

"That was unanswerable!"What a way for Tyrique George to open his account for Everton! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/c0HPRjWUia

If you largely try and defend a 1-0 lead and don’t go for that second goal, there’s always the danger of that happening. Superb finish from George to equalise but it’s been so passive from United. Asking for trouble and they’ve got it. Big 7 minutes plus injury time for them now.

Free-kick on the left, parallel with the penalty spot. Hackney bends it in with his right and Branthwaite heads it on target but too close to Lammens who oddly elects to punch.

Mykolenko gives the ball back from the throw-in as Fernandes serves his minute on the sidelines.

Dalot is booked for pulling Grealish’s shirt when the left winger had spun him.

Maitland-Niles receives a warm reception. I had forgotten that he has five England caps.

Bruno Fernandes goes down after kicking Tarkowski’s studs when his foot was raised. The referee does not stop play but books Maguire for complaining when the ball eventually goes out.

Garner almost immediately goes down and starts stretching his calves.

Mykolenko hurls a long throw into the Man Utd box. Dewsbury-Hall meets it with a shot that he catches sweetly but hits a defender. The ball rebounds to Armstrong who scuffs his attempt wide .

George has switched to the right to accommodate Grealish. I wonder if there was ever a possibility of him returning to Villa? Would Unai Emery treasure him?

“He’s back!” the stadium announcer has proclaimed, as Jack Grealish has entered the fray. The move has provided an immediate bounce but let’s see what the former England man can do to change the pattern of the game. Everton believe they have got a £100m player. It’s time to show it.

Grealish’s first contribution sends Mykolenko away on an overlap and Martinez messes up his clearance from the cross, shanking it behind for a corner that they defend soundly.

Manchester United corner on the left after Tielemans’ 25-yard shot was deflected behind. Fernandes plays it along the ground to Shaw in the D. The left-back’s control spoons the ball up with his left so he improvises a right-foot volley with his swinger, dragging it predictably wide.

Rohl is beaten yet again by Rashford and works his way into the book after pulling him back. It’s been hard going for the Everton right back against Rashford but United just haven’t taken advantage of it enough.

Jack Grealish is stripped and ready to come on.

Rashford jinks at pace 35 yards up the inside-left channel, chopping to the left and barrelling between defenders. He takes it too wide to shoot so cutely backheels to Cunha who pulls back his left foot to shoot from six yards but Tarkowski slides his leg through his gait and pokes the ball away. The away fans shout for a penalty but Cunha has no complaints.

Barry diddles Martinez by feinting to the right and then darting left to open a rout to goal. He hammers a shot from about 16 yards that Shaw slides across to block, diverting it to Dewsbury-Hall whose follow-up effort is a tame daisycutter that Lammens easily gathers.

It threatened to be the case that a Manchester United goal would puncture the atmosphere completely and so it has proven. The likelihood here is the away team will score again in the next 10 minutes to completely kill the game. Everton have endured a miserable week and this flat performance is entirely in keeping with the narrative.

Johnson cuts in off the right to run on to Garner’s pass and shoots from 18 yards. Martinez makes himself as big as possible and the shot clips his calf, sending it up before it dips threateningly, whistling over the bar.

Mbeumo heads out Garner’s corner. Dewsbury-Hall crosses it back into the box and Tarkowski tries to head it across into the middle. Manchester United clear their lines.

Shaw slides in to block Dewsbury-Hall’s shot after the attacking midfielder had manipulated an opportunity with a quick interchange with Johnson.

Key for Manchester United, who have taken the lead in a match for the first time this season, not to let up on the tempo with which they started this half.

Everton respond with a menacing cross in from the left, from George, I think, that eludes Johnson as he arrives in the middle a second late.

Everton 0 Manchester United 1 (Mbeumo) United were probing patiently from the kick-off, Mainoo the hub until he helped the ball down the right and Mbeumo drove in from the right touchline, splitting George and Mykolenko until he reached the 18-yard line and wrapped his left instep around a shot that he arrowed into the bottom left corner.

A brilliant run and a fine finish from Bryan Mbeumo! 👏 pic.twitter.com/IM9kVcdPkh

We hadn’t seen that Mbeumo in the first half – so much better, driving inside at pace and with intent. Good decoy run from Fernandes. Top finish from Mbeumo.

Both managers will want to see a lot more urgency from their sides in the second half. Rashford has been United’s most threatening outlet and has the beating of Rohl but Mbeumo and Cunha were poor in those opening 45 minutes and both guilty of turning over the ball cheaply when United were breaking late in the first period. Barry should have hit the target with a header from Rohl’s cross. But it’s been a lacklustre game, low in quality so far.

A drab match that came to life in the last few minutes of the half, creating good a good chance for Thierno Barry and Jarrad Branthwaite thwarting Marcus Rashford and Bruno Fernandes. Everton look wide open on the right side of their defence and Brennan Johnson is starting to make headway against Luke Shaw.

Brilliant sliding tackle from Branthwaite when Rashford, piling down the inside-left channel in full flight. Just as he was about to pull the trigger, Branthwaite launched himself to knock it away and leapt back to his feet to block Fernandes’ stinging follow-up with the his head.

Mykolenko’s long throw from the left raises the Man Utd blood pressure as they try to scramble it clear. The ball pinballs around the six-yard box, comes off Dalot last and straight to Branthwaite who catches it straight and true but clips the shot at Lammens.

There will be three additional minutes. Barry and Johnson link up again to send the rangey striker down the right but again he hits his cross/shot straight at a defender at close quarters. He can’t work an angle but tries to go through a defender.

Rohl and Barry link up in more orthodox fashion with an excellent, dipping cross from the right-back. Barry peels off Maguire and thumps his header wide. That’s the best chance of the game.

Neat one-two between Johnson and Barry sends the latter into the box on the right but his shot/cross is fired straight at Shaw. The crowd shouts ‘Hand ball!’ but it wasn’t and the ref waves play on.

Everton have had no spark at all so far. George goes down when challenged by Mbeumo to give them a free-kick on the left, 35 yards from goal. Garner hits a floaty cross to the right of the box and Barry heads it wide.

It was Johnson who was under scrutiny for a ‘foul’ on Martinez’ but it was just a hand on the back.

Branthwaite is winded when he collides with Pickford in midair defending a back-post cross. Seems to be OK.

Fernandes whips over a cross and Armstrong beats Martínez to head it clear. VAR is looking at Martínez’s claim that he was fouled. Now it’s been cleared.

Yellow card for Johnson for sliding into Cunha’s stride and raising his right boot to leg him up right by the byline on the left, 12 inches outside the area.

Shaw trips Rohl in the Everton penalty area as they fought for the ball from Branthwaite’s block of Rashford’s superb cross from the left. The winger was looking for a near-post runner but Branthwaite read it perfectly, certainly better than Cunha, and telescoped out a leg to intercept.

Given the chaotic end to Everton’s transfer window, the atmosphere was going to go one of two ways: bearpit or flat as a pancake. As of now, it’s very much the latter situation, and not even a first sight of Jack Grealish has enabled the volume to be pumped up. Everton are finding it difficult and special attention will need to be paid to Harrison Armstrong, who has been harshly booked but must now walk a disciplinary tightrope. The young midfielder has played encouragingly once again and is desperate to impress.

Ripples of applause for Grealish who comes off the bench to warm up. Armstrong is urged to shoot when fed by Garner’s curling pass up the inside-right channel. But he dithers and then plays it out to Johnson whose cross is no good.

Best move of the game to date should have ended with Cunha hitting the target. The silkiest bit about it was how Rashford lulled Rohl into a false sense of security with his first touch then tapped the ball past him in the next movement just as Rohl was engaging. Very clever.

Now Shaw reaches the byline down the left and cuts it back for Fernandes. Branthwaite again to the rescue, diligently doing his job and closing down the Man Utd captain. Merlin Röhl is a talented player but he’s no right-back against the well-grooved Rashford and Shaw combo.

Dalot let the Rashford pass through his legs to Cunha, probably deliberately but he might have been better placed to apply the finish himself. Cunha had the time and space to do much better than he did, though.

Cunha blazes a side-foot shot from 18 yards over the bar. It was put on a plate by Rashford’s cut-back from the byline after the winger was sent down the flank by Mbeumo’s clever pass.

Manchester united again open up Everton through the middle when Mainoo slips a pass to Bruno Fernandes who puts his laces through a 25-yard shot that Branthwaite bravely throws himself at and deflects wide and out for a corner.

Tielemans’ eyes widen as space opens up between Armstrong and Garner but he scuffs his 22-yard shot which floats gently down Pickford’s throat.

Shaw cuts out Branthwaite’s long pass to Armstrong who was running down the inside-left channel. Manchester United do not clear their lines convincingly and Everton come back at them, probing away with George and Armstrong.

Dalot is let off a booking inexplicably for pulling George’s arm after being spun by Everton’s left-winger. The crowd is irate at that and seething even more when Armstrong is yellow-carded moments later for wrapping an arm around Fernandes’ neck to stop him running away.

Big shout for a home penalty when Barry goes down, face first in the six-yard box when closed down ny Martínez but it was more of a belly flop than a foul.

Slick attacking move from Manchester United, zipping a dozen passes around Everton and ending with Shaw being slid down the left by Rashford. The left-back crosses from the byline and Mbeumo cushions a header to Bruno Fernandes who flashes a sidewinder volley into the crossbar.

In the grand scheme of things, this might sound the most ridiculous complaint you have read but Manchester United’s kit - really? When they play away at Everton, their kit has always been – and always should be – red shirts, black shorts and black socks. It looks odd with two teams playing in white shorts. This may seem a random observation but there we go... there hasn’t been any action to discuss in the opening four minutes!

Maguire returns to the fray as Everton pass the ball through midfield to Johnson on the right. His cross, aiming for Barry, is cut out by Maguire and cleared to halfway. Back come Everton until Dewsbury-Hall is too rough with Mainoo as the Man Utd midfielder tackled him. Free-kick.

Lammens kicks the ball the full length of the field and Pickford picks it up. Mbeumo momentarily is at right-back with Dalot at centre-half.

Maguire is OK to continue but he will be off the field for the mandatory minute.

Maguire headed the back of Barry’s head and splattered his nose. He should be all right though he might need the cotton wool nostril bungs for a while, like Blackadder, the pencils and ‘wibble’.

Big cheers goes around the stadium when Harrison Armstrong’s name has read out. Everton would likely have sold him had there not been a backlash from fans opposing his sale.

Concern here for Harry Maguire. Looks in distress on the ground, laying very still. Concerned players around.

Leny Yoro is warming up on the touchline.

Looks like he caught the back of Barry’s head as he went to challenge. Sat up nose receiving treatment on a very bloodied nose.

Everton kick off, attacking from right to left. The fans, as usual, are making a racket. Everton work the ball back to Pickford who clips a diagonal up the left. Everton play it towards Barry who collides with Maguire who takes a blow to the head.

The teams emerge from the tunnel, both teams in their home kits with the only twist Manchester United’s switch to white socks.

We’re looking forward to seeing what [Brennan Johnson] does. We know he is very capable [and shown it] in recent seasons. Let’s hope he can bring us goals and assists as he did for Tottenham.

We’ve needed them [the two deadline day signings]. Maitland-Niles is physically fine. I don’t think Jack should be yet. We’ve needed it.

That’s all gone now [deadline day]. It’s all about the football. That’s what people are coming to see and we’ll have to play as well as we have done in our opening two games, get a positive result. Hopefully we can continue to build on it.

Nothing different [expected from the fans today]. They’re always really good for us.

No surprise United remain unchanged from the 5-2 win over Ipswich although Carrick will be looking for his side to score first here and make life a little easier for themselves after going behind to Hull and Ipswich in their opening two games. Brennan Johnson comes in for the departed Iliman Ndiaye, who joined Manchester City for £65m on deadline day. Jack Grealish is on the bench for Everton.

Moyes issued a call to arms to Everton fans in his programme notes after a dismal transfer window that has left him with just 18 outfield players. The Everton manager warning there may be difficult times to come.

“Finally, I must stress the importance of us all pulling together,” Moyes wrote.

“We need to be strong again and there may be occasions when we may have to find a way to get through some difficult moments.

“It is something you have all done in recent seasons. Everyone has pulled together for the good of the football club and we may need to do so again.”

We did a lot of good things [against Ipswich]. No two games are ever the same. We have different challenges today. We have to be ready for that with some slightly different ideas. But the boys did well last week, trained well this week and we’re really looking forward to it.

The next result is always the most important one regardless of what’s happened. Building momentum, building a run, of course it’s important. It’s game-by-game, as you know, but this is as tough as it comes for us, Everton away.

It’s not a major deal, we’ve got the squad and we can cope with it [increase in numbers of fixtures with the return to European football].

Mason Mount is fit enough for the bench and takes Shea Lacey’s seat

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of Everton vs Manchester United from Hill Dickinson Stadium. The hosts have made a creditable start on the field but four points from their opening two games cannot gloss over the discontent fostered by the owners and executives because of the credibility gap between their talk about recruitment and their paltry achievements.

The fact that their comeback against Bournemouth to earn a draw last week was achieved with Beto, Tim Iroegbunum and Iliman Ndiaye on the field and all three have now been sold with only Jack Grealish returning on loan to compensate tells its own story.

Speak to supporters and it is emblematic of ownership, they fear, who are prioritising Roma and view the Hill Dickinson as a terrific multisport and concert venue with a heritage football club attached. The bullishness of Angus Kinnear, the chief executive, rings hollower with each pronouncement and it is little wonder that the fans are so disenchanted.

David Moyes will not walk away but once again he has been sent into the fray against teams with £250m midfields armed with a spud gun. Having said that, we should not underestimate his capacity to rally the old “dogs of war” spirit even if the crowd is still yearning more for a “school of science” revival.

Manchester United won on their first visit to the Hill Dickinson last season when Benjamin Sesko came off the bench to score the only goal of the game and give Michael Carrick a fifth win in six league games as caretaker manager. They were far more fluid in their forward play during the victory over Ipswich last week but it was against an error-stricken defence and they continued to be as worryingly open at the back as they had been against Hull City in the opening round of fixtures with Luke Shaw and Lisandro Martínez having brain fades.

Shaw is a doubt today, along with Mason Mount, while Amad Diallo, Matthijs de Ligt, Carlos Baleba and Manuel Ugarte have all been ruled out. Only Christian Norgaard is absent for Everton but so thin is their squad, they will cast covetous glances at Man Utd’s bench, not least at Joshua Zirkzee who was the subject of a very late rejected bid on deadline day.

#1435. Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1,2,3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

Large-scale genetic studies have implicated hundreds of genes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with many identified through rare mutations that result in loss of function of one allele1,2,3. This suggests that gene dosage plays an important part in ASD11 and makes it critical to determine how appropriate expression levels of ASD genes are maintained. Characterization of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) could provide important insights into mechanisms mediating the proper transcriptional dosage of these ASD genes. In addition, ASD is significantly male-biased in prevalence, and although some ASD genes have been identified on the X chromosome12, X-linked mutations alone cannot fully explain this sex bias8,13. Moreover, it has been consistently demonstrated that female individuals require greater autosomal genetic risk to manifest ASD compared with male individuals6,7, but the genetic mechanisms of this female protective effect (FPE) are unknown8,9.

Here we use GRN reconstruction to identify key drivers of expression of ASD genes, including CHD8 and REST. These analyses also identify female-biased transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and inactive X chromosome in female individuals10, as a key regulator of ASD genes, suggesting a direct transcriptional mechanism that could contribute to the FPE. This study provides a crucial framework for determining how variants in diverse genes can cause convergent molecular effects that ultimately result in ASD.

Functional interrogation of ASD genes revealed strongly overlapping effects on downstream targets in human neural progenitor cells (NPCs). Knockdown (KD) studies were performed for 20 ASD genes, including 18 genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) gene database14 and two long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) previously implicated in ASD (NR2F1-AS1 (ref. 15) and SOX2-OT16). RNA-degrading CRISPR enzyme CasRx17 and an array of three guide RNAs (gRNAs) per target (Supplementary Table 1) were used to induce individual KD of each target gene relative to non-targeting controls (NTCs) in NPC cultures from a control human male (XY) induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell line (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 1). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis after 24 h of KD demonstrated that nearly all perturbations led to substantial numbers of significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs; adjusted P (Padj) < 0.05), with a median of 920 DEGs per perturbation (25th percentile: 644, 75th percentile: 1,485) (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 2). To ensure sufficient statistical power for downstream analyses of these DEGs, we focused on the 18 perturbations (18 of 20, 90%) that resulted in more than 20 DEGs, excluding the ARHGAP5 and ARID2 KD samples from further analysis. The remaining perturbations each led to a minimum of 287 DEGs, which enabled robust characterization of these samples.

a, Experimental design schematic showing CasRx-based KD in NPCs. b, Immunocytochemistry of iPS cell-derived human NPC cultures, representative of three independent analyses with similar results. c, Bar plot depicting enrichment of SFARI genes or intellectual-disability-only genes among the DEGs for each KD condition, excluding the targeted gene itself. Bars indicate the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test; error bars indicate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. d, Circos plot depicting transcriptomic convergence of HC-SFARI DEGs shared between different KD conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3a). e, Heatmap showing the relative expression of HC-SFARI genes that were DEGs in at least ten KD conditions (recurrent dysregulation) (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Statistically significant DEGs were identified using DESeq2 (Wald test) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing and are indicated by an asterisk. Top ASD risk genes from ref. 1 are shown in bold. f, Relative CytoTrack dye intensity (−log2) over time. Only KD conditions that exhibited statistically significant effects on NPC proliferation that were consistent over time are displayed. Plot depicts mean ± s.e.m. Statistical significance was determined using ordinary two-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test. At least three biologically independent samples per condition were analysed for each time point. See Supplementary Table 10 for full statistical results. Scale bar, 50 μm. ID, intellectual disability; NS, not significant.

Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that ASD gene KDs caused remarkably widespread disruption of other ASD genes. Most sets of DEGs exhibited significant enrichment for known ASD genes in the SFARI Gene database (15 of 18, 83.3%) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3). By contrast, there was no significant enrichment for genes implicated in intellectual disability but not ASD (intellectual-disability-only genes) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3) (Methods), despite their comparable expression in NPCs (intellectual-disability-only genes: 1,062 of 1,242, 85.5% expressed; SFARI genes: 797 of 1230, 64.8% expressed). This suggests that perturbation of ASD genes particularly affects other ASD genes, as opposed to neurodevelopmental genes more broadly.

We observed a striking pattern of transcriptomic convergence across perturbations, which we defined as statistically significant overlap of the same DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 3). This was particularly evident for high-confidence SFARI (HC-SFARI) genes, the SFARI genes in the highest evidentiary tier for association with ASD (Fig. 1d). Moreover, HC-SFARI genes tended to shift in a concordant direction as a result of different perturbations even when they were not significant DEGs within a particular KD sample (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Such genes included prominent ASD risk gene CHD8 (ref. 18), which was significantly downregulated by most (11 of 18, 61.1%) of the KDs. Notably, 27 HC-SFARI genes were DEGs in at least 10 of the KDs (27 of 183, 14.8%, P = 4.1 × 10−9), and all were consistently downregulated (Fig. 1e), indicating convergent dysregulation of many of the strongest risk genes for ASD.

High levels of CasRx have been reported to cause non-specific RNA degradation of a magnitude that is correlated with the expression level of the KD target, whereas use of lower CasRx levels avoids this problem19. In our NPC transcriptomic studies, CasRx was expressed from only a single safe-harbour locus (AAVS1), which limited its expression. We also performed several further experiments to confirm that non-specific RNA degradation did not affect our results. First, we found no relationship between expression levels of KD targets and numbers of resulting DEGs when considering either the whole transcriptome (P = 0.990, R2 = 8 × 10−6, linear regression) or SFARI genes specifically (P = 0.784, R2 = 0.0043, linear regression) (Extended Data Fig. 4a). We next generated NPCs expressing fluorophores mKO2, mScarlet and iRFP670 and targeted each individually with CasRx (Supplementary Table 4); flow cytometry showed no collateral effects on the fluorescence intensity of non-targeted fluorophores (Extended Data Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 5). Finally, we confirmed strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs by performing further KD studies of a subset of our target genes using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) in NPCs (Extended Data Figs. 4c,d and 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Re-analysis of data from a study that used Cas9 to knock out ASD genes in iPS cells and iPS cell-derived excitatory neurons (ExNs)20 similarly demonstrated strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs both within each cell type and between cell types (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Recent studies published since our work was submitted have also noted convergence across diverse ASD models21,22. Together, these data confirm that disruption of ASD genes results in transcriptomic convergence across various cell types and experimental contexts.

The marked transcriptomic convergence we observed in our KD studies suggested that candidate ASD risk genes could be nominated by the following features: (1) consistent downregulation following ASD gene KDs; and (2) dosage sensitivity, as indicated by high genic constraint scores (Supplementary Table 7 and Methods). This approach yielded 397 genes (Supplementary Table 8), including 113 SFARI genes (odds ratio (OR) = 5.87, Padj = 1.85 × 10−39) and 49 HC-SFARI genes (OR = 11.17, Padj = 1.11 × 10−29), demonstrating that these criteria effectively prioritize known ASD genes. Notably, this set of genes showed no enrichment for intellectual-disability-only genes (OR = 1.01, Padj = 0.509). All of the remaining 284 non-SFARI genes exhibited significant co-expression with SFARI genes (all Padj < 0.05), which has previously been shown to help prioritize novel ASD risk genes4, further supporting their relevance to ASD. Moreover, at least 40 of these genes showed some association with ASD in at least 1 major sequencing study (Supplementary Table 9). For example, mutations in AKT3, although classically associated with brain overgrowth disorders such as megalencephaly, have recently been associated with ASD; other genes including KIF11, KIF2A and SOS1 have also been associated with ASD in multiple studies (see references in Supplementary Table 9). Therefore, the remaining genes merit consideration as candidate ASD risk genes.

Many ASD gene perturbations also caused similar phenotypic effects in NPCs. Proliferation analysis using heritable dye (CytoTrack) showed that 9 of 18 (50%) of the KDs led to a statistically significant decrease in proliferation (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 6a, Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Fig. 1), including several genes that have been implicated in microcephaly (SETD1B23, SETD2 (ref. 24), SETD5 (ref. 25), KMT2E26 and WAC27). By contrast, only 1 of 18 (5.6%) of the KDs led to a significant increase in NPC proliferation rate. This suggests that reduced NPC proliferation is a common phenotype that results from disruption of several different ASD genes, consistent with previous findings28. Deciphering the specific relationships between these molecular phenotypes and abnormal head size in ASD is complex, as reports implicate increased rates of both microcephaly and macrocephaly across individuals with autism29,30. Indeed, two KD targets that we found to decrease proliferation in NPCs, SETD2 (ref. 24) and KMT2E26, have been reported to be associated with either microcephaly or macrocephaly depending on the specific variants studied in these genes. Thus, although disruption of NPC proliferation is a convergent phenotype observed across many of our perturbations, how this relates to downstream changes in head size remains to be determined.

Inducible KD in cerebral organoids also revealed shared neurodevelopmental phenotypes. For these organoid studies, we created the FLEx-based inducible CRISPR knockdown (FLICK) construct. FLICK enables control over the timing of KD through doxycycline-inducible genetic recombination that results in constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter (Fig. 2a), providing robust KD (Extended Data Fig. 7a). The FLICK constructs also contain identifying sequences that can be captured during single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and used to determine the KD target in a given cell; this enables analysis of mosaic cerebral organoids.

For long-term studies, we targeted ASD genes whose KDs were not found to impair NPC proliferation in our CytoTrack experiments (Supplementary Table 10). FLICK constructs targeting these genes or expressing NTC gRNAs were each separately transposed into iPS cells. We then used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate cells that had integrated the FLICK constructs on the basis of their expression of fluorescent reporter TagBFP. Following FACS, we pooled an equal number of FLICK+ iPS cells for each KD target and for the NTCs, and cultured this mixed iPS cell population for 4 days to allow the cells to recover before generating mosaic organoids (day 0). Recombination of the FLICK construct, which leads to constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter, was induced in a subset of the cells (approximately 10%) by treatment with doxycycline from days 14–15, when the organoids predominantly consisted of PAX6+ NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These organoids were subsequently grown until either 1 or 2 months of development (Fig. 2b) and analysed by scRNA-seq; this analysis identified all expected cell types (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 7c,d) including radial glia, intermediate progenitor cells, inhibitory neurons and ExNs. Further scRNA-seq analysis confirmed that the FLICK construct could produce efficient KD (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

Long-term organoid KDs revealed shared phenotypes across several perturbations. Several KDs, particularly those targeting BAZ2B, CLASP1 and EHMT1, were depleted from the organoids compared with NTCs (Fig. 2e), even though these KDs did not impair proliferation in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Table 10). This discrepancy between our NPC cultures and organoids suggests that long-term organoids, which support progenitor proliferation as well as differentiation, can be used to identify neurodevelopmental phenotypes that are not apparent in short-term NPC cultures. Notably, microcephaly has been associated with pathogenic variants in these genes31,32,33, consistent with the organoid phenotypes. Furthermore, these KDs also altered cell type proportions in organoids, producing relatively greater numbers of ExNs and fewer radial glia (Padj = 0.021 for BAZ2B, 0.018 for CLASP1 and 0.012 for EHMT1; ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test) (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7f). Together, these results indicate that disruption of these genes may result in increased ExN differentiation at the expense of self-renewal of radial glial progenitors. Most of the other KDs also resulted in a trend towards an increased proportion of ExNs by the 2-month time point, suggesting that this is a convergent neurodevelopmental phenotype, in line with previous observations34,35.

Depletion of ASD genes also resulted in prominent transcriptomic convergence in cerebral organoids (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g). Radial glia with different KDs exhibited highly overlapping DEGs, further supporting our findings from NPC cultures. Indeed, the DEGs identified in organoid radial glial progenitors strongly overlapped with the DEGs identified from KD of the same target in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7h), suggesting that these effects on gene expression are not specific to a particular experimental context. Transcriptomic convergence was also observed in other cell types, including intermediate progenitor cells and ExNs (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g), demonstrating that the convergence of ASD genes on shared downstream effects is not unique to neural progenitors. This was consistent with findings of studies that identified shared ASD DEGs in postmortem brain tissue from individuals with distinct causes of ASD36,37,38, as well as with widespread observations of convergent ExN phenotypes such as disordered synaptic structure or activity upon disruption of distinct ASD genes20, suggesting that convergence does not reflect merely a shared alteration of cell type or fate of progenitor cells. Furthermore, we found that detection of overlapping DEGs using scRNA-seq was heavily dependent on the number of cells sequenced for each perturbation, as demonstrated by downsampling analysis (Fig. 3b). This sample-size dependence may partially explain the lack of robust transcriptomic convergence observed at the individual gene level in some previous studies with smaller sample sizes34,39. Our use of an isogenic background is also likely to have contributed to our detection of transcriptomic convergence, as different genetic backgrounds have been found to significantly affect neurodevelopmental phenotypes resulting from the disruption of ASD genes in organoids34. Finally, although some convergently disrupted genes were cell-type specific, many genes were consistently disrupted across several cell types, including SFARI DEGs (Fig. 3c). This suggests that although cell-type-specific features affect the transcriptomic consequences of ASD gene perturbations, certain effects could be broadly shared by diverse cell types.

Downsampling of the number of cells per condition to the number indicated above each pie chart decreased the transcriptomic convergence observed. c, Network visualization of SFARI DEGs in long-term organoids shared among different KDs conditions and cell types. Acute disruption of ASD genes in 2-month organoids revealed even greater convergence on shared DEGs. A further set of mosaic FLICK organoids was grown for 2 months before induction of KD with doxycycline treatment from days 61–62; this was followed by scRNA-seq 2 days later, to determine the acute effects of disruption of these genes in organoids that had developed normally. This approach resulted in similar numbers of cells per KD (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7i), enabling deeper analysis of the KDs that had been depleted from the organoids with long-term KD (Fig. 2e). As expected, these organoids contained a mixture of cell types (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7j), with ExNs by far the most abundant cell type at this developmental time point (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Many KDs resulted in ExN DEGs that were enriched for the DEGs identified from NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7l), again suggesting shared changes in gene expression across cell types upon KD of ASD genes. Furthermore, acute KD of the target genes that had been depleted from organoids over the course of long-term KD (Fig. 2e) allowed us to obtain much greater cell numbers for these perturbations, which showed that these KDs also resulted in strong transcriptomic convergence (Fig. 3f).

Transcriptional regulators that could mediate transcriptomic convergence in ASD were identified through MAGIC analysis (Methods), which uses chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) data from ENCODE to identify transcription factors and cofactors whose binding targets are enriched within a gene set of interest. This identified transcriptional regulators whose target genes were recurrently differentially expressed across many of the ASD gene KDs in NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11), including HC-SFARI genes such as CHD2 and SIN3A. Of the recurrent MAGIC regulators not previously implicated in ASD, several were both highly constrained (Supplementary Table 7) and co-expressed with known ASD genes (Extended Data Fig. 8a), features that have been demonstrated to be predictive of novel ASD risk genes4.

MAGIC analysis also identified consistent drivers of convergence in organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11). Of the top recurrent transcriptional regulators identified in NPCs, half (13 of 26, 50%) were also identified in organoid radial glial progenitors (Extended Data Fig. 8b). MAGIC also identified recurrent ExN regulators shared across developmental stages and across long-term versus acute KD timescales, including many SFARI genes. Nine of these genes were also identified as top transcriptional regulators in neural progenitors, indicating that they may be key drivers of convergence in various cellular contexts.

Of particular interest, the RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST) was significant according to MAGIC analysis in 17 of 18 (94.4%) NPC perturbations (Extended Data Fig. 8a) and consistently emerged as a top MAGIC regulator across all tested conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Although direct mutations in REST have not previously been associated with ASD, REST has critical neurodevelopmental roles and functions as a master negative regulator of neurogenesis40,41. Dysregulation of REST has also been reported following disruption of ASD genes including CHD8 (ref. 42) and Rett syndrome gene MECP2 (refs. 43,44). Re-analysis of human and mouse REST ChIP–seq binding sites (Methods) identified strong enrichment of SFARI genes (Padj = 3.6 × 10−67 and 7.7 × 10−50, respectively), including HC-SFARI genes (Padj = 2.2 × 10−13 and 3.7 × 10−8, respectively), among REST targets (Extended Data Fig. 8c), supporting a key role for REST in regulation of ASD-relevant gene expression.

De novo GRN reconstruction from our NPC RNA-seq data using ARACNe enabled association of further transcription factors and chromatin modifiers (together referred to as ‘regulators’) with their downstream targets (regulons) (Methods). We validated this approach by separately constructing ‘held-out’ GRNs that excluded data from samples in which the KD target itself was a potential regulator, thereby preventing circularity in regulon inference. Regulons predicted from these held-out GRNs strongly overlapped with the DEGs observed following KD of the corresponding target genes in NPCs (Padj < 3.98 × 10−116 for each, combined P = 4.08 × 10−937) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Thus, ARACNe effectively captures bona fide regulatory relationships.

The full NPC GRN revealed a high degree of interconnection between ASD genes and their upstream regulators (Fig. 4b). Indeed, ASD genes were strongly enriched among central genes of the NPC GRN (Padj = 9.81 × 10−6 for SFARI genes, 1.99 × 10−4 for HC-SFARI genes, centrality assessed using the PageRank algorithm, Methods) (Fig. 4c). By contrast, intellectual-disability-only genes did not exhibit enrichment among the central genes of the GRN (Padj = 0.19), consistent with the lack of enrichment that we observed among the DEGs resulting from ASD gene KDs (Fig. 1c). In addition, central GRN genes were enriched for pathways associated with the G2M checkpoint (Padj = 6.0 × 10−4) and mitotic spindle (Padj = 3.6 × 10−5), consistent with the NPC proliferation phenotypes we observed (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 10).

We next identified GRN regulators that acted as key drivers of ASD-associated transcriptomic convergence. This analysis revealed 70 top drivers of convergence whose activity was consistently altered by ASD gene KD (Methods) and whose targets were both enriched for SFARI genes and central to the GRN (Supplementary Table 12). Nearly half of these top drivers of convergence were SFARI genes (31 of 70, OR = 6.35, Padj = 3.9 × 10−11), and nearly one-third were HC-SFARI genes (22 of 70, OR = 10.61, Padj = 6.7 × 10−12). By contrast, only 7 of these top drivers of convergence were intellectual-disability-only genes (7 of 70, OR = 2.06, Padj = 0.078). Moreover, the top drivers of convergence were consistently downregulated across nearly all ASD gene KDs (Extended Data Fig. 9b). They were also highly interconnected in the GRN (P < 1 × 10−6) (Fig. 4d), as well as in the STRING database of protein–protein interactions (P = 2.0 × 10−9) (Methods). Taken together, these findings suggest that these genes both act as central regulators of many ASD genes and cross-regulate each other, driving transcriptomic convergence in ASD.

Iterative walktrap clustering identified 4 gene modules among the 70 top drivers of convergence (Fig. 4e), one of which (the blue module) was especially strongly interconnected. This module exhibited very high cross-interaction through STRING analysis (P < 1 × 10−16) and included REST (Extended Data Fig. 8) and several notable ASD genes including CHD8, one of the strongest known risk genes for ASD18. Notably, the inferred CHD8 regulon from the GRN was strongly enriched (first-degree regulon Padj = 4.6 × 10−7; second-degree regulon Padj = 3.9 × 10−20) for direct CHD8 target genes previously identified through ChIP–seq from NPCs45 (Fig. 4f), further supporting the validity of ARACNe-predicted regulatory relationships. Moreover, consistent with previous reports45,46, CHD8 ChIP–seq targets were also highly enriched for NPC-expressed SFARI genes (Padj = 2.6 × 10−8) and HC-SFARI genes (Padj = 8.5 × 10−8). The CHD8-containing module also included three transcriptional regulators (SETD2, SETD5 and KMT2E) that we had directly perturbed, and DEGs from these KDs exhibited significant enrichment for CHD8 ChIP–seq targets (Padj = 1.2 × 10−5, 7.8 × 10−8 and 2.6 × 10−4, respectively) (Fig. 4f), further demonstrating convergent regulation of shared targets by critical ASD genes. This analysis highlights CHD8, a high-confidence ASD risk gene, as a key driver of transcriptomic convergence in ASD.

Previous studies have found that genes downregulated in ASD tend to be more highly expressed in the neurotypical female versus male brain47,48, raising the possibility that this baseline female-biased expression may contribute to the FPE8,47,48. We identified 82 genes that were consistently downregulated by ASD gene KD and exhibited female-biased expression in the brain (Methods); 28 of these were highly constrained (Extended Data Fig. 10a), including 12 highly constrained SFARI genes (OR = 2.79, P = 8.65 × 10−3) (Fig. 5a). Re-analysis of single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) data (Methods) from the frontal cortex of neurotypical male controls and autistic male participants—including individuals with 15q duplication syndrome and genetically idiopathic ASD—revealed that many of these highly constrained genes were significantly downregulated in ExNs from autistic male individuals, further supporting their relevance to ASD (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 10a).
