In contrast to brain Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had increased frequencies of venous capillaries (Extended Data Fig. 8b–d) and marked upregulation of the key regulator of vein specification Nr2f2 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had decreased frequencies of activated and sprouting ECs and lower expression levels of several tip cell genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). The number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), particularly upregulated genes, was much higher (1,621 versus 569 DEGs) in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs; this is likely to represent a long-term adaptation response to loss of VEGFR2 function (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e with Fig. 3g). Whereas in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs, genetic pathways related to EC proliferation and cellular activity (E2F targets, MYC, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis) were paradoxically increased, in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs they were decreased (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e,f with Fig. 3g,h). This suggests that brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs adapt to the long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling through a decrease in cellular activity and upregulation of Nr2f2, which probably decreases their dependence on VEGF signalling for growth and survival.

In the heart, we confirmed previous histological analysis showing that heart Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs proliferated at levels similar to those of control cells and markedly higher than those of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (compare Fig. 3k,m with Fig. 4b–d). They also had many more DEGs (1,750 DEGs versus 242 DEGs), particularly upregulated genes (compare Fig. 3n with Fig. 4e). GSEA showed increased epithelial–mesenchymal transition, KRAS signalling and angiogenesis, and less expression of metabolic-pathway-related genes (Fig. 4e,f), as seen in the brain. Expression of tip or activated EC genes was not as compromised in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Fig. 4g), suggesting some adaptation over time to the loss of VEGFR2. Notably, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4c,d), similar to our observations in the retina (Fig. 1d–f), confirming that mosaic loss of Vegfr2 causes mutant ECs to expand more in veins. In comparison with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed strong upregulation of most venous-specific genes, including Nr2f2, Fbln2, Igf1 and Vwf (Fig. 4e). This was not caused only by the increased proportion of venous ECs in these mutants; capillary and angiogenic ECs also showed much higher expression of these venous marker genes, indicating venousization of mutant Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 capillary ECs over time (Fig. 4h,p).

In the lung, the same adaptation and venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was observed. Mutant cells were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4i–k), and even capillary or CAR4+ ECs showed significantly upregulated expression of lung venous genes including Vegfc, Nr2f2, Vwf and Fbln2 (Fig. 4l,m and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Similar to findings in the other organs, lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had significantly more DEGs than lung Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (3,116 vs 502), particularly upregulated genes (compare Extended Data Fig. 6k with Fig. 4m). Volcano plots and GSEA revealed upregulation of many venous-enriched and epithelial–mesenchymal transition genes, as well as oestrogen response genes. Lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had lower expression of E2F targets and metabolism genes, as seen in the other organs (Fig. 4m,n).

Notably, deletion of Vegfr2 for 2 weeks in adult organ blood vessels did not induce venousization of adult Vegfr2KO ECs; instead, it decreased expression of venous genes (Extended Data Fig. 8g–u), indicating that upregulation of Nr2f2 and venousization may represent a long-term adaptative response to VEGFR2 loss that occurs only during active angiogenesis.

The scRNA-seq data indicating venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs over time were confirmed by immunostaining for the master regulator of venous development NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII) (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). To understand the venousization requirement for long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs, we also analysed Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic Vegfr2Flox/Flox, Nr2f2Flox/Flox mice. When ECs lacked both VEGFR2 and NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), their capacity to expand was significantly reduced, particularly in veins (Fig. 4q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9e). This suggests that endothelial venousization is a key mechanism of adaptation to long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis that enables mutant cells to expand in veins and derived vessels over time.

In addition to analysing embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, we tested the capacity of Vegfr2KO ECs to form tumour vessels over a period of 2 weeks. When Vegfr2 deletion was induced a few days before tumour implantation, Vegfr2IECKO-day-3–adult ECs formed tumour vessels mainly at the tumour border and failed to penetrate deeper into the tumour, where they were 5.2-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10a). By contrast, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–adult ECs, which had undergone venousization throughout embryonic and postnatal development, could better reach inside the tumour and were only 2.6-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). These data show that although VEGFR2 signalling promotes tumour angiogenesis, ECs can progressively adapt to its absence and sustain tumour angiogenesis.

In addition to our findings with respect to venousization, we observed significant upregulation of expression of other VEGF receptor ligands in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11a), including PGF and VEGFC, which bind and activate VEGFR1 and VEGFR3, respectively1. In the absence of VEGFR2, VEGFR1 is the only other receptor that can bind VEGFA. However, all studies so far have shown that VEGFR1 kinase activity is too weak29,30, whereas its extracellular soluble form (sVEGFR1 or sFLT1) acts as a strong VEGF decoy receptor31. Therefore, when VEGFR2 is present, VEGFR1 is considered to mainly antagonize VEGFA–VEGFR2 signalling and angiogenesis. However, we found that Vegfr1 expression was much higher in ECs in the brain, the organ least sensitive to VEGFR2 loss (Extended Data Fig. 11b). We also found that during postnatal angiogenesis, sVegfr1 showed 2–5-fold lower expression than the membrane full-length Vegfr1 (flVegfr1) mRNA form, except in brain ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11c), suggesting a potential signalling role for flVEGFR1.

To evaluate whether VEGFR1 could compensate for loss of VEGFR2, we induced mosaic codeletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 in ECs with iSuRe-HadCre from P1 to P7 (Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1–P7). Compared with Vegfr2KO ECs, Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed a further decrease in ability to migrate and form retina capillaries, but not veins or arteries (Fig. 5a). In veins, Vegfr1/2KO ECs could clonally expand (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Brain and heart Vegfr1/2KO ECs proliferated less than Vegfr2KO ECs at P7 (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Deletion of both Vegfr2 and Vegfr1 had a stronger effect on endothelial and pup survival (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i), confirming the requirement for VEGFR1 signalling when VEGFR2 is absent in capillaries. Mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 alone also led to a decrease in EC migration towards the VEGF-rich front (Extended Data Fig. 11j). In contrast to deletion of Vegfr1 in all ECs, mosaic loss of Vegfr1 in single ECs did not increase VEGF signalling (as assessed by ESM1 expression), probably owing to normal levels of sFLT1 present in the mostly wild-type microenvironment (Extended Data Fig. 11k).

a,b, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from the indicated genetically distinct groups of mice induced at P1 and collected at P7, with cellular heatmaps, XY dot plot and related charts. c, Fold change in the contribution of Vegfr2/3KO-P1–P7 ECs relative to Vegfr2KO-P1–P7 ECs for artery cells. d, Representative confocal micrograph of a Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1–P7 retina immunostained for Ki-67 and ERG. Magnified insets show vein and AF. Yellow arrows indicate Tomato+Ki-67+ cells. e, High-magnification confocal micrographs of retinas stained for VEGFR3 and ERG, and violin plot indicating VEGFR3 immunostaining intensity in control and Tomato+Cre+ (gene KO) ECs normalized to background levels. f, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from mice induced at P1 and collected at P7, with cellular heatmaps, XY dot plot and related charts. g, Proportional stacked bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of Tomato+Cre+ (KO for the indicated genes) cells in distinct retinal vascular regions at P7. h, Bar plot showing fold change in the frequency of Tomato+Cre+ ECs in different vascular regions and mutant groups in relation to Vegfr2KO. Asterisks indicate complete loss of ECs (zero) at LE. i, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from P7 mice with the indicated alleles (n = 6 pups). The iFlpMosaicH2B-Reporter transgenic allele enabled stochastic labelling of a small fraction of individual nuclei with distinct fluorescent proteins, showing that individual Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs clonally expand in veins. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,b,d,f,i) and 10 μm (e).

In addition to VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, ECs express VEGFR3. Previous studies have shown that VEGFR3 is strongly expressed by capillary and venous ECs; however, this receptor cannot bind VEGF (VEGFA), only VEGFC and VEGFD, which are key molecules for lymphangiogenesis but less relevant to blood vessel angiogenesis. Vegfr2IECKO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed very strong upregulation of VEGFC (Extended Data Fig. 11a), which could signal to VEGFR3 in the absence of VEGFR2. Loss of VEGFR3 in growing retina ECs has been shown to induce angiogenesis, suggesting that VEGFR3 negatively regulates VEGFR2 signalling32. However, single Vegfr3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs also had decreased ability to migrate and reach the leading edge (Extended Data Fig. 11l–n). Arterial ECs and smooth muscle cells express high levels of VEGFC33,34,35 a ligand that can bind both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. Compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs had a very similar zonal distribution in capillaries and veins (Fig. 5b) but a 3.4-fold lower frequency in arteries (Fig. 5c); this suggests an important role for VEGFC to VEGFR3 signalling in arterial mobilization or survival, but only when VEGFR2 signalling is absent. Loss of both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 did not compromise the proliferation of surviving ECs in any vascular segments (Fig. 5d).

We also observed that Vegfr2KO ECs had decreased VEGFR3 expression only at the angiogenic front, where VEGFA levels are highest. By contrast Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed strong downregulation of VEGFR3 in all vascular segments, except in arteries (Fig. 5e). Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs behaved similarly to Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, except for a pronounced decrease in formation of arterial vessels (Fig. 5f–h). Taken together, our findings show that in the absence of VEGFR2 signalling, VEGFR1 is required to sustain VEGFR3 expression and growth and migration of capillary ECs. In arteries, VEGFR3 continues to be expressed after loss of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 and regulates development of arteries when the other VEGFA receptors are missing. Notably, vein ECs can survive and clonally expand in the complete absence of all VEGF receptor signalling (Fig. 5i).

Our study challenges the longstanding view that VEGFR2 signalling is indispensable for endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting during angiogenesis1,22. By using iFlpMosaics to induce ratiometric genetic mosaics of wild-type and Vegfr2KO ECs, we demonstrated that these mutant cells are capable of surviving, proliferating and competing with wild-type ECs during the entire embryonic and postnatal organ growth period (Extended Data Fig. 12). Contrary to previous studies suggesting that VEGFR2 is required for all forms of vascular differentiation and development10,12,36, our findings indicate that VEGFR2-independent mechanisms support angiogenesis in certain vascular beds, particularly the long-term development of venous and perivenous capillaries.

We identified significant organ-specific differences in adaptation to acute loss of VEGFR2 signalling (Extended Data Fig. 12a), thereby extending previous findings37,38. Whereas angiogenic retina ECs were strongly affected, brain ECs were the least affected, retaining high angiogenic potential, partially because of VEGFR1 compensation (Extended Data Fig. 12b). By contrast, postnatal heart, kidney and liver ECs were more sensitive to acute withdrawal of VEGFR2, showing partial depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs in capillaries, as well as a partial reduction in proliferation. The postnatal lung showed a distinct response, with no major changes in EC proliferation or cluster composition but instead a shift in transcriptional programs towards inflammation and metabolic adaptations. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of endothelial responses across different vascular beds and suggest that organ-specific factors influence EC resilience to perturbations in VEGF signalling.

The long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs was a notable observation. Although these cells initially had a competitive disadvantage during early embryonic and postnatal sprouting angiogenesis stages, they ultimately expanded and outcompeted wild-type cells in venous and perivenous regions, indicating that alternative pathways support their survival and proliferation in this niche. Veins are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for capillary angiogenesis and later arterialization20,23, and this venous dominance of Vegfr2KO ECs allows them to compete with wild-type cells over time. Our scRNA-seq analysis of different vascular beds further showed that ECs with prolonged loss of VEGFR2 exhibited a significant shift towards a venous transcriptional signature (venousization), marked by upregulation of many venous genes, including Nr2f2, a master regulator of veins development24,39. Vegfr2KONr2f2KO ECs were significantly less able to expand, particularly in veins, showing that venousization is a key adaptation mechanism that enables Vegfr2KO ECs to persist and contribute to vascular development (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d).

In addition to venousization, our findings demonstrate the compensatory roles of VEGFR1 and VEGFR3 in supporting survival and growth signalling when VEGFR2 is absent (Extended Data Fig. 12b). Previously, VEGFR1 has mainly been reported to negatively regulate VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis, because its soluble secreted version sFLT1 or VEGFR1 is a decoy receptor of VEGF1,22. In our mosaic Vegfr1KO and Vegfr1/2KO experiments, sFLT1 levels in the microenvironment were normal; this led us to find that membrane or full-length VEGFR1 acted as a positive regulator of angiogenesis and partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss, supporting both EC survival and migration. The mosaic single loss of VEGFR3 also showed that this receptor was a positive regulator of EC migration towards the leading edge. This was consistent with results obtained using VEGFR3-blocking antibodies40; however, our findings were contrary to results from pan-endothelial Vegfr3KO genetics experiments32 in which the receptor was lost from all ECs. In this case, VEGFC and/or VEGFD bioavailability in the whole body increases, thereby increasing VEGFC–VEGFR2 signalling, whereas in low-frequency Vegfr3KO mosaics this does not occur. In addition, Vegfr2/3KO ECs mobilized less to the angiogenic front and had decreased arterialization when compared with Vegfr2KO ECs. The ability of these alternative VEGF receptors to sustain EC survival, migration and proliferation at the single-cell level indicates potential functional plasticity and compensation within the VEGF signalling network, as suggested previously by studies using classical full-tissue conditional genetics12,32,37.

An important implication of our study is that EC sensitivity to VEGFR2 loss varies depending on the vascular context and the time since the loss. We found that acute loss of VEGFR2 during active angiogenesis resulted in significant EC depletion in the first 3 days, particularly depletion of tip cells and other ECs at the angiogenic front, where VEGF signalling is highest. However, Vegfr2KO ECs in VEGF-low areas and those that had undergone long-term adaptation were able to persist and even contribute to a substantial portion of capillary vessels, particularly those around veins. This suggests that ECs experiencing prolonged VEGFR2 deficiency undergo venousization in VEGF-low areas, enabling them to survive and then grow in the absence of canonical VEGF signalling. Our tumour models showed that Vegfr2KO ECs could form tumour vessels, particularly if they had previously undergone venousization during embryonic angiogenesis. The use of ratiometric and trackable iFlpMosaics was key to obtaining these findings.

Our work may also provide biomarkers and insights into resistance mechanisms to anti-VEGF therapies5,41,42,43. Adaptation of ECs to VEGFR2 loss by engaging alternative venous-related angiogenic pathways may also occur in tumours. If this is confirmed, therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block the compensatory and venous-related pathways identified here may be necessary to overcome resistance to anti-VEGF treatments.

In conclusion, our study reshapes our understanding of VEGFR2-dependent angiogenesis by demonstrating that ECs possess intrinsic mechanisms to adapt to long-term absence of VEGFR2 signalling. The discovery of endothelial venousization and compensatory VEGF receptor signalling provides a new framework for investigation of alternative modes of vascular development and resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

All mouse husbandry and experiments were conducted using protocols approved by local animal ethics committees and authorities (Comunidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid CAM-PROEX 164.8/20, PROEX 293.1/22 and PROEX-288.7/24). The mouse colonies were maintained in racked individual ventilation cages according to current national legislation. The mice had dust- and pathogen-free bedding and sufficient nesting and environmental enrichment material for development of species-specific behaviour. All mice had ad libitum access to food and water in environmental conditions of 45–65% relative humidity, temperatures of 21–24 °C and a 12 h/12 h light–dark cycle. For preservation of animal welfare, mouse health was monitored with an animal health surveillance programme that followed the recommendations of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations for specific-pathogen-free facilities

We used Mus musculus lines mostly on the C57BL6 genetic background, with some having a fraction of 129SV, or B6CBAF1 or DBA genetic backgrounds. Mice were backcrossed to C57Bl6 for several generations. To generate mice for analysis, we intercrossed mice aged between 7 weeks and 30 weeks. We did not anticipate any influence of mouse sex on our data, and both female and male mice were analysed. The initial sample size was determined taking into account the ‘3 Rs’ for animal experimentation and the expected experimental variability based on protocols (published and our own; refs. 13 and 14). The final sample size was defined a posteriori after statistical analysis of the data. Sample size and related statistical analysis methods are indicated in the figure legends or source data. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining.

The following mouse lines were used and intercrossed: Tg(Cdh5–CreERT2)44, Tg(iSuRe–HadCre)14, Vegfr2flox (ref. 45), Vegfr1flox (ref. 46), Vegfr3flox (ref. 47) (for this work, we also generated a new Vegfr3flox allele in the Vegfr1/2flox background, as indicated below), Nr2f2flox (ref. 48), iMb2–Mosaic16, Apln–FlpO15 and the iFlpMosaic lines13 (R26-iFlpMTomato-2A-Cre/MYFP and Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic).

To generate a new Vegfr3flox allele combined with Vegfr1/2flox we injected Cas9, donor DNAs containing LoxP sites and guide RNAs (TGTTAAAGACACGCATACCT/AGG and AGATGGGGTGAATAGCTCCG/TGG) into mouse eggs of the Vegfr1/2flox iSuRe–HadCre Cdh5–CreERT2 line. Founders containing LoxP sites flanking exon 1 in the same chromosome were screened by PCR, and inducible Vegfr3 deletion was confirmed by PCR and immunostaining for the VEGFR3 protein (Extended Data Fig. 11l,m).

For induction of CreERT2 activity in adult mice, 1 g tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, P5648_1G) was dissolved in 50 ml corn oil (stock tamoxifen concentration, 20 mg m−1), and aliquots were stored at −20 °C. Animals received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl of this stock solution (total dose: 2 mg tamoxifen per animal at 80 mg kg−1), as indicated in the figures. To activate recombination in pups, we injected 4-OHT at the indicated stages at a dose of 40 mg kg−1. For double (VEGFR1/2, VEGFR2/3) or triple (VEGFR1/2/3) mutants, 4-OHT was administered to pups at 15 mg kg−1. For activation of recombination during embryogenesis, pregnant dams were induced with 0.25 mg 4-OHT supplemented with 0.125 mg progesterone at E10.5 and E12.5. All mouse lines and primer sequences required for genotyping are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Lewis carcinoma cells were obtained from ATCC and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1× penicillin–streptomycin and 2 mM glutamine at 37 °C, 5% CO2. The cell medium was changed every other day, and cells were passaged every 3–4 days. Cells were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were used for tumour inoculation when they were at 75–80% confluency. Cells were trypsinized and resuspended in Matrigel solution (Biosciences). Age-matched (15–20 weeks) and sex-matched mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 105 tumour cells suspended in Matrigel (Corning, 354234). Mice were euthanized after 15 days, and tumours (less than 2 cm3) were extracted, fixed and processed for immunostaining.

For immunostaining of mouse retinas, eyes were dissected from mouse pups and fixed by incubation with agitation for 20 min in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (diluted from a stock of 16% PFA; EMS 15710). After two washes in PBS (5 min each), retinas were microdissected from the eyes; 4 incisions were made to enable later flat mounting, and the retinas were refixed in 4% PFA for 45 min with agitation. After two washes in PBS, retinas were blocked and permeabilized by incubation for 1 h in PBST (0.3% Triton X-100, 3% FBS and 3% donkey serum in PBS). Samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) diluted in PBST overnight at 4 °C with agitation. The next day, retinas were washed 5 times for 20 min in PBST diluted 1:2. Then, they were incubated in the same solution for 2 h at room temperature with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2). After washing (3 × 15 min) in PBS containing 0.15% Triton X-100, retinas were washed (2 × 15 min) in PBS and flat mounted in Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated with the Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For collection of organs and histological analysis, mice were euthanized in CO2 chambers, and 10 ml of PBS was injected into the left ventricles, followed by perfusion with 3.7–4% formaldehyde (ITW Reagents, 252931) at pH 7. The explanted organs were postfixed for 2 h in 4% PFA (Thermo Scientific, 043368.9M) in PBS at 4 °C with gentle rotation. After three washes in PBS for 10 min each, the organs were stored overnight in 30% sucrose (Sigma) in PBS. The organs were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura) and frozen at −80 °C. Cryosections of 30 µm were cut on a cryostat (Leica), washed three times for 10 min each time in PBS, and blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 10% donkey serum (Millipore), 10% FBS and 1% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) were diluted in the same buffer and incubated with sections overnight at 4 °C. This step was followed by three 10-min washes in PBS and incubation for 2 h with conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in PBS at room temperature. After three washes in PBS, the sections were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated first with the other primary rabbit antibodies, followed by Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then rabbit epitopes blocked with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally incubated with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For confocal scanning, immunostained organ sections or whole-mount retinas were imaged at high resolution with a Leica SP8 Navigator confocal microscope fitted with a ×10 or ×40 objective. Individual fields or tiles of large areas were acquired. All images shown are representative of the results obtained for each group and experiment. Animals were dissected and processed under identical conditions. Phenotypes or signal intensities were compared using images obtained with the same laser excitation and confocal scanner detection settings. We used ImageJ/Fiji v.1.54f to threshold, select and quantify the objects in confocal micrographs.

For arteriovenous mapping of ERG-labelled control and mutant ECs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), a semiautomatic Fiji script (available at https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab) was developed. First, six regions of interest were manually defined by the user: artery, vein, mature capillaries between the established arteries and veins, intermediate capillaries, angiogenic front and leading edge. ERG labelling was used to segment endothelial nuclei and classify each nucleus according to reporter or marker positivity (determined by the percentage of pixels within each nucleus above a given intensity threshold level), and the XY coordinates of nuclei were extracted. Then, arterial, venous, distal and proximal arteriovenous boundaries were defined by the user to determine the relative position of each segmented nucleus to each arteriovenous field boundary; this enabled compilation of data extracted from different arteriovenous fields into a single XY dot plot or heatmap.

The data collected in Fiji were post-analysed in R (v.4.5.2) for generation of graphs representing the spatial distribution of the cells of interest. For the XY plots and heatmaps, samples were randomly subsetted to enable us to display equal numbers of control and mutant cells (MYFP+ versus MTomato+ in the Apln–FlpO, iFlpMosaic background, and MTomato− versus MTomato+ in the Cdh5–CreERT2, iSuRe–HadCre background); this was to make clear the zonation differences between control and mutant cells. For visualization with XY dot plots, 2,000 randomly selected cells of each group were plotted; for the heatmap generation, the maximal number of cells (determined by the cell type (control or mutant) with fewer cells) was used. The percentage of each cell type in each arteriovenous region was calculated given its spatial distribution per field (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

We generated Fiji macro Script_Reporter_MarkerDetection_Mapping.ijm for spatial mapping of ERG and/or quantification of EC colocalization with reporters (MYFP or MTomato) and other markers (Ki-67) as in Figs. 1, 2, 5. R scripts were used for data quantification and heatmapping (Script_Spatial Heatmap; Figs. 1, 2, 5 and Extended Data Figs. 3, 4, 11) and are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab). Fiji, Adobe Photoshop CC 24.1.0 and Adobe Illustrator CC v.27.1.1 were used for downstream image processing, analysis and illustration.

To quantify the clonal expansion of single ECs expressing the iSuRe–HadCre and the Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic alleles, we segmented and analysed images with MTomato+H2B-Cherry+, MTomato+H2B-EGFP+ or MTomato+HA-H2B-Cerulean+ signals with the Clone_Identification_Quantification script, deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

Postnatal and adult tissues were dissociated before fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Enzymatic digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 20 min using a solution containing 2.5 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 mg ml−1 dispase II (Thermo Fisher) and 50 μg ml−1 DNase I (Roche). Following dissociation, samples were pelleted by centrifugation (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Pellets were gently resuspended in 1× blood lysis buffer (BioLegend, 420301) and incubated on ice for 5 min for lysis of erythroid cells. After lysis, cells were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged again (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Cells were resuspended in antibody incubation solution (PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+, supplemented with 2% dialysed FBS; Biowest, X0515), with primary antibodies (APC rat anti-mouse CD31 and APC-Cy7 anti-CD45; Supplementary Table 2) only or with the addition of Hashtag oligo (HTO) antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) when scRNA-seq was performed. Samples were then incubated at 4 °C with gentle agitation for 20 min.

After immunolabelling, cells were centrifuged (450g, 4 °C, 5 min), washed with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged again and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added immediately before FACS analysis. Cells were analysed using an LSRFortessa cell analyser or sorted using a FACS Aria Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). For an example of the FACS gating strategy, see Extended Data Fig. 1a. BD FACSDiva v.8.0.1 and FlowJo v.10 were used for data acquisition and analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, APC rat anti-mouse CD31 (which labels ECs), APC-Cy7 rat anti-CD45 (which labels blood cells) and HTO antibodies (BD Biosciences) (Supplementary Table 2) were used together to hashtag and distinguish the different organ Tomato+CD31+ ECs when loaded on the same 10x Genomics port (Extended Data Figs. 6a and 8a). After antibody incubation, samples were washed twice with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged (450g, 5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. Immediately before FACS analysis, DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added, and the cell suspension was passed slowly through a 70-µm cell strainer attached to a 1-ml syringe for removal of aggregates. Live, DAPI-negative, CD31+CD45− and endogenous-reporter-positive cells were sorted into cold 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 µl of sorting buffer. Cells were collected using a 100-µm nozzle at 20 PSI in high-purity mode with a flow rate of fewer than 3,000 events per second to preserve cell viability and minimize contamination. After sorting, cells were pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 30–40 µl cell-capture buffer (Ca2+- and Mg2+-free PBS supplemented with 0.04% ultrapure bovine serum albumin; Thermo Fisher, AM2616). Viability and cell concentration were determined using a Countess 3 Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before loading of the 10x Genomics port.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded on to the 10x Genomics Chromium Controller system for encapsulation into emulsion droplets. The 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell 3′ RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing were carried out at the CNIC Genomics Unit according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Each port was loaded with 20,000 to 50,000 cells. Final libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, with software v.1.7.2.

scRNA-seq data were aligned and quality controlled by the CNIC Bioinformatics Unit using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9). Clustering, cell type identification and downstream analysis were performed by I.G.-G. The following pipeline was applied for transcript alignment, quantification, quality control and cell type classification.

Reference transcriptomes were generated using the Ensembl GRCm38 mouse genome, build version 98 (sep2019.archive.ensembl.org). Genes metadata were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. To enable downstream analysis of gene deletion efficiency and soluble versus full-length isoform abundance, we appended Vegfr2 (also known as Kdr) exon 3, Kdr exon 30, Vegfr1 (also known as Flt1) exon 13b and Flt1 exon 30 to the reference transcriptome as custom metadata features. Gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. Raw sequencing reads from gene expression libraries, hashtag oligonucleotides and targeted transcript sequences were aligned and quantified using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9).

Downstream analyses were performed using R (v.4.5.0) and the Seurat package (v.5.5.1; https://satijalab.org/seurat/)49. Cells were filtered for removal of low-quality profiles and technical artifacts using the following criteria: 2,000–30,000 total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 800–6,000 detected genes, mitochondrial transcript content less than 25%, fewer than 65% of reads mapping to the top 50 expressed genes and fewer than 0.1% haemoglobin transcripts. Cells with fewer than 15 hashtag UMIs were excluded to improve sample assignment accuracy. To enrich for endothelial populations and exclude hematopoietic contamination, we also required cells to express Cdh5 (normalized expression greater than 0.1) and no or very low expression of Ptprc (normalized expression less than 0.1). Cells identified as doublets on the basis of hashtag antibody signals were removed. Demultiplexing by organ was performed using sample-specific hashtag oligonucleotide signals (Supplementary Table 2) and after confirmed by organ-specific EC markers, and all downstream analyses were conducted separately for each organ ECs.

Mitochondrial genes, haemoglobin genes and transgenes were removed before clustering to avoid biasing of normalization and dimensionality reduction. Filtered count data were log-normalized and scaled before analysis. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis, and batch effects across independent ports were corrected with the Harmony algorithm50.

We clustered cells by constructing a shared nearest neighbour graph and applying the Louvain community detection algorithm to identify distinct cell populations. The optimal number of principal components for dimensionality reduction was determined using an elbow plot, and clustering resolution parameters were selected on the basis of the EC complexity observed in each organ.

Clusters and cells were classified using the SingleR function from the SingleR package v.2.10.0 (ref. 51). Putative doublets were identified as cell clusters that had high total UMI or gene counts or unusual gene coexpression or were located in principal component analysis outliers. Cells classified as singlets were retained and reclustered. Final cluster identities were manually curated on the basis of known EC subtypes and literature-based markers. The FUNCTION_Dotplot_Markers custom function in R was used to find and plot top marker genes per cluster to determine cell identities.

To assess the rate of exon deletion in Vegfr2flox/flox samples, we computed the number of UMI reads aligned to each exon, including the floxed region and the terminal 3′ exon or untranslated region (which is typically overrepresented in 10x Genomics 3′ libraries). Only reads with valid barcodes, UMIs and matching strand orientation were retained.

Read counts for floxed exons were normalized to total UMI counts per cell. These values were added to the Seurat metadata. Deletion efficiency was visualized using dot plots and violin plots, comparing expression of the whole transcript (including the 3′ untranslated region). These visualizations were generated using the custom R function FUNCTION_violin_dotplot_deletion_FC.R, which combines violin plots of single-cell expression distributions with dot plots displaying total average expression numbers and signed fold change between conditions.

To obtain the ratio between the soluble (sVegfr1) and full-length (flVegfr1) isoforms, the normalized reads from exon 13b (the last exon in the soluble form) were divided by the normalized reads of exon 30 (the last exon in the full-length version).

We quantified differences in cell type composition between control and mutant samples for each organ by comparing relative proportions across conditions. For UMAP visualizations (both split and integrated), equal downsampling of the two conditions was performed to ensure identical cell numbers, thereby avoiding sampling bias in visual comparisons.

Differential gene expression between conditions was visualized using volcano plots. These were generated using R functions (FUNCTION_VolcanoPlot) developed in-house that built on the EnhancedVolcano package (v.1.26.0)52. For volcano plots and heatmaps, statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. GSEA was performed using FGSEA with a custom wrapper function (FUNCTION_Fgsea_TableFgsea) based on the FGSEA package. For hallmark pathways, statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea v.1.34.2)53 and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing.

Genes used for differential gene expression analysis were prefiltered using FUNCTION_FilterLowExpressionGenes_onlyTable; this removes genes with low and highly heterogeneous expression patterns across cells, which are often inconsistently detected between datasets and potentially reflect technical artefacts such as ambient RNA contamination. The function acts as an empirical, distribution-based filter to improve robustness of downstream differential expression analysis. Differential expression heatmaps were generated using a custom function (FUNCTION_Find_PlotGenesHeatmap_FC_Metadata), implemented in-house and based on the pheatmap package.

Most numerical data shown in charts were first compiled and processed with Microsoft Excel 2019 and 2024 and then analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism v.10.1.0. All bar graphs show mean ± s.d. Experiments were repeated with independent animals, as stated in the source data file or figure legends. Comparisons between two sample groups with a Gaussian distribution were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. Comparisons among more than two groups were made by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by multiple comparison tests. Data points were analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining. For mosaic analysis, only samples with less than 50% recombination were selected. The sample sizes were chosen according to the observed statistical variation and published protocols.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

a, Schematic of the iFlpMosaic and iSuRe-HadCre genetic systems used to induce and map genetic mosaics. Flow-chart depicting the main steps in image analysis used for the digital mapping of the identified cells, and the generation of heatmaps or XY dot plots, with an example of the analysis for a control retinal AV field with AplnFlpO, iFlpMTomato-Cre/MYFP or Cdh5-CreERT2, iSure-HadCre genetics. Definition of the 6 regions of interest, ERG-based segmentation (endothelial nuclei), nuclear-classification according to reporter or marker expression and relative distance of each nucleus to the AV limits are determined using a custom made semi-automatic FIJI script (steps i-iv). Once a minimum of 2000 cells per reporter group (Tomato+/−, YFP+) are analysed, data is then post-analysed in RStudio to determine the cell distribution of each reporter group in each region and the contribution of Tomato+ cells to each region when compared to control (YFP+ or Tomato- cells) (step v). XY dot plots (step vi) and heatmaps (step vii) are then generated. Note that dot plots (shown in vi) have a maximum of 2000 + 2000 mapped cells plotted as dots, to allow their spatial visualization, whereas heatmaps (shown in vii) are generated with maximal number of mapped cells (with equal cell number in control and mutant group).b,c, Representative confocal micrographs showing the loss of VEGFR2 protein (b), and its downstream target ESM1 (c), 24 h after 4-OHT administration. Data are presented as mean values +/−SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bars are 25 μm.

a, Schematic of the genetics and cell sorting gating strategy to isolate the cells used to perform the scRNAseq contrasts shown in Fig. 3 and this figure. b,c, UMAP showing the different brain endothelial clusters and their proportions (b) and the expression of canonical tip cell marker genes in the activated cell cluster (c). d,e, Umaps and violin plots showing the expression of two genes known to be highly expressed by sprouting tip cells, and downregulated after Vegfr2 deletion in brain ECs. f, Violins showing a tip cell genes score based on the combined expression of several tip cell genes (PlexinD1, Kcne3, Esm1) in brain ECs. g, Violin plots showing expression of the terminal exon 30 (highly detected in the 3′10x genomics library sequencing) and the upstream deleted floxed exon 3, used to assess Vegfr2 deletion efficiency from P4 to P7 in lung ECs. Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). h, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of lung endothelial cell clusters within each condition. i, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different lung EC clusters. j, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 lung ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. k, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs in lung ECs. Coloured genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. l, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in lung Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. m, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in lung ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. n, Violin plots showing expression of the terminal exon 30 (detected in the 3′10x genomics library sequencing) and the deleted floxed exon 3, used to assess Vegfr2 deletion efficiency from P4 to P7. Note that in some cells there is still some residual Vegfr2 mRNA given the short-term deletion nature of the assay, or some contamination with mRNA from wild-type kidney ECs. Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). o, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of kidney endothelial cell clusters within each condition. p, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different clusters. q, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 Kidney ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. r, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs. Colored genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. s, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in kidney Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. t, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in kidney ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. For volcano plots and heatmaps (k, m, r, t), statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For hallmark pathways (l, s), statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea) and Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) FDR correction for multiple testing.

a,b, Direct comparison between scRNAseq data of long- (Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7) and short-term (Vegfr2KO-P4-P7) Vegfr2 deletion in heart and lung tissues showing increased venousization in long-term Vegfr2 deleted cells by dot or volcano plots. Note that the genetics of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs is different and hence the comparisons should be done with their independent respective genetic controls, as shown in Fig. 4h,l. c,d, Representative confocal micrographs of immunostained P7 mouse retinas and hearts (n = 3 pups) showing the upregulation of NR2F2/COUP-TFII specifically in Tomato+/Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ERG+ ECs (white arrowheads) and not in control YFP+/ERG+ ECs (yellow arrowheads), and quantification chart of signal intensity per nuclei (white insets also shown in main Fig. 4o,p). e, Representative FACS gatings of CD31-APC+ ECs collected at P7 from the indicated organs (n = 3 pups), and corresponding to the chart numbers showed in Fig. 4q. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bars 100 μm (c) and 50 μm (d). For volcano plots (b), statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

a, Schematic of the iSure-HadCre, Cdh5-CreERT2 genetics used to analyse the ability of ECs with short-term (2–3 days before implanting the tumor) deletion of Vegfr2 to contribute to Lewis Lung carcinoma (LLC) tumor vessels. Quantifications show that upon short-term deletion, VEGFR2KO ECs(Tomato+ERG+) contribute less to intratumoral vessels when compared to vessels in extratumoral region of the tumor. b, Schematic of the iFlpMosaic genetics used to analyse the ability of ECs (ERG+ nuclei) with long-term (since embryogenesis) deletion of Vegfr2 to contribute to LLC tumor vessels. Quantifications show that upon long-term deletion, the disadvantage of VEGFR2KO ECs(Tomato+ERG+) to contribute to intratumoral vessels when compared to vessels in extratumoral region of the tumor, is smaller than upon short-term deletion. Note that the Apln-FlpO allele also drives the recombination of the iFlpMosaic allele in other cell types besides ECs, and hence the need to use ERG staining (labels the EC nuclei). Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bar 250 microns.

a, Table showing the average log2 Fold change in expression of VEGF ligands and receptors in Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs when compared with Control E8.5-P7 ECs. b, Violins showing the expression of Vegfr1 mRNA in single ECs obtained at P7 from the indicated organs. c, Ratios of soluble and full-length Vegfr1 mRNA expression in the indicated organs single ECs (bulk analysis). d, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from P7 mice with the indicated alleles. The iFlpMosaicH2B-Reporter allele enables the stochastic labelling of a small fraction of individual nuclei with distinct fluorescent proteins, showing that individual Vegfr1/2KO-P1-P7 ECs clonally expand in veins (n = 4 pups). e, Representative confocal micrographs of Vegfr1/2KO-P1-P7 retina immunostained for Ki67 and ERG. Magnified insets of vein and AF are shown. Yellow arrows indicate Tomato+Ki67+ cells. Chart with quantifications showing no significant difference in Ki67 positivity between control and Vegfr1/2KO-P1-P7 ECs in the indicated vascular areas (note that these mutant cells were rarely found at the angiogenic front, and never at the leading edge, and hence no data could be presented for this region). f, Representative confocal micrographs and quantifications of the % of Ki67+ ECs in the indicated organs of Vegfr1/2KO-P4-P7 mice. Arrows indicate Tomato+Ki67+ cells (yellow) or Tomato+Ki67- (white). g, Representative confocal micrograph of Vegfr1/2KO-P4-P7 retinas immunostained with ERG and respective quantification charts, showing a further decrease in EC/vascular density when compared to Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 retinas. h, Representative confocal micrographs of Vegfr1/2KO-P4-P7 retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 (CC3), and respective quantification chart showing a similar increase in EC apoptosis to Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. i, Newborns survival plot showing that double deletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 induced at P1, leads to 100% lethality of pups before P20. j, Representative confocal micrograph of retinas with mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 in ECs from P1 to P7. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing the position and relative % of Tomato+ (KO) and Tomato negative (WT) cells. k, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from Vegfr1 heterozygous floxed (flox/wt; n = 3 pups) and Vegfr1 homozygous mice, with complete (n = 6 pups) or mosaic deletion (n = 5 pups) in ECs induced at P1 with 4-OHT. Note the much higher expression of ESM1 in Tomato+ ECs when Vegfr1 is deleted in all/most ECs, but not when deleted mosaically. l, Vegfr3 floxed gene structure and the guide RNAs sequences used to produce it. m, Validation of Vegfr3 deletion in retina ECs by immunostaining (n = 3 pups). Note the presence of VEGFR3 protein in angiogenic front Tomato negative (EC nuclei ERG+) cells. n, Representative confocal micrograph of retinas with mosaic deletion of Vegfr3 in ECs from P1 to P7. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing the position and relative % of Tomato+ (KO) and Tomato negative (WT) cells. Data are presented as mean values +/−SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bar 100 microns. Abbreviations: LE – leading edge, AF – angiogenic front, IntCap – intermediate capillaries, MA – mature area, A – artery, V- vein.

a, Single cell RNAseq and histological analysis of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs (gene deletion induced at P4 and analysis at P7) in distinct organs revealed common but also distinct transcriptional programs and functions for VEGFR2. b, Loss of VEGFR2 affects the migration of ECs towards VEGF produced by hypoxic tissues, during the first wave of angiogenesis. This leads to the accumulation of Vegfr2KO ECs in more mature vessels and veins, which provides for a continuous source of mutant ECs during subsequent waves of angiogenesis derived from veins. The additional loss of VEGFR1 compromises capillary angiogenesis, whereas the additional loss of VEGFR3 compromises arterialization. c, The comparison of scRNAseq data from ECs with short-term (P4 to P7) and long-term (embryonic to P7) deletion of Vegfr2 revealed that over time Vegfr2KO ECs undergo significant transcriptional changes and upregulate the expression of many venous genes (venousization), particularly Nr2f2. d, The upregulation of Nr2f2, and venousization, enables Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs to compete with wildtype ECs over time, and form veins and many other venous-derived vessels, such as capillaries, tip cells and even arteries. Note that these cells adapt over time to the loss of VEGFR2 and become more capable of angiogenesis than Vegfr2KO-P1-P7 ECs. The additional loss of the master regulator of vein specification Nr2f2, prevents the venousization and growth of Vegfr2KO ECs.

#1418. Xabi Alonso hits out at ‘soft’ Chelsea players

Xabi Alonso accused his Chelsea players of being “soft” after they failed to keep a clean sheet for the 20th successive Premier League game.

Chelsea threw away an early lead to draw 2-2 with Hull City and have conceded two or more goals in each of their four Premier League games.

Alonso has tried different systems and different players in those games, but suggested Chelsea’s biggest problem is mental.

The club’s dreadful clean-sheet record pre-dates him and is the first time in 65 years Chelsea have gone 20 league games without keeping the opposition out.

Hull’s first goal from Mohamed Belloumi came after the ball had bounced over Jorrel Hato and Alonso said: “We need to be aware that from any situation, any team in the Premier League can hurt you. Today it was from a long ball, two bounces, the way it happened. You need to be very aware, very ready that the danger can come from any situation. If you are soft or if you are not prepared, you will get punished and we have been punished that way.”

Chelsea have shared 30 goals with their opponents in the club’s six games in all competitions so far this season.

“Yeah, it’s all maybe entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win and we don’t give these entertaining moments,” he said.

“But, for sure, it kind of repeats some patterns that we are making. It will take time to... or it will take moments to fix them when we get the lead and you still need to be competing and not give the chance so easily for them to come back, especially in the first goal, we can do much better.

“It was too soft to give them this hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances. But that momentum that we had changed the mood and the score of the game, and it’s something that we need to be talking [about], we address and we will get better. But it’s having an impact on our performances at the moment.”

Asked if his players have a real desire to defend and keep clean sheets, Alonso said: “We can do better, we can do better for sure. We need to know that even when we have the lead, a very important part of the game is to hold together, to keep the distance, to go intense in the situations to defend. I’m sure that we can do better.

“Overall, I think that we are attacking better than defending in every part. We know that it’s a big topic and a big theme for us. For sure, it’s just four games. But the dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it and we need to do much better. Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”

Needing three goals or more to win games is not sustainable, as Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso is finding out.

This is not a problem of Alonso’s making, given Chelsea have now gone 20 Premier League games without a clean sheet. But he is certainly not improving the issue yet.

Chelsea beat Fulham with three goals and Brighton with four but left themselves far too much to do against Arsenal and were taken advantage of by Hull City, who will be slightly disappointed they did not leave Stamford Bridge with all three points.

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez has now conceded seven goals in three games since joining from Aston Villa, while central defender Maxence Lacroix, who joined for £52m from Crystal Palace in the summer, was relegated to the substitutes’ bench.

Martínez was at fault for Mohamed Belloumi’s second goal, but the Argentine did make a crucial save at his back post to stop substitute Mohamed-Ali Cho grabbing a winner that Chelsea could have had no complaints about.

Hull finished the game with more shots on goal than their hosts and a higher expected-goals rate. Chelsea are far too open and in some ways far too entertaining.

Defensive midfielder Moisés Caicedo cannot return from injury quickly enough, but this does not feel like a problem that will be solved by one man. Alonso needs to find a balance and instil a real desire in his team to defend.

Caicedo has that desire, but there are no defenders at the club who have shown that absolute desperation to keep the ball out of the net that Chelsea fans became so used to in the days of John Terry, Gary Cahill and César Azpilicueta.

None of this should diminish Hull’s performance. They were not only spirited and full of character but also showed quality and a threat. The joke is currently on those who laughed at their hopes of survival before a ball had been kicked.

It is now two wins and two draws for Sergej Jakirovic’s team and they are already a fifth of the way to 40 points. Jakirovic had promised his staff a week off in the international break if they reached eight points after five games. With that target already met, there may be a new reward if Hull can make it 11 points against Newcastle United next weekend.

“Before the season, I said to my staff that we will take seven, eight points in these first five and then I will give them seven days off,” Jakirovic said. “That was our target and now we are in a very good position, eight points.

“Especially today, it’s very, very difficult to play here, and now we will try to get even more. Of course, I’m a little bit worried about the international break because we have 13 national team players. But we will see who will come back and in what condition. So this is my concern right now.” Asked if his staff’s seven-day break will be extended if Hull can beat Newcastle, Jakirovic added: “I will tell them. But I know already.”

While his five-game target may need modifying, Jakirovic is not deviating from his goal for the season for Hull. “Our target is always to stay in the league and collect as many points as possible,” he said. “Forty points, 38 to 41, this is the average we need. Then it’s easier to play. You can play more relaxed, with more joy and happiness. So [get to] this as soon as possible, so that we are safe.”

Hull had not conceded a league goal before this and there had been predictions they might crumble when they finally let the ball into their net. They did so after just seven minutes but they kept their heads and came back stronger.

It was far too easy for Morgan Rogers to make a yard of space for himself to shoot after collecting the ball from João Pedro, and Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis may not have been happy to have been beaten at his near post.

Chelsea have now scored inside the first 10 minutes in all of their four league games, but Hull were in no mood to crumble and hit back with two goals in six minutes from Belloumi to take a half-time lead. Both Hull goals were shockers from Chelsea’s perspective. The first, in the 28th minute, came as a result of Jorrel Hato letting the ball bounce over him from a Ryan Giles cross and Belloumi finished brilliantly.

Belloumi’s second came after Martínez had flapped at a corner and Semi Ajayi had hit the bar with a header. The ball fell to Belloumi again and his shot was deflected into the net.

It was no surprise that Hato did not reappear for the second half, as he was replaced by Pep Chavarría at left-back. But Chelsea remained vulnerable and Martínez had to recover from spilling a Regan Slater shot to prevent Ollie McBurnie extending Hull’s advantage.

When Palmer and Pedro combined for Pedro to sweep the ball into the net and equalise with 24 minutes remaining, it seemed like it would be Chelsea who would provide the grandstand finish.

But it was Hull who got a second wind and Chelsea were indebted to Martínez for making a save to stop Cho securing all three points and sending the visiting fans home even happier.

I feel good. We have to be happy. It’s a huge result for us.

We had 2-1 at half-time and we had a 100 per cent chance with McBurnie but Martinez’s save was excellent. We have to control play better in the box because we can stop this [Chelsea goal]. We had an excellent chance for Cho – Martinez saved again. Player of the match.

We can be very happy. We took a point in a very demanding match.

Eight points against very difficult opponents. We have to continue like this.

There have been 12 Premier League games at Anfield in 2026, Liverpool have only won 4 of them to date. This was seventh draw and Fulham deserves their share of the spoils. This was very much a learning experience for Andoni Iraola.

Not a single home win in the Premier League, today.

Aston Villa 1 Nottingham Forest 2Bournemouth 2 Brentford 2Chelsea 2 Hull City 2Crystal Palace 2 Ipswich Town 3Liverpool 0 Fulham 0

What a result for Hull, who remain unbeaten and they have taken five points from fixtures against United, Villa and Chelsea.

That is the first really poor result of the Alonso era, points dropped.

What a thriller in SE25, both teams have been going for it in the closing stages, but Ipswich have surely score the winner through Zian Flemming.

Fulham were pointless before this game, but they have kept a clean sheet at Anfield with a disciplined display and they could well have score one or two. Underwhelming for Liverpool, who have not won just one of their first four games and their fixtures have not been the most taxing.

And as we predicted at the beginning of the game... Liverpool 0 Fulham 0. If this reporter ever gives you advice on a horse to back or a team to follow, make sure you take the opposite stance. Fulham deserve their reward and their fans are singing “We got a point!”

Villa are finishing the game with 10 men because Ian Maatsen pulled up after Emery had made his five substitutions, and Forest have punished them through Igor Jesus with just a few minutes of normal time to play.

Alexander Isak heads over the bar when he perhaps should have hit the target. Has time run out for Liverpool?

You might imagine Chelsea are battering down the door, but Mohamed-Ali Cho has just forced Emi Martinez into a save at the other end. Hull will remain unbeaten if they can hold out.

Strand Larsen has had his critics, but he has scored his first goal of the season to set up a grandstand finish with 15 minutes plus stoppage time to play at Selhurst Park.

Short corner, McGinn whipped in an inswinging cross that is glanced into the bottom corner by Alysson.

Liverpool continue to toil at Anfield, but no opening goal. Iraola has thrown on Frimpong, Mac Allister, Ngumoha and Gakpo in the second half. Fulham have had the chances to score at least one, and Josh King has just brought a save out of Alisson.

Hull are a little lucky they still have 11 men on the pitch. Already on a booking, my man Crooks bundled down Rogers. It could easily have been another yellow car but the referee let him off and now he’s been replaced by Iroegbunam.

Joao Pedro finds the smallest of gaps to be the goalkeeper and find the roof of the net with a brilliant, instinctive finish.

That had not really been coming for Chelsea. It all felt a bit easy for Palmer to get his low cross into the box and Pedro to sweep the ball in. The home fans have woken up again.

Martinez was lucky to get away with another slip up, there. He spilt Slater’s shot but reacted before McBurnie to stop the Hull striker scoring the rebound. Just a day after his nasty looking crash, Sorba Thomas is on for Hull.

This game is absolutely here for Fulham to win. Quietness has descended around Anfield, the hosts have no fluency in their play and Fulham are growing in confidence. Why wouldn’t they after getting to 65 minutes with a clean sheet?

Just like in the first half, four minutes after one of these teams taking the lead there has been an equaliser. Kevin Scahde is in a rich vein of form.

Bournemouth have have never beaten Brentford in the Premier League, but they might well be on their way to changing that record having trailed earlier in the game. Marcus Tavernier has just scored their second goal.

Matt Davidson Rider Crooks has just been booked for a very cynical foul on Rogers. It gave Chelsea a free-kick in a dangerous position Reece James had an effort tipped away. Chelsea have started the second half well

Within a minute of the restart, Villa lose the ball in midfield and Delap punishes them to the maximum. Cracking finish from just outside the box, and a much-needed goal by Delap. The Glasner curse striking for Emery again?

Liam Delap has just started paying back that £50m transfer fee with a fine goal.

Delap picked the ball up on the left and set himself up on the edge of the box before crashing a 25-yard shot past Zion Suzuki.

Unai Emery has made a couple of changes at half-time, taking off Nicolas Jackson who picked up a silly booking just before half-time.

Tammy Abraham is on in his place. George Hemmings is also off and replaced by Alysson.

Pep Chavarria on for Chelsea at half-time. He’s replaced Jorrel Hato, who had a bit of a stinker in the first half.

Andoni Iraola hasn’t hung about here. Milos Kerkez has come on immediately after half-time for Kostas Tsimikas and you can say with certainty that Liverpool will be shopping for a new left-back in due course.

So at half-time, Hull City are top of the Premier League and don’t their supporters know it? They were singing “we are top of the League” for the full two minutes of time added on for stoppages at the end of the first period. Alonso has some work to do at the break.

Forest did need a brilliant double save from Matz Sels to deny Victor Lindelof and have recovered to slow the match down.

Neco Williams wasted a decent chance for Forest from outside the penalty area shortly before the break.

Referee Andrew Madley has irritated both teams with a number of weird decisions - but that’s sadly par for the course with officials nowadays.

Villa 0 Forest 0Bournemouth 1 Brentford 1Chelsea 1 Hull City 2Palace 1 Ipswich 2Liverpool 0 Fulham 0

Palace in some trouble now, level with Ipswich and down to 10 men. Disasi was sent off in the 34th minute for a reckless challenge on Jack Clarke, caught him with studs on shin.

Things got worse for Palace just before half-time, with Leif Davis heading home at the back post to give Ipswich the league.

Apologies for the lack of updates, some technical gremlins at Telegraph Towers. A nip and tuck game as expected at at the Vitality: Kevin Schade gave Brentford the lead before Justin Kluivert equalised four minutes later.

One way to put it is that Kostas Tsimikas isn’t playing well. Another way to say it would be that his efforts are making Milos Kerkez look like Roberto Carlos. The Greek left-back is having a dreadful afternoon and Fulham are getting plenty of joy out of him. We suggested there was no chance of this game finishing goalless, and it’s anomalous that we have reached 40 minutes without score. Fulham, certainly, have a sense of adventure and have been into Liverpool’s 18-yard box plenty of times. Let’s see if the picture changes before the interval.

That’s now seven goals Emi Martinez has conceded in three games since joining from Villa to supposedly solve Chelsea’s goalkeeping crisis. Martinez won’t be pleased with Hull’s second goal, here. He was beaten to a corner by Ajayi. His header hit the bar and Belloumi’s shot was deflected past him. The Hull fans are in dreamland.

This is a turn up for the books. Chelsea undone by a long ball forward, and Hato lets the ball bounce over his head, and Belloumi finishes with aplomb.

That’s now 20 Premier League games Chelsea have gone without keeping a clean sheet. What an earth was Jorrel Hato doing, letting the ball bounce over him for Belloumi? Amateur stuff at the back from the home side. It was Hull’s first meaningful attack.

Emersonn has struggled in some games so far this season, but he has just planted a header into the corner from a Davis cross.

There is a VAR check for offside... but the goal stands.

5 - Morgan Rogers is the fifth different player to score or assist in each of Chelsea's first four games of a Premier League season, after Didier Drogba (2010-11), Cesc Fàbregas (2014-15), Diego Costa (2014-15 & 2016-17), and Eden Hazard (2018-19).Famous. pic.twitter.com/0cuThzH472

A sweet strike from one of Palace’s summer signings, recruited from Union Saint Gilloise, and that is his first Palace goal. The 22-year-old Israeli came through at Maccabi Haifa. Uphill task for Gary O’Neill and Ipswich.

Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s flamboyant set-piece coach, just motioned for Xabi Alonso to sit down when the Blues manager momentarily got up from his seat when the home side were preparing to take a corner. It seems MacPhee wears the (correct length) trousers when it comes to set pieces.

An almighty let off for Alisson and Liverpool after pass from the goalkeeper played Gravenberch into trouble, but Jacquet cleared off the line to keep the game goalless. That was Fulham’s first foray forward.

A bright start in this game and there is no chance it will end goalless (famous last words). Andoni Iraola has made three changes from the team that beat Atletico Madrid on Wednesday and it’s a pattern of his early management that he is making the kind of decisions that supporters are nodding along in approval with. Liverpool should already be one up but Alexander Isak’s shot has just drifted across the face of goal but the signs are encouraging. It could be a long afternoon for Alvaro Arbeloa.

Wow. Unbelievable double save from Forest’s Matz Sels there to keep out Victor Lindelof.

The first was the most impressive, a reflex stop after a deflection.

Morgan Rogers is the first player to score against Hull City this season. Emi Martinez launched the ball forward after claiming a corner, and Rogers’ shot from the edge of the area crept under the goalkeeper Tzolakis. He will not want to watch that one again.

We’re past five minutes and it’s the longest Chelsea have gone without scoring in the league this season. Back on Matt Crooks – one of his middle names is Rider.

Although Rogers scored in the seventh minute...so the early goals continue for Chelsea. It will be difficult for Hull now.

Twelve seconds in and the chant “where were you in Istanbul” gets a very early airing from Villa’s home fans.

That is of course a reference to Villa’s 4-0 win over Forest in the Europa League semi-final second leg last season.

The early indications are that Reece James is playing in midfield with Malo Gusto at right-back in a conventional back four.

Xabi Alonso has made an encouraging start to life as Chelsea manager. But his trousers upset me. They are three inches too short and a bit baggy above the ankle.

We are under way in the five Premier League 3pm kick-offs. Goals and further updates from around the grounds as they happen.

Some early #analysis from Matt at the Bridge, about one of Hull’s midfielders.

One player who has really shone for Villa so far this season is teenage midfielder George Hemmings.

Unai Emery has been very impressed with the academy graduate, who made his Champions League debut on Tuesday night.

There is also a big buzz around £51m signing Johan Manzambi, who is on the bench today after recovering from a knee injury.

Will we get another fast start from Chelsea today? They have scored inside the first five minutes in all three of their League games this season. Hull are yet to concede.

Dominic King writes that there were signs of promise in the relationship between Barcola, Wirtz and Isak in Liverpool’s win over Atletico Madrid, and all three forwards start against Fulham. Timothy Castagne, Fulham’s right-back will need to have his sprinting boots on against Barcola, who is grease lightning.

Cole Palmer has 15 goal involvements in his 15 Premier League games for Chelsea against newly promoted sides.9 goals ⚽6 assists 🅰️ pic.twitter.com/PJIU0YxIhQ

I’m having real fun. I’ve got a smile on face and I’m enjoying my football. Playing with players like [Palmer and Joao Pedro] inspire you to be better and make you do better and do well for the team. We are in a good moment and we want to keep it going.

Hull are really tough to beat. They have played against some good opponents and they’ve kept them out - they haven’t conceded yet. It is going to be difficult because they are really organised but we are at home and it is on us to make the game about us.

We know it is always tough against Brentford. We can expect a tight game today, definitely. We both want to win so it’ll be a nice game.

We are very excited about our first European game coming up but we haven’t really spoken about it lately because we have just spoken about this game. This is a big game and we are looking for our first three points of the season. We have been close in every game so we hope to get it today.

Unai Emery is possibly the best coach in the Premier League but has found past encounters with Oliver Glasner very uncomfortable.

Since Glasner’s arrival in English football with Crystal Palace in February 2024, he has faced Emery’s Villa seven times and never lost.

With five victories and two draws, it is an impressive record albeit with a different set of players.

Aston Villa and Forest are two teams in transition, and meet for the first time since that two-legged Europa League semi-final last season.

Villa are building a new chapter after a summer of significant change, while Forest are implementing a totally different style of play under Oliver Glasner.

There have been signs of progress at both of the former European Cup winners. Villa secured an impressive victory over Club Brugge in the Champions League on Tuesday. Forest are improving under Glasner, with their best performance the 2-2 draw at Liverpool.

Returning to Villa Park will have some bitter memories for a number of the Forest players, after that 4-0 defeat in the second leg of the Europa League.

Brentford XI: Kelleher; Hickey, Schuster, Ajer, Lewis-Potter; Yarmoliuk, Sangare, Janelt; Anthony, Schade, Thiago

Subs: Valdimarsson, Henry, Ouattara, Wilson, Carvalho, Damsgaard, Diouf, Kayode, Nunes

Aston Villa XI: Suzuki; Wan-Bissaka, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Barkley, Kamara, McGinn, Buendia, Hemmings; Jackson

Subs: John; Sangare, Hudson-Odoi, Domínguez, Wood, Igor Jesus, Kalimuendo, Yates, Netz

The Reds to take on Fulham 🔴 #LIVFUL pic.twitter.com/PpuyPkkNxU

Ollie Watkins and Emi Martinez departed for pastures new in the transfer window.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this afternoon’s Premier League three o’clock kick-offs, and home bankers would appear to be the theme of the day.

Liverpool will be strongly fancied to put Fulham to the sword at Anfield, with confidence low at the London club and new manager Alvaro Arbeloa (once a player at Anfield) already under pressure amid reports of dressing room unrest. Andoni Iraola secured his first Premier League victory as Liverpool manager at Ipswich last time out, and backed up that result with a come-from-behind win against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League.

Chelsea host Hull City, who are unbeaten after three games and have yet to concede a goal. It is a remarkable start to the season for Sergej Jakirović‘s side, who continue to defy expectations as well as the underlying data. For all their spirit and defensive organisation, keeping out Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro at Stamford Bridge promises to be a tall order, though.

Aston Villa’s rocky start to the campaign took a turn for the better with a 3-2 Champions League victory at Club Brugge, and as the weeks go by Unai Emery’s team should grow stronger as their raft of young signings bed in. Nottingham Forest could be obdurate opponents, although Villa swept them aside in the second leg of last season’s Europa League semi-final. Oliver Glasner’s Crystal Palace were a bogey team for Villa though, with the Austrian coach undefeated against Emery having notched up some resounding victories.

Glasner’s former club Palace could do with a home win against Ipswich Town, while there is cigarette paper between Bournemouth and Brentford, two of the league’s smartest operators who play at the Vitality Stadium this afternoon. Bournemouth qualified for Europe at Brentford’s expense last season, but Marco Rose is looking for his first league win despite some encouraging performances.
