To integrate the evidence from the two independent Mtb screens (experiment 1 and experiment 2) into a single, directly interpretable probability, a joint Bayesian mixture model was fitted to the paired GI scores. For each gene pair, the GI score in each experiment and its standard error (that is, mean GI score and the standard deviation of Δ′ from the Bayesian two-line model) were taken as the x,y coordinates and their measurement uncertainties.

The mixture consisted of five components defined over the range of GI scores: a null component and four interaction components, one for each quadrant. The null hypothesis of no interaction was represented by a bivariate normal distribution centred near the origin, with a correlation parameter, ρ, given a weakly informative prior centred at zero. Allowing ρ to be a free parameter allowed the model to learn any existing correlation observed in the null distribution, owing to each screen using the same library and protocols. Per-pair measurement error was incorporated into the null by adding each pair’s squared standard error to the variance on the corresponding axis and scaling ρ accordingly (see Stan model code for implementation details). This approach incorporates the uncertainty associated with each GI-score estimate, down-weighting imprecise measurements while integrating both the consistency and the precision of observed effects across the two screens.

The four interaction components corresponded to the concordant negative quadrant, the concordant positive quadrant and the two discordant quadrants in which the two experiments disagreed in sign (one positive and the other negative). Each quadrant was modelled as a product of per-axis uniform densities over the range of observed scores, which were winsorized at the 0.1st and 99.9th percentiles to reduce the influence of outliers. Because pairs near a quadrant edge could belong to a neighbouring quadrant owing to measurement uncertainty, the uniform densities were convolved with the per-pair measurement error at the origin. Thus, a pair lying near an axis is assigned partly to each quadrant, and the model identifies the most likely membership from the mixture. The mixture weights were given a Dirichlet(2, 2, 36) prior over the concordant, discordant and null components, placing an 18-fold higher weight on the null, reflecting the expectation that most gene pairs do not interact. Concordant and discordant weights were divided evenly between their two respective quadrants (two discordant quadrants and the concordant positive and concordant negative quadrants). The model was fitted using Stan (cmdstan v.2.35, cmdstanpy v.1.2.4). For each gene pair, the posterior probability of belonging to each component was computed and summarized as the probability of a negative, positive or discordant interaction, and of no interaction. As in the single-experiment analysis, a pair was classified as a likely interaction when the largest of its interaction-class probabilities exceeded 0.5 and as a confident interaction when it exceeded 0.95, and was labelled negative, positive or discordant according to the dominant class.

To explore patterns of similarity in GI profiles, the GI matrix was hierarchically clustered using average linkage with Pearson correlation as the similarity measure, as implemented in SciPy86. At each internal node of the clustering hierarchy, the descendant genes were tested for Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment using GOATOOLS87. GO annotations were obtained from UniProt and mapped to the go-basic ontology, with the full set of genes in the GI map used as the background. Enrichment P values were calculated using Fisher’s exact test and corrected for multiple-hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Nodes were designated as key nodes when they represented the most significant occurrence (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for at least one biological process term. Each key node was labelled with its most significant GO term, and a GO-DAG specificity constraint was enforced such that no parent node carried a more specific term than its descendants. To reduce redundancy, key nodes with highly overlapping parent gene sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.8) were removed. Distinct colours were assigned to the remaining key nodes and propagated through their descendant branches, producing functionally labelled dendrograms in which leaves inherited the most specific term in their lineage.

Pathways were defined using a combination of KEGG and PATRIC pathways together with manual curation (Supplementary Table 4). Genes were assigned to pathways on the basis of manual curation and AI-assisted literature review (Claude Sonnet 4.5). Gene pairs were categorized as having a significant GI (p > 0.5) or not, and Fisher’s exact test was used to assess the association between pathway pairs and significant GIs. Self-interactions, in which a gene is targeted twice (that is, A + A), were excluded from the analysis. The resulting P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The analysis was performed twice: once using all gene pairs and once excluding potential polar effects (defined as pairs in which the genes were five genes or fewer apart), to assess how significance changed.

Sequences for selected genes were co-folded with AlphaFold-Multimer28 (v.3) to predict protein complex structures and AlphaFold34 to predict PPIs. All model inputs for Mtb used amino acid sequences from the H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584). All model inputs for Msm used amino acid sequences translated using BioPython from strain mc2155 (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), with the following exceptions. MSMEG5414 in the reference genome was split into proteins MSMEG5414A and MSMEG5414B. Four genes are misannotated in the reference genome as pseudogenes, and their translations were manually included: MSMEG4629:folC and MSMEG1828 from another genome (GenBank: CP009494); MSMEG1843:ahcY from UniProt (accession A4ZHR8); and MSMEG1400:fusA1 from a previously reported sequence88,89. All sequence inputs for Msm can be found in the file msm_essential_proteome.fa in our linked GitHub repository (see ‘Code availability’). AlphaFold-Multimer inputs were formatted as pairs of monomers28. These complexes were predicted using LocalColabFold90 v.1.5.5 (https://github.com/YoshitakaMo/localcolabfold)90 on an NVIDIA L40S GPU and 16 24-GB CPUs. The model was run with three recycles and AMBER relaxation. AlphaFold3 inputs were prepared following a modified pooled AlphaFold3 approach27. Within the bin-packing strategy, smaller protein sequences were prioritized to maximize the number of monomers per pool. In both cases, five predicted structures were generated per input. Predicted TM scores (pTMs) and interface predicted TM scores (ipTMs) for any given gene or gene pair, respectively, were taken as a mean across all models. ipTMs were corrected for combined protein length as previously described27. In Supplementary Tables 2 and 3, columns from pooled inputs on the web server have the suffix or infix ‘_webserver’.

Structures and scores were also generated locally for Mtb using the same pooled inputs as the AlphaFold3 web server. Per-chain multiple sequence alignments were generated with ColabFold v.1.5.590 using MMseqs2 18.8cc5c91 against the UniRef30 (2023-02) and ColabFold environmental clusters (2021-08; comprising filtered BFD, MGnify, MetaEuk and SMAG sub-databases), with GPU-accelerated prefiltering (--gpu 1 --prefilter-mode 1). The output was written directly in AlphaFold3-compatible JSON form (--af3-json), yielding one unpaired multiple sequence alignment per chain. To avoid recomputing identical alignments across the many overlapping pools in this study, sequences were keyed by SHA-256 hash and computed only once; an indexed central cache of all previously generated alignments (about 3,800 unique sequences) was consulted on every job, with cache hits delivering byte-identical multiple sequence alignments and cache misses triggering a fresh ColabFold run that subsequently updated the cache. Co-folding was performed with AlphaFold3 v.3.0.14 executed inside an Apptainer/Singularity container on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs. For each pool, the per-chain multiple sequence alignments were combined into a single AlphaFold3 input JSON (dialect alphafold3, version 1), populating unpairedMsa from the ColabFold output; pairedMsa was left empty, deferring to AlphaFold3’s internal pairing logic. AlphaFold3 was invoked via run_alphafold.py with --flash_attention_implementation=triton and --resolve_msa_overlaps=false; all other parameters retained their AlphaFold3 defaults. A single random seed (modelSeeds = [1]) was used per input, producing five diffusion-sampled structures per pool from which downstream pTM and ipTM statistics were derived as described above. In Supplementary Table 3, the resulting columns have the suffix or infix ‘_local’.

For both the local and the web-server results, the total number of predicted PPIs for each single protein is listed with the prefix ‘degree’, following notation from graph theory. Each of these columns is suffixed with 1 or 2 to indicate the monomer to which it corresponds. These degrees are calculated cumulatively at three ipTM cut-offs (see Fig. 3f): for example, ‘degree_low_webserver1’ refers to all PPIs predicted for gene 1 with low or higher confidence using the web server.

All compounds were dissolved in DMSO (VWR, V0231) and dispensed using an HP D300e digital dispenser in a 384-well plate format using a twofold dilution series. DMSO did not exceed 1% of the final culture volume and was maintained at the same concentration across all samples. Cultures were synchronized in late logarithmic phase (OD600 nm = 0.2 to 1) and then back-diluted to a starting OD600 nm of 0.01 or 0.05. Fifty microlitres of cell suspension was plated in triplicate in wells containing the test compound. Plates were incubated standing at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The OD600 nm was evaluated using a Tecan Spark or Molecular Devices SpectraMax M2 microplate reader 7–14 days after plating, and the percentage growth was calculated relative to the DMSO vehicle control for each strain. MIC90 and MIC50 measurements were calculated in R using the drm function from the drc package92, with a four-parameter log-logistic model (LL.4). For all MIC curves, data are mean ± s.e.m. for triplicates.

Compounds were dispensed in a 384-well plate as described above for the MIC assays. For each pair of drugs, all combinations of the two-dilution series were plated, including dilution series in which each drug is present alone and a DMSO control in which neither drug is present. Each combination of concentrations was plated in triplicate. Cultures were grown and plated and the relative growth was measured as described for MIC assays, except that the cultures were seeded at OD600 nm = 0.025. Drug synergy was quantified using the synergyfinder v.3.14.0 R package93. For each checkerboard, mean percentage viability values were used to calculate the Bliss independence score94,95 at each combination of drug concentrations. The resulting scores were then scanned to find the most synergistic area (MSA) and most antagonistic area (MAA). These areas were defined as the 3 × 3 contiguous areas of the plate with the highest and lowest mean Bliss scores, respectively. The mean Bliss scores of the MSA and MAA are reported for each drug combination. Both metrics are reported to avoid bias in calling a drug pair synergistic or antagonistic. Following recommended guidelines96, drug pairs with an MSA mean Bliss score higher than 15 were considered synergistic, and drug pairs with an MAA mean Bliss score lower than –15 were considered antagonistic.

A wild-type H37Rv culture was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.05, and 500 μl of culture was added to each well of 24-well plates. Vertex-49 (6.25 μM or 12.5 μM) was added alone or in combination with either bedaquiline (0.45 μM or 0.89 μM) or ethambutol (3.61 μM or 7.21 μM) in triplicate for each concentration combination. Cultures were grown standing at 37 °C for 6 days and then plated in serial dilutions from 10−1 to 10−7 on 7H10 charcoal plates. Plates were grown for 21 days, and then colony-forming units (CFU) were counted. Because we did not have a full panel of concentration combinations, we opted to use the highest single agent (HSA) method of quantifying drug synergy97. In brief, the amount of killing (measured as the change in CFU per ml versus the no-drug control) with the combination of the two drugs is compared to the drug that shows the highest growth inhibition (the HSA) when used alone at the same concentration. The drug pair is considered synergistic if the combination of drugs results in more than 100-fold more killing than the HSA.

Cultures were grown for 5 days in 7H9-OADC with 100 ng ml−1 ATc to pre-deplete protein targets. The cultures were then washed twice in PBS containing 0.05% Tween-80 and adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.15 with fresh 7H9-OADC. After dilution, 4-ml screw-cap glass vials were filled with the cultures, and methylene blue dye was added at a final concentration of 0.001% (w/v). All vials were sealed tightly using a PTFE–rubber seal (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C4015-21), wrapped with parafilm and incubated shaking at 60 rpm at 37 °C in an anaerobic pouch (Becton Dickinson GasPak EZ container systems, BD 260683) for 3–4 days, after which photos were taken to determine whether the cultures turned clear (intact respiration) or remained blue (impaired respiration).

A 20-ml preculture of Msm in Middlebrook 7H9 medium (Sigma) supplemented with 0.5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin, 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80 was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm to saturation. Msm with pKM444 but no other genetic modification was grown without antibiotic in the preculture medium, whereas Msm modified with a 3×Flag tag encoded in its gDNA was grown with 50 µg ml−1 hygromycin in the preculture medium. Each preculture was used to inoculate 6 l of Middlebrook 7H9 supplemented with 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose, 1% (w/v) tryptone and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80, and was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm for 48–72 h. The cells were collected by centrifugation at 6,500g for 20 min, and pellets were resuspended in 100 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM benzamidine HCl, 5 mM aminocaproic acid and 1 mM PMSF. The cells were lysed with the Avestin EmulsiFlex-C3 homogenizer at 20–25 kpsi, and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 39,000g for 30 min, followed by isolation of the membranes by centrifugation at 200,000g for 1 h. The membranes were resuspended in TBS (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) and solubilized for 1 h with 1% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. Solubilized membranes were centrifuged at 200,000g for 1 h to remove insoluble material before binding to around 1 ml anti-Flag M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma) in a plastic column. The column was washed with ten column volumes of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside before eluting the bound protein with three column volumes of 150 µg ml−1 3×Flag peptide in TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside, followed by one column volume of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. The eluted protein was concentrated with a centrifugal concentrator with 10-kDa molecular weight cut-off.

Protein (10 µg) was reduced with 20 mM dithiothreitol for 10 min at 95 °C and alkylated with 40 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min in the dark. Samples were diluted to a final concentration of 5% (w/v) SDS, and phosphoric acid was added to a final concentration of 1.2% (v/v). S-Trap protein binding buffer (165 µl) containing 90% (v/v) methanol and 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) was added to 27.5 µl acidified sample. The resulting mixture was passed through an S-trap micro column at 4,000g. The micro column was washed four times with the S-Trap protein binding buffer. Each sample was digested with 4 µg of trypsin in 20 µl of 50 mM TEAB for 1 h at 47 °C. Before elution, 4 µl of 50 mM TEAB pH 8 was added to the column. Peptides were eluted by centrifugation at 4,000g. Peptides were eluted from the column two more times with 40 µl of 0.2% (v/v) formic acid and 40 µl of 50% (v/v) acetonitrile with 0.2% (v/v) formic acid. Eluted peptides were dried and stored at –40 °C before mass-spectrometry analysis at the Network Biology Collaborative Centre at the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute using standard protocols for data-dependent acquisition.

The SAINTexpress98,99 software package was used to score protein interactions. In brief, peptide-level counts are summed for all detected proteins for both the tagged and the untagged samples (two replicates per condition). These were then used to obtain the protein-level L2FC of counts in the tagged samples relative to the untagged samples. The SAINTexpress package uses a Bayesian model to calculate the probability of an interaction for each protein and uses these probabilities to estimate the FDR.

IMV acidification assays were performed as previously described51. In brief, the membrane fraction from wild-type, ∆qcrB and ∆ms2764 Msm strains were isolated and resuspended in IMV resuspension buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM 6-aminocaproic acid, 5 mM benzamidine hydrochloride and 20% [v/v] glycerol). IMV acidification experiments were performed in 96-well plates (BRANDplates pureGrade 96-well black microplates). NADH and succinate were prepared as electron donors as follows. NADH was prepared immediately before use by dissolving disodium NADH in water to a final concentration of 4 mM. Succinate was prepared by dissolving sodium succinate in water to a final concentration of 20 mM. A master solution containing ACMA assay buffer (10 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl and 5 mM MgCl2), 9-amino-6-chloro-2-methoxyacridine (ACMA) dye (3.125 µM), IMVs (5 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for succinate-driven acidification; 2 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for NADH-driven acidification) and 10 µM of Q203 (with a final concentration of 2% [v/v] DMSO) or an equivalent volume of compound-free DMSO vehicle was prepared and transferred into each well of the 96-well plate. The plate was incubated in the dark for approximately 15 min at room temperature before the start of the experiment. ACMA fluorescence was measured at 25 °C with a BioTek Synergy Neo2 Hybrid Multimode plate reader (Agilent Technologies), using an excitation wavelength of 410 nm and an emission wavelength of 480 nm. IMV acidification was initiated by the addition of NADH or succinate. Fluorescence was monitored for 20 min before the addition of nigericin in ethanol to a final concentration of 2 µM with 0.02% (v/v) ethanol. Fluorescence recovery was monitored for an additional 10 min. Fluorescence recovery was calculated as the absolute difference between the fluorescence immediately before and 10 min after nigericin addition. All IMV acidification experiments were performed with at least three replicates.

Sensor spot assays were performed as described previously100.

Cultures were grown and passaged twice to closely match optical densities. Final cultures were diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.17 (around 50,000 cells per μl), and tenfold serial dilutions were made. Multichannel pipettes were used to spot 2 μl of culture for each dilution onto 7H10 with or without ATc, with the appropriate selection of antibiotics. Images were taken after approximately 20 generations.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Raw sequencing data have ben deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under project numbers PRJNA1337647, PRJNA1338999 and PRJNA1346122. Pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding used the Mtb H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584) and translated sequences from the Msm mc2155 reference genome (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), unless noted otherwise in the Methods. Mass-spectrometry analysis used the Msm mc2155 reference proteome (UniProt: UP000000757). sgRNA sequences were designed using the Mtb H37Rv and Msm mc2155 reference genomes (RefSeq: NC_018143.2 and RefSeq: NC_008596.1, respectively).

a, Construction of dual-sgRNA libraries. Single-sgRNA constructs were cloned individually. To assemble the dual-sgRNA library, all single-sgRNA plasmids were pooled and subjected to two parallel digestions: (1) MfeI + XhoI to generate a backbone library, and (2) EcoRI + SalI to excise the sgRNA–barcode fragment and generate an insert library. Ligation of these two products places two sgRNA cassettes in tandem, followed by their corresponding unique barcodes. To quantify sgRNA abundance, the barcode region is amplified using flanking NGS primers. b, Overview of the pilot GI library design. Up to 24 sgRNAs were selected for each of 16 target genes. The resulting dual-sgRNA library was transformed into Msm and serially passaged +/–ATc, with samples collected every 2.5 to 5 generations. The relative abundance of each sgRNA pair was quantified by sequencing the barcode region. c, Density plot of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2. d, Heat map of GI scores for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Each row and column corresponds to a single sgRNA, and each cell represents a dual-targeting construct. sgRNAs are grouped by target gene and, within each gene, are ordered by sgRNA strength, as defined by the L2FC of the sgRNA when paired with a non-targeting sgRNA at 25 generations (weaker sgRNAs at the top/left; stronger sgRNAs at the bottom/right). Gene pairs highlighted in e–h are marked with dashed boxes. e–h, Scatter plots of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-sgRNA constructs targeting glgB and glgE (e), ponA1 and ponA2 (f), folA and folP1 (g) and rpoB and macE (h). Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2.

a, Library metrics. Metrics are shown for the plasmid library after cloning in E. coli and for the corresponding mycobacterial library after transformation into either Msm or Mtb. Mycobacterial libraries were sequenced from the initial (Generation 0, G0) sample of the uninduced (–ATc) condition. Mtb experiment 1 and experiment 2 were derived from the same plasmid library. b,c,g,h,l,m, Heat maps of the Pearson correlation between sgRNA counts across all time points and replicates for the (b,c) Msm, (g,h) Mtb experiment 1 and (l,m) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. For each experiment, the (b,g,l) –ATc samples and (c,h,m) +ATc samples are shown on separate heat maps. d,i,n, Density plots of uncorrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (d) Msm, (i) Mtb experiment 1 and (n) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. e,j,o, Density plots of corrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (e) Msm, (j) Mtb experiment 1 and (o) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Corrected ΔL2FC values are calculated as the residual (observed – GAM-predicted L2FC) for each dual-targeting construct. For more information, see Methods: ‘Quantification of GIs’ and Figs. 1f and 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4c. f,k,p, Density plots of GI score versus combined gene vulnerability for all gene pairs in the (f) Msm, (k) Mtb experiment 1 and (p) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Combined gene vulnerability is defined as the sum of the vulnerabilities of the two genes in each pair.

a–l, GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 (a–f) and Mtb experiment 2 (g–l) for all genes paired with whiB7 (a,g), with ftsR (b,h), with mtrA (c,i), with ndh (d,j), with ponA1 (e,k) or with dnaE1 (f,l). Arrows mark specific interactions.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual-NT, single-targeting, and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. g, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, Dendrogram of all genes (left), clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Representative clusters (right, from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, DNA replication, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis, and protein degradation). k, Scatter plot comparing GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 and Mtb experiment 2, coloured by joint model hit class. See Methods for additional details. l, Distribution of GI scores for gene pairs grouped into 10 equal-width bins by GI profile correlation. Gene pairs separated by five or fewer genes were excluded to minimize potential polar effects. Boxes indicate the interquartile range (IQR), centre lines indicate the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR; outliers are not shown.

a–c, GI scores in the Msm GI screen (left) and the Mtb GI screen (right) for all genes paired with crp (a), with fumC (b) or with whiA (c). d,e, Density plots of GI scores in Msm versus Mtb for (d) all homologous gene pairs and (e) homologous gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (“category” in Supplementary Table 4, excluding “Unknown”). The total number of gene pairs included in each analysis (n) is indicated in the plot titles. f, Percent of Mtb GIs conserved in Msm. The two gene pair sets defined in d,e were first filtered to retain only Mtb GIs (p > 0.5 in experiment 2). An Mtb GI was considered conserved if the corresponding gene pair in Msm was also called as a significant interaction (p > 0.5) with the same sign (positive or negative). For each set, percent conservation was calculated as the number of conserved GIs divided by the number of Mtb GIs. The analysis was performed twice: once without additional filters (corresponding to the full bar height) and once excluding potential polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart; corresponding to the filled portion). g, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 3c. Only results with q < 0.05 are shown. Hollow circles indicate pathway pairs that fail this threshold after removing possible polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart).

a, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. All pools have exactly one copy of each monomer (that is, the co-folding screen captures only heterodimers). Six additional pools with >25 monomers not shown. b, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. 40 additional pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. c, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in a. Five pools with >25 monomers not shown. d, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in b. 36 pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. e, Uncorrected mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. Red line is the correction factor, calculated as (0.0044 × \(\sqrt{{l}_{1}\,+\,{l}_{2}}\,\)) − 0.036, where (l1, l2) are the lengths of each protein in the pair. f, Size-corrected (s.c.) mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. g,h, Distribution of s.c. ipTMs for co-folded Msm protein pairs with mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.2 (g) and all protein pairs (h). Black dots and grey lines represent the mean and s.d. of s.c. ipTMs across all pools.

a, Volcano plot showing results from an Mtb CRISPRi-based CGI screen with the KasA and KasB inhibitor thiolactomycin. Knockdown of kasA and pptT sensitizes Mtb to thiolactomycin, whereas knockdown of rpoB does not. FDR was calculated using α-RRA with one-sided tests for enrichment and depletion. b–k, Checkerboard assay heat maps showing Bliss scores for the indicated drug pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 4g,i,j,l. b, Known synergistic pair: RpoB inhibitor rifampicin (RIF) and EmbA and EmbB inhibitor ethambutol (EMB); c, Known additive pair: ribosome inhibitor linezolid (LZD) and EMB; d, Thiolactomycin (TLM) and LZD; e, TLM and EMB; f, PptT inhibitor 8918 and LZD; g, 8918 and EMB; h, Pks13 inhibitor mCMX410 and LZD; i, EfpA inhibitor BRD-8000.3 and LZD; j, PknA and PknB inhibitor Vertex-49 (V49) and EMB; and k, V49 and ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline (BDQ). n = 3 biological replicates.

#1399. Manchester United hounded off pitch by own fans

After a humiliating defeat by Grimsby Town in their previous League Cup campaign, Manchester United found a different way to exit the competition this time around. The jeers heard at the full-time whistle after throwing away a two-goal lead pointed to more worrying times a year on from Blundell Park.

For the first time in half a century, United lost a game at Old Trafford having led 2-0, highlighting the defensive problems Michael Carrick needs to solve after turning results around last season.

“What the f---ing hell was that?” shouted the home fans, in a chant that may have been aimed at the referee but equally applied to United’s players, who led through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount’s early goals.

Brighton cut through Carrick’s defence several times before staging their comeback with goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. Carrick and his analysts will rewatch the footage of all three goals in horror at how they conceded.

Kostoulas halves the deficit! 🔵Brighton score on the stroke of half-time. pic.twitter.com/bGjN1w6s6c

“I totally understand the feelings of the supporters,” Carrick said. “We have to accept it. I totally accept it. It’s on me ultimately: as a team what we look like, how we play and what results you get. I take that. I’ll take the praise, I’ll take the criticism and the upset.”

Erik ten Hag used the domestic cups to taste success while struggling in the Premier League, but one of those opportunities is now lost to Carrick, who must be careful not to spiral from a poor start to the campaign into crisis. Sunday’s trip to Fulham before the international break now feels like a big game for United and Carrick.

“We’ve gone out of the cup and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that,” Carrick said. “I’ll be honest about that, that’s how it feels, but it doesn’t have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction.

“We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches.

“It doesn’t feel good at the moment. It doesn’t feel good. We have to go back to winning football matches. We want to win and want to win quickly. The next game is Sunday. That’s all I’m thinking about right now.”

At the start of the evening it seemed that the tie would be remembered for Lacey scoring on his first start for United, the first teenager to do so since Marcus Rashford. In the week when JJ Gabriel, one of United’s great academy talents, asked to leave the club, a different United teenager was kissing the badge when he found the net.

SHEA LACEY ON HIS FIRST START!!! 🔴🌟What a hit from the 19-year-old to open the scoring for Man Utd! pic.twitter.com/Ex2ceXaUge

Mason Mount DOUBLES Man Utd's lead! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/c83ggCb8Bf

And after Mount’s strike it looked like United were cruising into the fourth round for their first knockout win in 19 months, since defeating Leicester City in the FA Cup last year. But Brighton’s way back into the game was to get Gross, 35, on the ball and the veteran German controlled the game.

Gross took his chance when United carelessly played the ball out of defence again, with Diogo Dalot’s clearance mishit. Luka Vuskovic’s header went straight into the United penalty area, with their centre-backs failing to react quickly enough.

Pascal Gross takes advantage of a gifted opportunity to level the score! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Qu2E0B6060

The turnaround was completed a few minutes later when De Cuyper found the net, finishing off a counter-attack in which Diego Gómez and Kostoulas raided the left flank of United before cutting the ball back.

Brighton have turned it around!!! 🔵A sensational comeback as Maxim De Cuyper makes it 3-2 at Old Trafford. pic.twitter.com/Bfcr4N7mTL

Fabian Hürzeler’s side can be considered this season’s entertainers, with this comeback going with their seven-goal thriller against Chelsea, putting four past Aston Villa and five past Coventry at the weekend. Next for them in the League Cup is Manchester City or Norwich away, although they are unlikely to fear any opponents.

“We take it how it is. We want to go as far as possible but if you want to win something you have to win at the highest level,” Hürzeler said. “We have to stay very, very humble and get an understanding why we are at the place we are and getting the basics right and the small margins right. It is so vital we stay humble and then we can grow into the game.”

For Carrick, matches such as this can define a United manager’s reign if he cannot turn results around. The image of Ruben Amorim in the dugout at Grimsby was one of the lasting impressions of last season before Carrick was brought in to salvage the campaign.

“We can’t put ourselves in that position after being ahead in the game and the game finishing like it did,” he said. “So we’ve got to react to it. We’ve got another game on Sunday, we’ve got to react to it.”

"We can't accept that" ❌"I take responsibility for that" 🗣️ Michael Carrick reacts to his side's defeat👇 pic.twitter.com/OheT8yUK7y

2 league one teams and 13 premier league teams in a cup draw.. You couldn't write it Ridiculous 😡😡😡I give up on cup draws after 20 years waiting for one 😂

I think we’ve got to be a little bit careful on that one. He’s a 15-year-old boy. It’s more about the welfare and the care of JJ as a child really, or certainly a young man. The situation is what it is, but we’ve got to be a little bit careful of the exposure and how we jump on that.

The start of the game and the end of the game was completely different, didn’t feel like the same game or the same emotions at all. We had the game exactly where we wanted it and let it get away from us in a big way.

There’s a number of things we’ll look at, we’ll dissect and I know quite a bit of where it went wrong. We can’t accept that as a group. I take responsibility, the performance towards the second half that’s on me. We’ll have to get better, we have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to get back to winning football matches.

We’ve got to keep evolving as a group. We have to keep learning and dealing with situations. Sometimes they come a bit easier than others. Tonight was a tough one. We didn’t find a way out of it. That’s up to me and the staff to help the players and guide them through it. I think we all know that in the end tonight feels like a big disappointment.

We’ve had small, little things that have gone against us in the last week or two and then it accumulates to feel that it’s a lot bigger. I think we have to be honest and say that. The late goal against Everton from outside the box. The [Manchester] City goal the other day. It can all of a sudden roll into something a bit greater but I understand the disappointment because we shouldn’t finish the game in that manner with the position we were in and we have to be humble and take that.

Fleetwood vs ArsenalMan City or Norwich vs BrightonEverton vs NewcastleSunderland vs BrentfordLiverpool vs ChelseaBradford City vs PeterboroughFulham vs Crystal PalaceBournemouth vs Aston Villa

Bradford City vs PeterboroughFulham vs Crystal PalaceBournemouth vs Aston Villa

Plenty of Carabao heritage in that one, they played in the 2019, 2022 and 2024 finals. That’s the glamour draw.

That promises to be a tight one. Many people fancy Brentford for this competition.

The team with a long trophy drought against the club who ended theirs in this competition a few years ago.

Brighton’s reward for a comeback is another trip to Manchester (or Norwich).

The first team out are Fleetwood Town! They will host Arsenal at Highbury, which feels appropriate.

Should be getting started in the next couple of minutes.

The Brighton man has now scored eight times against them, all for Brighton, which is quite amazing. The first of came back in May, 2018. He is not even a striker.

It was frustrating because it’s not the first time this season, it’s the third time this season where we started slow. We have to improve that because we always have to climb a mountain but today we did that.

We played here before last season a similar match that we won and that gives you belief in a stadium where you won before. The experience we try to give it to the lads. It was a really good performance and I have to say [Jason] Steeley’s save at the end was unbelievable.

His impassive demeanour was viewed as a virtue last season, bringing calm to a club that was a circus. Now some will be wondering if standing motionless on the touchline is indicative of a lack of answers. That is probably unfair, you can only be yourself, but we know the script. He’s on a slippery slope, like so many of his predecessors.

Boos ring around Old Trafford. Manchester United are out of the Carabao Cup, but of greater significance is that this defeat continues a poor start to the season and a general mood of deflation around the club. For the first time in 50 years, they lose a game at Old Trafford after leading 2-0. Another proud record falls in the post-Ferguson era.

Brighton have now won five of their last six games at Old Trafford, and are one of the best front-footed sides in the league on form.

As United push everyone forward, Heaven is penalised for a push on Vuskovic, and that is surely that now.

Mbeumo tees up Fernandes for a Hail Mary from 25 yards but he balloons the shot miles over the bar. Brighton fans can see the finish line and a place in the fourth round now.

Five minutes of added time to play, but Brighton have a corner after their press ensnares Tielemans on the edge of United’s defensive third. Dalot got a toe to the ball to prevent Rutter a sight at goal. Darlow claims the delivery, but some time has ticked away.

Tielemans slices his cross over the bar while off balance. This would be the first time since 1976 that United have led 2-0 in a game at Old Trafford and gone on to lose. At the moment, an equaliser does not look to be on its way.

Old Trafford growing impatient with how slowly United are moving the ball, a lack of options for the player in possession and they are being caught on it repeatedly by a sharp Brighton team.

Diego Gomez really should have sealed the victory, picked out by another clever Gross pass, but with so much time to take aim he blasted straight at Darlow. United still alive in the tie, but only just.

Lovely Brighton interplay again, Gross just keeps making the right decision around the box. This time his cut-back finds Kostoulas but Yoro blocks his goal-bound shot. Now Brighton make their fifth change: Rutter replaces Kostoulas.

Brighton still swinging punches. Costinha swings in a teasing cross to the back post, headed down by Gross, but De Cuyper cannot get over his volley. Carrick has made his final change: Cunha is on for Rashford.

Big miss by Rashford, but a big save from Jason Steele. It was a lovely touch by Fernandes while half stumbling that released Rashford, and he had so much time to think when through against the goalkeeper, but Steele stuck out a right boot to save.

Hurzeler making two more Brighton changes: Ayari and Kadioglu on for Hadjam and Boscagli, which probably makes their XI on the pitch even stronger. Kadioglu was voted Brighton’s player of the season for 2025-26.

Bruno Fernandes is stripped and ready to come on, Carrick calling for the man he would rather was resting on the bench. Fernandes replaces Mount.

De Cuyper, only on for a few minutes, scores the goal, but it was the off-the-shoulder threat of Kostoulas that made the goal. It looked as if the striker had the ball stuck under his feet, but he squeezed in a low cross that deflected off Mazraoui into the path of De Cuyper who had the simplest of finishes.

Brighton have turned it around!!! 🔵A sensational comeback as Maxim De Cuyper makes it 3-2 at Old Trafford. pic.twitter.com/Bfcr4N7mTL

Changes all round: Mainoo, Mbeumo and Zirkzee replace Sesko, Lacey and Andrey Santos.

For Brighton: De Cuyper and Diego Gomez on for Yalouye and Matt O’Riley.

He has been the scourge of United on so many occasions, and so it has proved again. United tried to play out from deep against Brighton’s press, hooked a longer pass around the corner towards Sesko but Vuskovic nipped in front of him to win a booming header back to Gross at the edge of the box. Nice touch to shift the ball left, before finishing across Darlow.

Pascal Gross takes advantage of a gifted opportunity to level the score! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Qu2E0B6060

Short corner from United after good work from Rashford, but Tielemans could not keep his curling shot under the bar. Brighton break, but it is better defending from Heaven against Kostoulas this time. Carrick is preparing a triple sub.

Sesko with space to drive forward and look to pass or shot, but he dallies and dawdles before losing possession, much to the frustration of Old Trafford. Sesko has looked short of sharpness and confidence so far.

Delicious pieces of skill from Lacey, a Cruyff turn against the touchline when he was facing away from goal. Hadjam thought he had the winger boxed in, and dragged him down at the expense of a yellow card. Crowd enjoyed that.

Vuskovic with a shot from distance which is always rising; a number of Brighton players have tried their luck from range tonight, perhaps inspired by Lewis Dunk’s screamer at Coventry. This second half has a been a bit of a non-event thus far.

Matt O’Riley clips Heaven, which enabled the United defender to get out jail because he did not have control of the ball and was scrambling. Then Struijk very nearly sells Steele short with a back pass, had Sesko have won the first touch it was a red card or a goal, but Steele went to ground to win the ball well outside his area.

Rashford has been a bright spark for United, but he is having to do too much of the heavy lifting on his own at the moment. This time he finds Lacey on the overlap, but his cross is volleyed clear. Moments before that, the Old Trafford crowd were unhappy that Lacey was not awarded a free-kick. Looked like Hadjam took a swipe.

Brighton continue to apply the squeeze, but Kostoulas fouls Mazraoui to enable Darlow to boot the ball long and United to push up the pitch. Carrick’s team are still not exerting much control on the contest, though.

That is something of a rarity at this stage of the League Cup.

Plenty of entertainment for the paying punters at Old Trafford, with Shea Lacey and Mason Mount scoring twice in two minutes to put United in a commanding position. Given the JJ Gabriel story, the home fans enjoyed seeing a 19-year-old kiss the badge after scoring on his full debut.

Brighton have probably been the better team in general play though, and scored a deserved goal on the stroke of half-time.

United’s second-string back four looking very shaky, understandably.

Carrick and United wanted a foul on Sesko on halfway, but the referee said nothing doing. Hadjam then floats a diagonal pass over the head of Heaven to find the run of Kostoulas, but goalkeeper Darlow surely had the chance to come off his line and claim? Passive goalkeeping, and Kostoulas slips the ball under Darlow into the far corner. Game on.

Kostoulas halves the deficit! 🔵Brighton score on the stroke of half-time. pic.twitter.com/bGjN1w6s6c

Chema Andres, signed by Brighton from Stuttgart on deadline day and known by the moniker “Baby Rodri”, has just been booked for a reckless challenge in midfield. Then Rashford shows he still has plenty in the locker with a touch and shimmy to beat Costinha.

Tielemans with an important challenge on Kostoulas, after more unconvincing United involving Dalot misjudging a bouncing ball. Then Kostoulas fizzes a cross all the way through the six-yard box and Gross fires over at the back post. Brighton have had the chances to be level.

Yalcouye was very dangerous for Brighton against Coventry, and he is proving difficult to contain again. Gross’s through ball releases him into space behind Dalot, but his side-footed shot was shoved wide of the post. He tried to “Henry” one around Darlow with his right instep and failed to find the curl.

Clean hit from almost 35 yards from Boscagli, but his left-footed attempt whistles just over the bar. Yoro heads away a temping Gross cross when Brighton had three blue shirts in promising positions. Rashford then puts the ball through the legs of Chema Andres, and United have a corner.

Lacey goes down hoping for free-kick, anticipating the contact from Gross but it was not forthcoming. Since 2013-14, United have been 2-0 up at Old Trafford 145 times, winning 143 and drawing just two.

Brighton well on top now, and Ayden Heaven goes to ground hoping for a free-kick but the referee is having none of it. O’Riley’s cross is turned behind for a corner, which United scramble away. Feels like a Brighton goal is on the way, despite the comfortable scoreline for United.

Brighton’s corner swung in from the right was far too deep and loopy, drifting harmlessly behind for a United goal kick. Brighton are soon back on the front foot, and Gross picks out Kostoulas in the middle but the forward’s touch let him down. Edgy defending from Yoro but United clear their lines eventually.

Mazraoui is now back on the pitch but he does not look 100 per cent. Brighton enjoying some long passages of possession now, but you sense United are happy to drop off and let them have the ball. More promising build-up play ends with Mazraoui heading a cross over the bar for a Brighton corner.

There has been a lengthy stoppage in play while Mazraoui receives treatment for a bang on the head. United’s left-back looks a little shaken and is off the pitch now, and Mason Mount has dropped into the left-back position.

Sesko and Vuskovic are enjoying a good battle early on. Andrey Santos then sells Tielemans a little short in midfield and Brighton take advantage, but O’Riley does not have the pace to get away from Mazraoui.

There are usually chances at both ends when Brighton are involved and so it has proved so far. A pleasant surprise for any Manchester United fans who feared the worst arriving at Old Trafford tonight.

Shea Lacey is the first teenager to score on their full Man Utd debut since Marcus Rashford back in 2016. And they even got to celebrate together 🥺 pic.twitter.com/hBeXpCr4Tc

Brighton playing their way into trouble in their own defensive third, and it is great work from Rashford to drive into the penalty area from the left. Steele makes a save with his feet, but the ball runs kindly for Mount to power his shot into the ground and into the roof of the net.

Mason Mount DOUBLES Man Utd's lead! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/c83ggCb8Bf

The 19-year-old, sent off against Brighton in the FA Cup last season, has powered a left-footed shot from the edge of the box beyond Steele. That is a moment to lift the Old Trafford crowd.

SHEA LACEY ON HIS FIRST START!!! 🔴🌟What a hit from the 19-year-old to open the scoring for Man Utd! pic.twitter.com/Ex2ceXaUge

Really slick, one-touch football from Brighton through midfield, players bumping off passes blind around the corner knowing their team-mate has read the next move, but the move breaks down at the edge of the box. Brighton tend to have plenty of possession and they have made a confident start. Boscagli then tries to chip Darlow from about 70 yards but it was never really on.

Some sound early defending from Brighton right-back Constinha, just when it looked like Rashford was going to break into space down the left flank. Yalcouye with a flick around the corner in midfield but his touch gets away from him and he commits a foul.

Then Yalcouye’s directness causes Yoro a problem near the left touchline, with the French defender hacking him down.

Tonight promises to be a test for Ayden Heaven and Leny Yoro who are a young centre-back partnership for United. Looks a good crowd for a third-round League Cup game.

Meanwhile, some interesting news on JJ Gabriel’s future from our man at Old Trafford:

Barcelona are leading the race for JJ Gabriel after the 15-year-old requested to quit Manchester United.

Telegraph Sport revealed this week that Gabriel has told the club he wants to cancel his registration and move as a free agent, with Europe’s biggest club well aware of the teenager.

Gabriel travelled to Barcelona last season when he was shown around their training ground and met Wojciech Szczesny and club legend Sergio Busquets.

Sources at rival Premier League suitors believe that Barça have stolen a march in the race for the England Under-17 forward.

Should he move abroad, United may only get around £300,000 in training compensation as Gabriel has a European Union passport.

United would be expected to look into whether there was any influence from football agents before September 1 when Gabriel was allowed to have a representative.

They are the Premier League’s top scorers with 13 goals in four games and they also lead the division when it comes to expected goals amassed. Brighton have also won four of their last five visits to Old Trafford in all competitions.

We’ve got the squad to do it, we feel its important and the boys are desperate to play. We’ve got a very good team out.

We’ve moved on [from the Manchester derby]. On the day, you have to deal with it, I think there’s been enough said about it [the VAR decision] and we move on.

They’re a very good team, the way they play, you make you work for it, we’ll be ready for that. They play some very good football, and score an awful lot of goals.

Youri Tielemans has been given the armband for the evening in an interesting Manchester United line-up named by Michael Carrick. Karl Darlow gets his club debut and Mason Mount is back from injury. Shea Lacey gets a start too, a home-grown talent given his chance in the week JJ Gabriel, 15, has requested to leave Old Trafford.

Eight changes by Carrick, with Karl Darlow between the sticks. Mazraoui, Yoro, Heaven, Andrey Santos, Mount, Sesko and Lacey the other players to come in. No JJ Gabriel in the squad.

United starting XI: Darlow; Dalot, Yoro, Heaven, Mazraoui; Santos, Tielemans; Lacey, Mount, Rashford; Sesko.

Subs: Lammens, Maguire, Amass, Fernandes, Mainoo, T Fletcher, Cunha, Zirkzee, Mbeumo

Lewis Steele replaces Bart Verbruggen in goal, and O’Riley, Costinha, O’Riley, Chema and Hadjam are the other players to come in. With the Conference League not starting until after the international break, Brighton do not have a pressing need to rotate.

Brighton XI: Steele, Costinha Vuskovic, Struijk, Boscagli, Chema, Gross, O’Reilly, Yalcouye, Hadjam, Kostoulas

Subs: Verbruggen, Dunk, Georginio, Promise, Osman, Kadioglu, Gomez, Ayari, De Cuyper

TEAM NEWS! 🚨 Our starting XI for #MUNBHA. 👊 pic.twitter.com/gK5tUVYJ7L

Talents like Gabriel offer United fans hope of a brighter future after years of failure and underachievement.

No one can be certain he will fulfil the vast potential everyone in football circles can see. But United would love to have a good stab at helping him realise it.

The notion of him doing it somewhere else will send chills down the spines of the Old Trafford hierarchy.

Here are the numbers. Man City vs Norwich is tomorrow night, so their last-16 tie will be clarified then. Spurs, Leeds and Forest three Premier League teams who have already fallen by the wayside.

The joke goes that Michael Carrick has already bettered Ruben Amorim’s efforts by reaching the third round of the League Cup, but Manchester United will need to find a way past free-flowing Brighton if they are to go any further.

United were eliminated in the second round by League Two Grimsby Town last season, but start the competition a stage later because they are one of nine Premier League clubs playing in European competition.

Brighton knocked United out of the FA Cup in the third round, with Danny Welbeck scoring at Old Trafford, meaning the club played just 40 matches in 2025-26.

Carrick will want to make a better fist of the cup competitions, but he could really use a win of any kind after taking just four points from United’s first four league games of the new season.

The no-show at Hull and derby defeat by City’s 10 men were especially dispiriting, and the relationship between the club and supporters is becoming increasingly strained.

There were no flags on the Stretford End for the game against City, as fans voiced their opposition to what they view as a heavy-handed ticketing policy. The club says the measures are to stop ticket-touting but critics believe many innocent season-ticket holders are being caught in the crossfire and having their tickets revoked.

Discontent is never too far away given the continued presence of the Glazer family, and confidence is fragile regarding the club’s sporting direction under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The news that 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, possibly the country’s outstanding academy player in his year group, wants out (broken by Matt Law in a Telegraph Sport exclusive) nagged at some of those fears. Gabriel could have been in contention for a place on the bench this evening, but that is now surely out of the question even if United say they have not given up hope of persuading him to stay.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1398. 'This club's not used to losing' - keeper Johnstone opens up on Celtic struggles

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:00 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 13:48 EDT, 7 November 2026

Sam Johnstone has warned that Thursday's dramatic win over Besiktas must be seen as just the first step on Celtic's road to recovery.

The pulsating 3-2 triumph over the Turks came after Martin O'Neill's men had lost four straight matches in Europe with just three wins in the previous ten matches in all competitions.

As timely as the result was, the keeper believes there's a lot of hard work for the side to get through before anyone can talk about it being a turning point in what's been a trying season to this stage.

Asked if the spirit in the camp had been affected by a string of adverse results, Johnstone said: 'Of course it has. I think the results affect it.

'This club's not used to losing and we've probably lost too many games for this club.

'We all realise that, but we have to put things right in each game.

'The lads go out to win every game, so the camp's good.

'It was tough. We're honest players, we're honest people and honest with each other.

'You could see on Thursday night that the lads put a good fight in and got the result.'

Signed on loan from Wolves for the season, Johnstone was handed his chance by O'Neill only to drop out of the team following an indifferent display in the 3-0 loss at Ibrox on September 13.

Celtic goalkeeper is finding his feet in Scottish football after a difficult start

But having been selected ahead of Viljami Sinisalo in the past five matches, the former England goalkeeper believes he's steadily making progress.

'To get a run of games for any player, you find your rhythm,' Johnstone explained.

'It was a new club for me, a new team, so that takes probably a couple of games to get used to as well.

'I think I've got to get used to them (defenders), they've got to get used to me and that only happens through playing and through games. It's great to be in the team.

'It's good. I love playing. It's a great team to play in, a great club to play for and we keep taking it game by game. We go again on Sunday.'

Johnstone moved to Celtic at the start of a difficult period which saw the side struggle for consistency.

Adamant that he's never regretted moving up to Scotland for a minute, however, he added: 'The expectation, rightly so, for this place is to win games.

'Unfortunately, we hadn't quite met that expectation and the lads know that.

'Like I said, we try to win every game and put things right.

Celtic fought back for a much-needed Europa League victory against Besiktas

'It's brilliant to play for this club. The passion of the fans, good and bad. The standard of players on the pitch, day in, day out at training.

'When I came, I said I didn't have to think twice about coming here.'

Having heard so much about Celtic Park on the night of a big European win, the keeper was glad to finally witness it for himself.

'It was unbelievable to experience this place, rocking and get the win,' he reflected.

'It's a great feeling. It's great to play in front of and feel the passion of the fans. That does help the lads and drives the lads on.

'As you could see, there were times in the game where we struggled a little bit, but the lads dug in. It's never going to be easy.

'In the Europa League, you're playing top teams and, after last week's result as well, we were under a lot of pressure. The lads came up with the goods.

'We've still got a chance to qualify, and that's our aim, so we'll take the next game the same as any other game, that we go to win.'

#1397. Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9,10,11,12,13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

The capacity of cancer cells to switch phenotypic states, also called cellular plasticity, is a hallmark of cancer and is involved in tumour initiation and progression, including therapeutic resistance1. Glioblastoma (GB), the most common primary brain tumour in adults, is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and a dismal prognosis2,3. Although the genomic landscape of GB has been catalogued extensively, actionable genetic drivers remain scarce, and clinical responses to targeted therapies have been minimal4,5,6. Longitudinal studies have underscored the limited contribution of therapy-induced genetic evolution in GB and revealed remarkable clonal stability despite treatment7,8, suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic plasticity and transcriptional reprogramming, are central to adaptation and treatment resistance in GB. Seminal single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown that malignant GB cells occupy a continuum of cellular states resembling developmental progenitors (for example, oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-like and neural progenitor cell (NPC)-like), as well as astrocytic and mesenchymal-like phenotypes9,10. Patient-derived xenograft models have demonstrated that individual GB cells can give rise to multiple states, implying substantial plasticity10,11. However, whether these state transitions follow stereotyped routes or variable trajectories12,13, and how gene-regulatory mechanisms promote or constrain them, remain poorly understood.

Here, and in a companion study14, we address these questions by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing; snATAC-seq) profiles from more than one million cells from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type primary GBs. Using a computational approach (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference; scDORI) and systematic transcription factor (TF) perturbations, we decode enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks (eGRNs) at single-cell resolution and map the regulatory landscape that underlies the identity and plasticity of GB cells. Specifically, we model the gene-regulatory processes that govern GB cell states, identify key transcriptional regulators for each state, elucidate their roles in driving cell-state conversions and reconstruct a hierarchical roadmap of GB transitions. Our analyses reveal a structured landscape of GB state transitions shaped by epigenetic ‘highways’ and ‘barriers’. Neuronal-like cells emerge as a constrained, low-plasticity state stabilized by a network of transcriptional repressors that actively silences alternative malignant fates. We identify MYT1L as the key repressor in this network: gain-of-function of MYT1L restricts plasticity and induces a neuronal-like identity in patient-derived GB cells, and reduces tumour growth after transplantation in mice; by contrast, removal of MYT1L enhances plasticity and malignant features. These findings suggest that enforcing repressive barriers could lock GB cells into less adaptive states, and identify plasticity restriction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Together with our companion study mapping spatio-temporal trajectories in GB tumours14, our findings reveal a conserved, epigenetically controlled hierarchy of cell states and transition routes in GB. Our work establishes transcriptional repressors as key suppressors of plasticity and underscores the potential of targeting the epigenetic foundations of state switching in brain cancer.

To characterize the regulatory landscape of GB, we generated a multiome snRNA–snATAC-seq atlas (see the companion study14), spanning parallel gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiles of more than one million cells collected across multiple sites (4–15) from 12 IDH-wild-type primary GB tumours, including peritumoral regions. In line with previous studies10, malignant GB cells exhibited vastly heterogeneous transcriptional profiles, ranging from developmental-like (OPC-NPC-like, OPC-like, OPC-neuronal-like, NPC-neuronal-like and astrocyte (AC)-progenitor-like) to glial injury response and hypoxia-associated (AC-gliosis-like, gliosis-like and hypoxia) phenotypes, as well as cycling signatures (proliferative) (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a).

a, Experimental set-up, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot and annotation of the RNA modality of 368,054 TME and 657,275 GB cells from 12 patients with IDH-wild-type GB profiled by snRNA–snATAC-seq. Colours and labels denote states of the indicated malignant GB and TME cells. b, Schematic of computation of the epigenetic plasticity score. A linear classifier trained on gene expression to predict transcriptional states is applied to gene accessibility profiles, with ambiguity of predictions indicating epigenetic plasticity. c, Epigenetic plasticity score determined using the approach in b, visualized for all cells on the UMAP plot in a. High scores denote high epigenetic plasticity. d, Confusion matrix for the accessibility-based predictions from the classifier in b: state prediction probability on the basis of gene accessibility profiles (rows), averaged across cells from each transcriptionally defined state (columns). Off-diagonal mass reflects accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states, the ambiguity that drives the epigenetic plasticity score in b. Malignant states (yellow box) show the lowest accuracy, indicating increased epigenetic plasticity. e, Average epigenetic plasticity score for the indicated cell states across n = 12 patients. Malignant states differ in plasticity, with NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like states showing the lowest levels (P = 5.0 × 10−6, two-sided t-test). Box plots show the median and interquartile range (IQR); whiskers are 1.5× IQR. f, Variance component analysis of epigenetic plasticity, assessing the contribution of patient, cell type and other sources of variation (residuals). Illustrations in a,b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

First, we investigated the epigenetic plasticity of GB cells, assuming that accessible gene regions without active transcription indicate epigenetic plasticity. Inspired by a previous study15, we quantified how well accessibility profiles of cell-state markers predict transcriptionally defined cell states (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1b,c, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). Cells whose chromatin profiles yield uncertain predictions are scored as more epigenetically plastic. Our analysis revealed that malignant cells exhibit greater epigenetic plasticity than non-malignant tumour microenvironment (TME) cells and analogous neurodevelopmental cell types (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f), with chromatin accessibility in malignant cells often being compatible with multiple cell states (Fig. 1d). However, the extent of this plasticity varied significantly across GB cell states (Fig. 1e), and NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like cells stood out as the least plastic states. The variations in epigenetic plasticity could not be explained by differences in global coupling between gene expression and accessibility, were robust to differences in cell numbers per state and were consistently observed across patients (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). These data suggest that specific regulatory mechanisms underlie GB plasticity and govern cell-state heterogeneity.

To determine the specific gene-regulatory processes that underlie the observed differences in epigenetic plasticity, we aimed to identify relevant TFs, cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their interplay across GB states using eGRNs. Established eGRN inference methods are not designed for the heterogeneity of a single-cell tumour atlas like ours16,17,18,19,20,21,22. Specifically, existing methods assume discrete, predefined cell-types and therefore cannot capture the continuous, cell-state-specific variation in eGRNs that defines malignant heterogeneity. Many also scale poorly to datasets of this size23. Moreover, previous methods focus mainly on signatures of transcriptional activation, despite the growing recognition of gene repression as a key regulator of cell identity and plasticity in cancer24,25.

To address these limitations, we developed scDORI, a computational approach for inferring continuous eGRNs and their relationships across cell populations using single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and scATAC-seq multiome data (Fig. 2a and Methods). Building on autoencoders26, scDORI performs joint dimensionality reduction of gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles, decomposing both into gene-regulatory modules16,27,28,29,30,31,32 that are hereafter referred to as ‘Topics’. Each scDORI Topic encodes an eGRN in which TFs bind to CREs to control target gene expression, so the factors carry regulatory meaning rather than describing co-variation alone (Fig. 2a). Coupled decoders enforce this structure through established eGRN signatures: peak co-accessibility, TF chromatin binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that distinguish activation from repression16,17,18,19,20,21,22 (Extended Data Fig. 2a). By modelling each cell as a mixture of Topics, scDORI can capture continuous variations in eGRNs across cell states, without relying on predefined annotations. Conversely, a single Topic can be active across multiple cell states, enabling the identification of shared aspects of gene regulation. scDORI scales to datasets comprising millions of cells, and performs favourably, compared with existing eGRN inference methods, on benchmarks such as the prediction of enhancer–gene links33 (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Overview of the scDORI model, inferring continuous eGRNs from scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq multiome data. scDORI models each cell as a linear combination of co-active Topics, with each Topic encoding an eGRN that links TFs, CREs and target genes. Auxiliary decoders impose mechanistic constraints from peak co-accessibility, TF binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that separate activation from repression. b, Activity of selected Topics in malignant cells, visualized on the UMAP representation from Fig. 1a. c, Heat map with hierarchical clustering of selected Topic activation patterns across GB states, revealing an activation continuum. Colour denotes average Topic activation, scaled across states. For complete Topic scores, see Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2. d, Chromatin accessibility of Topic-associated ATAC peaks (blue) and expression of their predicted cis-linked genes (orange) across cell states. Rows correspond to peak and cis-linked gene pairs, grouped by the Topic with the highest peak association. e, Annotation of scDORI Topics by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), using genes ranked by Topic-association score. The normalized enrichment score (NES) is shown for two representative pathways per Topic (P < 0.05). Expanded analysis in Supplementary Table 2. ChS, chondroitin sulfate; ECM, extracellular matrix; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transition; PCP, planar cell polarity. f, GB TRs: TFs with the highest cumulative activation of genes in each Topic-specific eGRN. Topic activation scores are shown for selected TRs and Topics. TFs previously reported as GB cell-state markers or as being highly expressed in developmental (dev.) cell types are indicated in the top panels. g, TSs: TFs that repress Topic programs of at least two alternative states. Rows show the predicted repression of alternative Topics exerted by each TF. The source Topic is labelled at the bottom. TFs previously reported as GB or developmental markers are indicated in the top panels. Neftel states10: NPC1-like; NPC2-like; AC-like; OPC-like; MES, mesenchymal; Verhaak states4: CL, classical; PN, proneural; MS, mesenchymal. NSC, neural stem cell. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

Applied to our GB atlas, scDORI identified 31 active Topics with distinct patterns of activity across cells and patients (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2), each capturing co-accessible chromatin regions that were cis-linked to co-expressed genes (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the mechanistic constraints came at no cost to descriptive power: scDORI Topics explained transcriptional variation in tumour cells as well as or better than conventional dimensionality reduction methods did18,29 (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Clustering transcriptional GB states according to Topic activity patterns revealed four major regulatory states alongside a distinct proliferative (cycling) population, including developmental states (neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like) and AC–gliosis–hypoxia states (AC-like and gliosis–hypoxia) (Fig. 2c). Topics specific to individual states reflected gene programs that are characteristic of their developmental counterparts, such as neurotransmitter release in neuronal-like cells (Topic 37), PDGF signalling in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 34) and calcium ion homeostasis in AC-like cells (Topic 20)34,35,36 (Fig. 2e, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2). These programs were also active in corresponding TME cell types, consistent with tumour cells co-opting developmental pathways.

As well as explaining differences between GB states, scDORI resolved functional heterogeneity within individual malignant states. For instance, in gliosis–hypoxia cells, distinct Topics captured hallmark features such as hypoxic stress (Topic 11), cytokine signalling (Topic 19) and vascular wound healing (Topic 12)37,38,39 (Fig. 2e). scDORI also identified ‘inter-state’ Topics (7, 9, 25, 29, 33, 36 and 49) that span several GB states. Most of these were enriched for programs linked to fate commitment and differentiation, indicating a potential role in mediating state transitions (Fig. 2c,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Finally, scDORI identified Topics that were broadly active across most tumour cells, reflecting tumour-wide programs, such as inflammatory response (Topic 31) and cell adhesion (Topic 18)40 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). The inferred Topics were reproducible across model restarts, consistently represented across patients with GB and transferable to independent single-cell GB atlases10 (Extended Data Figs. 3c and 4d–f). Notably, scDORI Topic-specific eGRNs accurately captured differential expression between GB cell states of these independent atlases (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h).

The eGRN encoded by each Topic directly yielded Topic regulators (TRs), defined as the TFs with the strongest predicted activation of the Topic-specific gene program. On average, scDORI identified about nine TRs per Topic (Fig. 2f, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). These included known GB cell-state markers, such as ASCL1 in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 36), SOX11 in neuronal-like cells (Topic 24) and FOSL1 in gliosis–hypoxia cells (Topic 19), as well as TFs associated with the respective Topic programs, such as hypoxia (NFKB1, Topic 19) and stress response (JUND, Topic 11)10,41,42,43,44. State-specific TRs included lineage-specific TFs, such as SOX6 (Topic 34, OPCs) and TRPS1 (Topic 9, ACs), further supporting the idea that GB cells reuse developmental TFs and gene programs45,46,47. Besides positive regulation, scDORI-inferred repressive links and identified Topic safeguards (TSs): TFs that regulate an identity by silencing gene programs of states distinct from their state of activity; that is, alternative states (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). For instance, ST18 and SOX10 emerged as putative repressors of alternative state programs in neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like programs, respectively. Several TSs also act as TRs of their own Topic, revealing factors that both activate their own identity program and repress those of alternative states. Collectively, scDORI redefines GB heterogeneity from a gene-regulation standpoint and reveals state-specific activators and repressors, many of which have not yet been described in GB.

The extent to which GB state transitions follow defined regulatory rules, and which TFs drive them, remain central questions in GB biology9,10. We reasoned that if scDORI faithfully captures these processes, then activating the predicted regulators should induce the associated cell states. To test this, we performed a pooled single-cell lentiviral overexpression (OE) screen of 55 TR and TS candidates across three patient-derived GB cell (PDGC) lines, co-cultured with primary cortical cells to provide a neural microenvironment (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 3 and Methods).
