#1386. Moyes' Programme Notes For Record-Equalling Everton Fixture

Good evening and welcome back to Hill Dickinson Stadium for a Premier League fixture staged, unusually, on a Friday night.

I’m told the last time Everton hosted a home game on a Friday night was when Tottenham Hotspur visited Goodison Park in 2021, when games were still being played behind closed doors due to Covid.

Now we find ourselves here this evening, just four days after a really good victory at Newcastle United in the Premier League.

We were in good spirits on our journey back from Tyneside on Monday after we had secured three valuable points in a league where, with the table so tight, one win can make a big difference to your Premier League position.

On the night, we produced some very good performances and were really pleased to come back from St James’ Park having secured what was our second victory over Newcastle United in four days.

There was a lot of scrutiny of our goal on the night, which we all felt was undoubtedly legitimate and which eventually proved to be the case. But after looking back on the non-penalty award which also involved Thierno Barry I could question whether VAR could have easily asked the referee to have another look at the incident, but chose not to.

Last Thursday we reached the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup with victory over Newcastle.

The timing of the tie meant both teams knew the winners on the night would go to Fleetwood Town in the last eight, after they had produced a remarkable result to knock out the league champions Arsenal.

In the event, we scored three goals on the night, which was really encouraging, to go through and we will now treat the next round of the cup with as much respect as we have every round so far.

Tonight I am fully aware I equal Harry Catterick’s record of most matches as Everton manager. I am incredibly thrilled and honoured to have been given the opportunity to manage this football club in so many matches and for so many years. Seeing my name alongside Harry Catterick’s is hugely humbling and I hope I can continue to add to that figure. What I really hope, though, is that I can bring trophies to the Club like Harry Catterick did in his period as Everton manager.

After tonight we head into another international break. Thankfully, for most people, the break is not as long as the last one, and on our return all clubs will face a really packed period of football leading up to Christmas and the new year. Hopefully all of our international players who are away on duty will return fit and well.

It is important we keep our squad strong and fit, with all of our players ready to perform when required to the standard we all want for Everton, as they have showed in the past few games.

It is important for us that we continue to try to show improvement week on week.

Tonight we welcome some ex-Evertonians and a former Everton manager back to the Club and I am sure they will get a good reception from you supporters.

Frank Lampard has done a great job in lifting Coventry out of the Championship and into the Premier League and we have no doubts tonight will be another competitive game.

One of the more pleasing aspects of being a manager is when you see players go on to have good careers, when it can’t always be at the club where they started, and we have a few former players in the Coventry squad who I am sure you will all warmly welcome back.

The performances of our own players in recent games has been excellent and you supporters have picked up on that. The effort they have put into getting those back-to-back results has been clearly noticeable on the field and you have responded.

Your support in the cup game was magnificent, as it was on Monday at Newcastle, and we will need every one of you again tonight to help us along, to give us that extra boost of energy and be the extra man when required.

#1385. Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players

Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

“I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”

Asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

Even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel said. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

“I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel said. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.

“It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

“So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I said, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”

Tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he said: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”

On Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always said he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”

Tuchel said that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”

Tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

It was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

“I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”

“It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

“It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”

“The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”

“That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a new level of pressure.”

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

Again, not something anyone has said to me. Where is Tuchel finding these people?!

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”

Tuchel says that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

Sorry, Thomas, that’s not my experience at all. Everyone I speak to says he blew the Argentina game. This sounds a bit deluded. According to Tuchel, I must speak to 0.01 per cent of England fans....

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”

Tuchel says he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”

Tuchel says he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel says the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”

Tuchel says his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s important to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He says the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has said the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

No questions from the broadcasters about blowing the lead against Argentina and Tuchel’s opinion about the World Cup. Weird.

Ben White pulled out with an injury after being back to his best. It is unfortunately, a bit of a story for him. Josh King was very close and is on the radar.

Tuchel seems to be referring to notes as he speaks. He keeps looking down at a piece of paper he brought in with him.

“The door is always open through performance, behaviour and commitment.”

“They had a good start to the season. Now it’s a new competition. Some positions have injuries. Palmer has his numbers back and a point to prove. Trent was never non-selectable and comes in as a right back.”

We will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

5 - Alex Scott is the only midfielder in the Premier League this season to rank in the top five for times he has won possession (3rd), for the number of duels contested (=4th) and for total distance covered (5th).Sprightly. pic.twitter.com/xfVzme7JXj

Jason Steele’s inclusion is effectively a call-up. He was at the World Cup as a “fourth” goalkeeper for training – and going to country and western gigs in Kansas – but was not part of the official 26-man squad.

The big ‘loser’ from the World Cup squad in being left out by Thomas Tuchel is Arsenal’s Noni Madueke. It is understood the place of his club team-mate Eberechi Eze was also in question, but the 28-year-old has been included, partly because of the unavailability of other players. Hopefully Thomas Tuchel will explain all later.

The absence of Nottingham Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White is puzzling.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the top-scoring Englishman in the Premier League since the start of last season.

🎯 "CALVERT-LEWIN STICKS IT IN!" pic.twitter.com/UJ54wPGytV

Thomas Tuchel has named his England squad for the first games of the 2026-27 season, as the Three Lions begin a new Uefa Nations League campaign.

The head coach has selected a 27-man squad for the four-game window, which takes place between September 21 and October 6.

There’s a return to the Three Lions squad for a number of players following the start of the new campaign with their clubs, with the likes of Cole Palmer, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Lewis Hall, Rio Ngumoha, Jarrad Branthwaite, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Alex Scott all selected.

And there’s a place in the squad for Trent Alexander-Arnold, alongside his Real Madrid teammate Jude Bellingham.

Here it is! 🤩Thomas Tuchel's first #ThreeLions squad of the 2026-27 season 🦁 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

Ivan Toney likely to miss out as he is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on September 24.

Nine weeks have passed since the agonising semi-final collapse to Argentina and Tuchel can expect a grilling about his reflections.

He will need to rebuild trust with supporters heading into a cycle that culminates with a home Euros in 2028.

Eberechi Eze could be left out of the England squad announced this morning by Thomas Tuchel ahead of the forthcoming Nations League campaign. The Arsenal midfielder has made six appearances for his club so far this season but has only started two of those games and none in the Premier League.

The 28-year-old played four times for England during the last World Cup but Tuchel is expected to shake up his forward options. There is an expectation that there will be a recall for Chelsea’s Cole Palmer.

#1383. ST MIRREN 0 RANGERS 2: It's back to the grind for McInnes' men as they show grit to see off Buddies

By KEVIN MCKENNA AT MARBILL COACHES STADIUM

Published: 17:42 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 17:51 EDT, 7 November 2026

At some stage, you would suspect Rangers are going to find their groove under Derek McInnes.

But until then, they will happily settle for just getting points on the board. How they go about it doesn’t really matter in the grand scheme of things.

This hard-fought victory in Paisley — much like so many of Rangers’ Premiership wins this season — was all about substance over style.

Yes, there were flashes of quality here and there. But it was more to do with doing the ugly stuff well than anything else. Fortunately for McInnes, his side are proving to be adept at doing so.

It’s a handy habit to have at their disposal. We saw it in recent draws at Dundee and Hearts last month, managing to come away with something when they probably deserved nothing.

With nobody knowing what version of Celtic are going to turn up on any given week, all Rangers can do is stay within touching distance of the league leaders — a point in front ahead of their meeting with Kilmarnock this afternoon — until they come to blows again in the new year.

Rangers skipper Neil nets with the aid of a deflection to put his side two goals up

Rangers wasted no time getting themselves on the front foot. St Mirren barely got a kick in the opening exchanges, and on the odd occasion they did, possession was turned over far too easily.

Badredine Bouanani had the visitors’ first effort of the night on six minutes, cutting inside from the right flank before pulling the trigger from 20 yards, but it lacked the power to properly test Jacob Chapman in the Saints goal.

The keeper had to be far more alert five minutes later, pulling off a wonderful reaction stop to deny Ryan Naderi finishing off Kevin Kelsy’s headed knockdown. You would have put your house on the in-form Czech finding the net.

Emmanuel Fernandez headed over from the resulting corner.

Having finally settled down, St Mirren gave their opponents a perfect opportunity to take the lead, when Samuel Ramos brought down James Penrice on the angle of the Buddies’ box.

There didn’t appear to be a great deal of contact, but it didn’t take long for VAR to confirm referee Nick Walsh’s decision.

Naderi stepped up to do what he failed to do moments earlier, coolly slotting into the bottom corner to register his ninth goal in all competitions this season.

From looking as if he was likely to be on his way out of Ibrox over the summer, the 23-year-old has become one of the first names on McInnes’ team sheet.

Penrice goes down under Ramos' challenge to earn Rangers a penalty in the first half

And perhaps the most exciting thing from a Rangers perspective is that he is still a million miles from being the finished article. But playing with this sort of confidence, he’s only going to get better.

He was involved in a lovely free-flowing counter shortly after the half-hour mark, with the ball eventually falling to Kim Min-su on the penalty spot. However, the South Korean delayed getting his shot off and the chance was gone.

When running full-flight at defences, the 20-year-old is a delight to watch in that No10 role.

There isn’t anyone in the country better at finding pockets of space between the lines and taking the ball on the turn. But for all that there is to enjoy about his game, his decision-making in the key moments undoubtedly needs work.

A woeful ball out from Olwethu Makhanya set up a two-v-two for the hosts before the break, with Ramos drilling straight at Ivor Pandur from inside the area. With the whole goal to aim at, the Spaniard should have done much better.

The same goes for Jake Young, who blasted high and wide from a promising position a minute later.

Naderi is hailed by Min-su after putting the visitors ahead from the spot

As dominant as Rangers were, you never got the feeling their lead was particularly secure, such is their tendency to play themselves into trouble every now and then.

Fernandez is the worst culprit for it. Fortunately for him, his recovery pace gets him out of jail more often than not. He needed it on a couple of occasions here.

A delightful threaded ball from Bouanani found the feet of Min-su inside the box on 47 minutes but under heavy pressure, he was unable to prod beyond Chapman who’d rushed off his line to meet him. It was hard to be too critical of the Rangers midfielder this time.

Chapman was once again called into action to thwart Kelsy from close range after the Venezuelan escaped the clutches of his marker to collect Min-su’s pass in behind.

He then skewed an effort wide at the back post from an excellent Nico Raskin delivery from the right. It was a night on which very little came off for the big man in front of goal.

To his credit, he kept plugging away, and played a key role in Rangers’ doubling their advantage just after the hour mark, with his driving run causing a bit of chaos in the Buddies backline, before captain Dan Neil swept a loose ball into the bottom corner via the aid of a big deflection to give Chapman absolutely no chance of saving.

With his first touch, substitute Eseosa Sule wasted a glorious chance to reduce the deficit after being left all alone at the back post to stab home Declan John’s cross.

With the ball seemingly destined for the back of the net, Rangers keeper Pandur produced a stunning save on the stretch to turn the ball round the post.

The Croatian’s signing went somewhat under the radar over the summer, but he has demonstrated time and time again that he is a man for the big occasion. He’ll win this side plenty of points between now and the end of the season.

McInnes applauds the away support after signing off for the international break with a win

St Mirren came into this one having won just once in their past eight, but you wouldn’t have guessed they were struggling for confidence given the way in which they threw everything at the game in an effort to get a result.

It wasn’t for lack of trying, with Luke Thomas testing Pandur from range before Calvin Ramsay’s follow-up header clipped the post.

That would be as close as Saints would come, as Rangers dug in to grind out an ugly — but ultimately deserved — win on the road.

They will need to be far better, far more consistently if they want to get their hands on the Premiership title come May. But that’s a worry for another day.

#1382. An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1,2,3,4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

#1381. Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal

Overpowered and overrun, Arsenal were subjected to the sort of gruelling treatment they usually inflict on their opponents. Mikel Arteta’s side did not look anything like Premier League champions here, as Brighton and Hove Albion produced a stunning performance full of swarming energy and breathless bravery.

In the biggest test of their season so far, Arsenal fell woefully short of the standards they have set themselves over the past few campaigns. This sort of thing simply does not happen to Arteta’s side. Well, it did not happen. Not before this monstering on the south coast, where the Brighton fans were whipped into a frenzy by the brilliance of Fabian Hürzeler’s players.

Brighton were everything that Arsenal are expected to be: aggressive, inventive and dominant across the field. They even scored with a set-piece, as one of Arsenal’s great strengths became a sudden weakness. Everywhere Arteta looked, the foundational truths of his team were being shaken by a Brighton storm. It was their first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023, also against Brighton.

Remarkably, this is now the third consecutive season in which Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions. They are rarely happier than when they are on the hunt against more illustrious opponents, working as a team to snap at heels and then attacking in numbers. They are known as the Seagulls, but they played more like a pack of bloodthirsty wolves. The ferocity of their off-the-ball work, especially in the first half, was extraordinary.

Not for a long time have Arsenal been as rattled as they were here. David Raya misplaced passes, Gabriel Magalhães lost duels and Bruno Guimarães chased the ball in vain. It was Brighton’s Pascal Gross, rather than Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard, who shaped the game in midfield. It was Brighton’s Charalampos Kostoulas, rather than Arsenal’s Kai Havertz, who offered incisive class in attack.

Gross and Kostoulas both struck from range in a one-sided first half, before Chema Andrés added the third after the break. At half-time, Arteta had sprinted down the tunnel towards the dressing room. Whatever messages he gave to his players, they either did not sink in or did not work. By the end, Arsenal were lucky the scoreline was not even more humiliating.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

It was the first time that Rice and Guimarães had started alongside each other for Arsenal and it quickly became clear that their £180m partnership will need some work. Arsenal would have hoped their experience in the Premier League would allow for an instant connection but, evidently, that is not the case. Guimarães was hooked after 60 minutes, but might easily have been removed at the break.

Both managers had a similar assessment of the match and how it was won: Brighton did the basics far better than Arsenal. “How we wanted to approach this game was getting into it through small wins,” Hürzeler said. “Everyone speaks about a goal or chance as a win, but a small win can be the first throw-in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle. These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

It was typical of Brighton that one of their new signings produced an excellent performance in midfield. Andrés, a 21-year-old Spaniard signed from Stuttgart at the end of the transfer window, looks to be the latest gem identified by their data-led recruitment model. No one inside the Amex Stadium was thinking about Carlos Baleba, sold to Manchester United, when Andrés made his tackles and won his headers.

Another new signing, centre-back Luka Vuskovic, was similarly impressive at the back. Signed for £46m from Tottenham Hotspur, Vuskovic looks more than capable of going to the top of the game.

This was perhaps the first occasion this season in which Arsenal missed William Saliba, the injured centre-back who has been so fundamental to their success in recent years. The Frenchman can always be relied on to provide calmness and composure at the back, even under intense pressure. Without him, Arsenal were uncharacteristically jittery.

“The amount of technical errors we did in our own half...” Arteta bemoaned. “We didn’t respect any principle of play that you have to get out of those man-to-man situations. That put us always on the back foot.”

Gross, who at 35 is playing as well as ever, opened the scoring with a low shot from range after 31 minutes. Kostoulas then struck the second, from a similar distance, after some end-to-end action resulted in Arsenal’s midfield and defence melting away. The third was the most simple, as Andrés headed in at the back post from an inswinging corner.

Arsenal did have some chances, with Havertz missing the best of them, but there was never a sense that Brighton were vulnerable. The pressure on the home side was never sustained. For Arteta, who now has an extended international break in which to ruminate on this defeat, it all made for an unfamiliar and unexpected pain.

Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players failed to “respect the game” as their perfect start to the season was ended in stunning style by a brilliant Brighton performance.

Arsenal’s capitulation on the south coast led to their first defeat of the campaign and Arteta admitted that Brighton had a different “edge” and “bite” throughout the match. The Arsenal manager also said the 3-0 loss represented a “big lesson” for his players.

“There are certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League, that we were very far from,” Arteta said. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“It was a really disappointing result and performance. Brighton were another gear up from us. We were extremely poor technically and were not respecting the game.

“It is not going to take away what the team has done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup. What we have done and the way we have competed, and the amount of games we have won, has been remarkable. But this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level.”

Arteta added that his team did not “respect the principles of play” that were required against Brighton’s intense pressing, and also said his players were guilty of numerous technical errors.

“Credit to Brighton for what they have done because they have overcome us and they had another edge,” Arteta said. “There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50/50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them.”

Brighton are the Premier League’s top scorers this season with 16 goals in five matches so far, and this emphatic victory took them up to third place in the table.

“It was a special win,” Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, said. “Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance. I am really proud of my team. It’s always important to enjoy these moments. We were horrible to play against. My players really trust each other on the pitch.”

Two things, one give credit to them. In the manner that they played and committed to every single action. We were below the standards that are required for us but in the Premier League as well.

When you miss chances like we did it becomes impossible. I want to congratulate Brighton for what they’ve done. It’s a big lesson for us to learn. If I have to describe how the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks, has been expectational but today has been a big lesson.

A very disappointing result and performance. Full credit to Brighton the manner they went about the game, they were a different gear from us. We didn’t do the basics right for long periods, especially in the first half. We didn’t win enough duels, and any second balls and that stretches you.

We were poor technically when we had the ball in our own half, we didn’t apply the principles that you need against a team that wants to press you man to man.

Arteta: "There are certain basics that you need to accomplish in the Premier League that we were very far from. The amount of technical errors we did... we didn't respect any principle of play. We were always on the back foot. They had another edge."

Beating the current champions and maybe the best team in England is something special. The result is nice but the performance is what makes it special, the boys showed real courage, real intensity and they were horrible to play against because we did the basics right.

Intensity, intensity, winning the personal duels...we have to have the belief to compete with the best teams in the league. My players really trust each other on the pitch. If one player is out then another can replace him.

Overall we wanted to be really good in every phase. We needed to be at the highest level. We go game by game. After the international break we have a lot of games. After wins like this we have to stay humble and understand why we had this win. We have to keep on going.

Our 125 anniversary & one of the best days! 💫 pic.twitter.com/YbZLTFPpWN

I thought we showed great intensity, waited for mistakes and punished Arsenal. It was a strong performance, a very complete performance.

We won the ball high up and attacked really fast. After the last two wins we are full of confidence and wanted to finish really strong before the international break.

I feel really good. I can’t complain. I just try to help the team when I can. I really enjoy life in Brighton, I’m loving it.

I know after the international break we play every three days and a lot of the lads are not used to that. It will be tough. I hope we can compete. We have a big squad this season.

Pascal Gross pulling the strings. 🔎 @Microsoft pic.twitter.com/DAgVsG2B3W

Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions in three consecutive seasons.

Like Everton, Newcastle labour to a home win which should have been more comfortable. It would have been had Wissa scored his penalty, but it was a nervy finish as Hull pushed for an equaliser after Cho’s goal.

Everton up to fifth but they made hard work of that against Ipswich’s 10 men, but Thierno Barry’s goal proves the difference. Barry unfortunate that his second did not stand because of a contentious offside check.

One of the outstanding team performances of the season so far from Brighton, and it will take some beating between now and May. Arsenal were loose defensively in open play and from set-pieces, and were smothered by Brighton’s pressing. Arteta’s team beaten for the first time this season and emphatically so. Arsenal’s first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023.

Just three minutes of stoppage time remaining, but Hull are still pushing bodies forward.

Hull are knocking on the door at St James’ Park, and Newcastle are hanging on to their lead rather than pressing for a third goal.

Matt O’Riley has missed two great chances to make it four. Brighton have not given Arsenal a sniff. It will be interesting to hear how stern Arteta is in his post-match assessment.

Kai Havertz shoots straight at the goalkeeper when clean through, and that is surely Arsenal’s last chance of an unlikely comeback gone. Brighton have pushed Arsenal back for much of the season half, they have not been sitting on a lead.

At St James’ Park, Hull have pulled a goal back through Cho to set up a nervy finish for Newcastle.

The forward is shown a second yellow card for diving, and Ipswich’s hopes appear to be dwindling at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

What a farcical five minutes we have had, from an absurd disallowed goal for Everton to a ridiculous red card for Abdul Fatawu, banished for a second bookable offence - which was diving. There is going to be plenty said about Thierno Barry’s second goal being chalked out because, when you see it, you will wonder what it was for. These are the situations with which I struggle most - if players do not appeal for a wrongdoing, if they don’t feel they have been the victims of an injustice, why are officials getting involved?

Thierno Barry thought he had made it two for Everton, but the goal has been ruled out because Brennan Johnson was judged to be interfering with play and offside. You’re never getting those this weekend after the Enzo Fernandez incident.

Arsenal undone from a corner, swung to the back post and Chema Andres rose above everyone to head home.

This is a remarkable performance by Brighton, who have battered and bullied the champions from the start. Three-nil, and they have even beaten Arsenal at their own game by scoring a set-piece.

I am struggling to remember the last time Arsenal were overrun and outplayed as comprehensively as this. It’s a thrashing.

No half-time subs from Mikel Arteta, which is a little surprising given Arsenal’s predicament.

The undisputed highlight of the afternoon so far – Raspberry Beret has just been played during the half-time interval and you will agree that this is Prince’s finest work. We feel the need to bring this to your attention because, really, the final 15 minutes of the first half were a hotchpotch and if Everton don’t raise themselves, they will find trouble.

Another shot from outside the box as Arsenal’s defenders backed off, and the Greek striker found the bottom corner. What a first half for Brighton, Arsenal need to pull something out of the fire in the second half. Just before the goal, Saka had a chance after a deflected Odegaard shot.

Brighton’s second goal was an even better hit than their first. End-to-end football resulted in Kostoulas having space 20 yards from Arsenal’s goal. It’s another thumping low finish. Brilliant, breathless half of football by Brighton.

As half-time approaches, Arsenal have mustered just one shot on goal worth 0.03 expected goals. When they have moved the ball beyond Brighton’s press, they have not done anywhere near enough with it.

This fixture last season was especially bad-tempered, with the Brighton fans (and manager) repeatedly accusing Arsenal of time-wasting. The memories of that defeat are clearly still fresh in the minds of the Brighton supporters, who are roaring with rage at every perceived delay by the visitors, despite the fact that Arsenal are losing. The bad blood is adding to the intensity of the occasion.

Ipswich don’t play like a team that is short of confidence and quality. You might assume, if you haven’t seen much of them, that they are destined for a season of toil but there is definite quality with Gary O’Neill’s ranks, including Abdul Fatawu, who has been magnetic in drawing your eye to him. They might be a goal down but they are playing as if they are a goal in front.

Arsenal had just enjoyed a spell of control, but trail to a goal from one of the league’s in-form players. Gross whips a shot from just outside the box around Raya and in off the post.

Brighton have the lead at the Amex and it’s their captain, Pascal Gross, who has provided it. Superb long-range effort, in off the near post. On the overall balance of play, Brighton deserve that. It’s reward for their courage and willingness to go after Arsenal, rather than sitting back.

It took almost 20 minutes but Arsenal have found their feet in this game now. They are starting to find avenues through Brighton’s aggressive pressing and have made a few promising runs in behind, through Havertz and Saka. This is a high quality match.

No goals at the Amex, but Brighton are the team making the running, Arsenal struggling to play out from their own half and are yet to register a shot on goal.

Barry kept himself onside and turned the ball into the back of the net with his stomach. He did well to avoid a handball.

Bright start from Everton and they have the goal they deserve, albeit it came in fortuitous circumstances. James Tarkowski’s volley clattered into Thierno Barry and the deflection took it away from Christian Walton in Ipswich’s goal. Barry now has five goals for the season and, while he is raw, it’s an invaluable contribution.

A storming response to a bad night at Leeds from Newcastle, and it looks like being a long afternoon for Hull. Two down in seven minutes.

What a start for Newcastle United and what will really please manager Matthias Jaissle is the way both goals have come from his players winning important tackles.

The German was incensed by the lack of physicality and intensity in the heavy defeat to Leeds on Monday but the first goal for Joe Wilock came when Lewis Miley won a tackle on the edge of the Hull penalty box.

The second came when Sven Botman came away with the ball just inside his own half. On both occasions Harvey Barnes provided the assist. A short, intricate pass to Willock inside the box and then a surging, twisting run from the halfway line and the perfectly timed pass to Lewis Hall who stroked a first time shot into the bottom corner.

Hull have been outfought so far which is precisely the response Newcastle’s manager had demanded.

The home team are pressing high and all over Arsenal in the early stages. Raya has just made a save to deny Kostoulas.

Brighton have started brilliantly against the champions. They are hunting like wolves, pressing Arsenal with remarkable intensity. We have played seven minutes and I don’t think the ball has left Arsenal’s half.

Big chance for Everton to take the lead, but after great skill to turn his man at the edge of the box Brennan Johnson shoots wide with only the goalkeeper to beat.

The perfect start for Newcastle with all their injuries: Joe Willock has put the home side in a strong position against Hull with a clean strike inside three minutes.

We are under way at the Amex, St James’ Park and the Hill Dickinson.

Another famous face in the stands at Hill Dickinson Stadium today but this time it’s not about politicians. Wayne Rooney is here to watch his boyhood club and he will be hoping Everton can go into the international break unbeaten. An extra special cheer too before kick-off for Jarrad Branthwaite, who has just been called up for England duty. Plenty of Premier League clubs would like to sign Branthwaite, if they were given half a chance, but David Moyes has made it quite clear that Branthwaite: “Isn’t for sale - I want to keep my best players.”

He was not part of the match-day squad at Sunderland but Ben White’s injury has opened up a place, and Dowman fully deserves it after his two goals against Ipswich in the League Cup. Sam Dean has the story of his rise to stardom as well as what Arsenal are doing to nurture such a special talent.

Brighton are wearing a special “125 anniversary” kit today, to mark 125 years since the club was formed in 1901. It’s inspired by the colours of their first ever kit, which means an all-blue shirt, pale gold shorts and dark socks. Personally I would not allow such nonsense. But I don’t make the rules.

Spurs scored two late goals to salvage some pride against Aston Villa, but it is another defeat for Roberto De Zerbi’s team who have two points from five games. This Emi Buendia screamer put the game out of reach.

It has been a term tossed around liberally at Newcastle United since Matthias Jaissle arrived as manager, but what does “vertical football” actually mean?

It is the new buzzword in football analysis, the latest fashionable phrase to describe a “new” style of football, and it has been referenced multiple times by both Jaissle and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, since the German coach’s appointment last month.

For some of us of a certain age, vertical football just seems like clever new terminology to describe an old idea.

We are getting to the stage where we really need to start asking questions about Tino Livramento’s injury record.

The right back was due to start for Newcastle against Hull City this afternoon – his first start since April – but has picked up another injury.

That will surely mean he is out of the England squad for the Nations League having also picked up a tournament-ending injury at the World Cup in the summer before the first group game.

Livramento only played 17 Premier League games for Newcastle last season, scuppering his chances of a summer move to Arsenal, missing huge chunks of the season with groin and hamstring issues.

Injuries are already cutting deep into the Newcastle squad, with four teenagers on the bench for the visit of Hull. None have played in the first team before and three of them – Michael Mills, Mason Miley and Kyrian Thompson are just 17–years-old.

Newcastle wanted a younger team this season but not this young. It was interesting to hear Matthias Jaissle talk before the game. He knows how tough this season could be with so little experience in the side.

Lewis Dunk is a surprise absentee for Brighton, it can only be because of injury, and Hurzeler has preferred Diego Gomez to the lively Yalcouye who was very threatening at Old Trafford and Coventry. He could be a handful off the bench.

Good news for Arsenal: Jurrien Timber is finally fit enough to start a match again. This is his first start since mid-March and his return is timely, given the absence of Ben White through injury. It’s also a first Premier League start for Arsenal for Bruno Guimaraes, who comes into the midfield after his impressive performance off the bench at Sunderland last weekend.

Very excited for this one today. Arsenal have won all seven of their matches so far. Only once before in their history have they won their first eight games of a season - that was in 1903, when they were playing in the Second Division as Woolwich Arsenal. pic.twitter.com/iNBxoHl4Gc

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1380. Everton Women To Honour Armed Forces For Remembrance Fixture At Goodison Park

Everton Women will pay tribute to the Armed Forces during their Subway Players Cup fixture against Durham at Goodison Park on Wednesday 11 November (19:00 kick-off) – with free tickets on offer to serving military personnel as part of the Club’s annual Remembrance fixture.

In recognition of their service, members of the Armed Forces are invited to attend free of charge, with tickets available via Tickets For Troops.

Service personnel can check their eligibility for Tickets For Troops membership by clicking here.

Those eligible can then register here, before accessing Everton Women tickets at ticketsfortroops.org.uk.

This initiative builds on the Club’s long-standing support for the Tickets for Troops charity, which provides sporting and entertainment tickets to UK Armed Forces personnel and veterans.

The match will see veterans from Everton in the Community's Veterans’ Hub take part in a pre-match tribute, which will include a performance of The Last Post. This will be followed by a moment of silence and reflection as players, supporters and staff from both sides unite to remember those who have lost their lives in conflict and those who continue to serve today.

Everton in the Community’s Veterans’ Hub provides vital support to ex-service personnel through mental health provision, social activities and employability programmes, and representatives from the charity will be present at the fixture to raise awareness of their work.

This year’s Remembrance fixtures continue Everton’s proud tradition of honouring the Armed Forces community across both men’s and women’s football – reflecting a commitment to respect, inclusion and the deep-rooted connection with its local community.

Everton’s Men’s team took part in a tribute to the fallen ahead of Friday’s Premier League fixture against Coventry City at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Poppy shirts from all men’s and women’s fixtures during the Remembrance period will be signed and auctioned in aid of the Royal British Legion. To find out more - or to bid for a shirt - click here.

#1378. Rangers boss Derek McInnes piles the praise on in-form striker Ryan Naderi

Published: 18:30 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 7 November 2026

Rangers manager Derek McInnes heaped praise on Ryan Naderi after the Czech added another goal to his tally in the 2-0 win over St Mirren – but insisted there is still far more to come from his in-form striker.

The 23-year-old stepped up to slot home a first-half penalty to take his total to nine for the season in all competitions, with skipper Dan Neil adding a second shortly after the hour-mark to seal a valuable three points on the road.

The result moves McInnes’ men to within a point of Premiership leaders Celtic – who take on Kilmarnock this afternoon – ahead of the international break.

And the manager was delighted with the way in which his frontman shrugged off an earlier miss to take responsibility for the spot-kick which set Rangers on their way in what was a potential banana-skin encounter in Paisley.

‘His first port of call is to make sure he’s a handful to play against and I thought he was that,’ said McInnes. ‘I thought he ran the gaps, he made sure every one of their centre-backs knew he was there, which is very important.

‘He needs to build that reputation for being horrible to play against, but equally at a club like Rangers you’re going to get judged on the goals.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes (pictured) is thrilled with Ryan Naderi's performances

The Czech striker (left) celebrates with Kim Min-su after breaking the deadlock in Paisley

‘If you’re going to lead the line for us, then getting those goals is so important and thankfully with his stats he’s really contributing.

‘He’s probably a bit annoyed he never added to it, but I thought he was terrific.

‘You can’t be unsure, you can’t be thinking, “Do I belong here?”.

‘I think he’s totally shown that he’s somebody you can depend on, somebody that can be trusted, somebody that you can rely on to get goals as well as bring in good performances.’

Rangers are now unbeaten in their last 12, but although McInnes is pleased with his side’s progress after a sticky start to the season, he is under no illusions that there is much to improve on.

‘That type of form gets you close to where you want to get to,’ he said. ‘There’s still loads of work to do and loads of improvements in the team, as you can see.

‘If we take our chances, we take the game away from St Mirren and while it’s still 1-0, they are always going to keep going.

‘I still think that if we can win games and keep improving as we go along, then that’s the nature of the job for us. It’s just all about winning here.

‘The form has been really good, but we’re conscious that we’re not home and dry. We’re not the real deal yet. We’ve got loads of work to do to maintain that.

Dan Neil scored the second goal just after the hour-mark to put the game beyond St Mirren

‘Every game we’ve won has been hard-fought and we’ve had to play well to get the win.’

Saints boss Craig McLeish wasn’t happy with referee Nick Walsh’s decision to award the visitors a first-half penalty after James Penrice went down under the challenge of Samuel Ramos.

‘If that’s the criteria for contact in the box, then fine,’ he said.

‘But Kabs [Ismael Kabia] gets wiped out in the second half after he puts a cross in. I don’t even know if anyone looks at it.

‘I get that if the ref gives it on the field, then it’s maybe difficult for VAR to overturn it.

‘I think if he doesn’t give it there and then, I don’t think VAR gets involved to give it.

‘It’s a difficult one and it’s a frustrating one from our point of view, but there’s also bits leading up to it getting to that situation that we need to deal with better.

‘I need to be careful with what I’m saying.

‘Somebody just told me that there, it’s like our seventh penalty we’ve given away in 13 games, which from our point of view is not good enough. We can’t give teams goals and put ourselves in a hole like that.’

Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1,2,3,4,5,6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Social cues are essential for coordinating interactions between individuals, facilitating the emergence of group dynamics including mating, aggression and collective foraging8,9,10. Yet social interactions do not occur in isolation. Rather, they unfold in a broader environmental context that structures when, where and how social behaviours are expressed. Courtship and mating, for example, often take place at ecologically privileged locations—food sources1,2, prominent visual landmarks3,4 or suitable nesting sites5,6—where many individuals aggregate, either to increase their encounters with prospective sexual partners or to access key resources that promote reproductive success. In these settings, a central component of the environment is the social collective itself: the multisensory backdrop that emerges from the movement, sensory signals and interactions across all individuals in a group11,12,13,14. Social behaviours are therefore likely shaped by both the static properties of the physical environment and the dynamic features of the social landscape. Yet the neural mechanisms that integrate these distinct sensory streams to regulate social arousal states and structure interindividual interactions remain largely unknown.

The mating behaviours of Drosophila offer a powerful inroad to explore how animals adapt to complex ecological and social landscapes. Species in the Drosophila genus vary widely in their ecology and geographic distribution15,16,17,18,19,20, raising the possibility that mating strategies have evolved in concert with the diverse sensory environments in which reproduction occurs. Many species, including members of the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup, mate on their host plants, typically decaying ephemeral substrates where many individuals congregate17, creating a complex social backdrop for reproduction. Other species reproduce in more isolated social settings. Drosophila elegans, for example, establish individual territories and mate on their host flowers19, whereas species of the Hawaiian subgroup perform competitive lekking in the vegetation surrounding their hosts20. The evolution of Drosophila courtship behaviours may therefore have been shaped by the distinct sensory ecology of a species’ mating site and the structure and dynamics of the social groups that form there.

Reproduction and population density in Drosophila erecta, a close relative of D. melanogaster, are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of its host fruit—the screwpine Pandanus21—creating a narrow window of opportunity for individuals to meet and mate22. Such restricted access raises the possibility that D. erecta has evolved behavioural adaptations that couple reproduction to sensory cues emanating from its host, allowing environmental signals not associated with sexual communication to shape mating behaviour. Here we show that the olfactory volatiles emanating from a food patch exert both direct and indirect control over courtship in D. erecta. We find that food volatiles serve as a potent environmental trigger in this species, driving aggregation and serving as a stringent sensory gate to control a male’s sexual arousal. In parallel, environmental food odours shape the visual landscape in which courtship unfolds by encouraging males to approach and sample prospective mates, amplifying visual motion to transform the sensory backdrop of the social scene. D. erecta males are highly sensitive to this increase in visual motion, in contrast to D. melanogaster, pointing to the evolution of a multisensory feedback loop that coordinates male sexual arousal across members of the group, linking courtship to the broader social context. We show that species-specific differences in the sensitivity to environmental cues seem to arise from variation in how olfactory information impinges on conserved components of the courtship circuitry, indicating a potential neural substrate for the rapid tuning of sensory thresholds that govern sexual arousal. Together, these findings show how both ecological and social cues shape species-specific reproductive strategies. Moreover, our observations underscore that the social landscape forms an integral part of the environment—both reflecting the collective dynamics of the group and actively shaping the sensory experience of each individual in it.

To investigate how environmental factors shape the reproductive decisions of species with different ecological preferences, we compared the dynamics of groups of D. erecta and D. melanogaster (five males and five females) provided with a small patch of agar perfumed with food volatiles (diameter 21.5 mm) at the centre of a large arena (diameter 190 mm), a configuration intended to mimic the presence of a localized feeding site (Fig. 1a). Although D. erecta and D. melanogaster have distinct hosts and divergent olfactory preferences16,23, both feed on the yeast microbiota that metabolize decaying fruits and thus display attraction to volatiles arising from fermentation15,24. We therefore used apple cider vinegar (ACV), a broadly appetitive fermentation product, as a generic ‘host’ odour to compare how the chemical environment influences mating behaviours. Flies were fed and maintained as virgins in these assays to minimize their motivation to track towards the odour source for purely metabolic needs or in search of an oviposition site.

We found that in the context of the localized ACV patch, these two ecologically disparate species displayed distinct patterns of behaviour. D. melanogaster broadly explored the arena, giving rise to a dispersed spatial distribution where individuals interacted mostly in pairs and only intermittently in larger groups (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1a–e and Supplementary Video 1). By contrast, D. erecta individuals rapidly approached the central ACV patch and remained there for extended bouts (Fig. 1b,e and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), forming dynamic clusters of three or more interacting flies (Extended Data Fig. 1c–e). D. erecta did not congregate on a patch composed of agar alone (Fig. 1b,e, Extended Data Fig. 1b,f,g and Supplementary Video 1), indicating that food volatiles act as a potent aggregation cue in this species. Consistent with the notion that aggregation serves a social function in D. erecta, more than 90% of their copulations occurred on the ACV patch, in comparison to the spatially dispersed mating observed in D. melanogaster (Fig. 1d,f and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Comparable differences in aggregation and mating behaviour were also apparent when D. erecta and D. melanogaster were presented with a food patch made from the ripe pulp of D. erecta’s native host Pandanus candelabrum (Extended Data Fig. 1i–l), aligned with evidence that ACV shares several key volatiles with the bouquet of fermenting Pandanus fruit25,26,27. Notably, D. erecta refrained from mating entirely in the absence of ACV or Pandanus (Fig. 1f), highlighting the importance of the food patch as a site of reproductive opportunities in this species.

The ACV patch could facilitate mating in D. erecta by simply aggregating individuals, creating a dense social landscape where interactions between males and females are enhanced by proximity. Alternatively, ACV may directly elevate the sexual arousal of males or females on their arrival to the patch. To differentiate between these possibilities, we assessed the courtship dynamics of groups of five males and five females confined to a smaller chamber (diameter 38 mm, 4% area of the large arena; Fig. 1g), allowing us to decouple the effect of spatial proximity from the influence of the chemosensory environment. D. melanogaster males courted vigorously in this arena, independent of the presence of ACV (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Video 2). By contrast, D. erecta males courted only when ACV was present but rarely in its absence, despite the high density of flies (Fig. 1h,i and Supplementary Video 2). Indeed, D. erecta remained dispersed on an agar-only patch (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 2a), with males rarely approaching or pursuing individuals of either sex (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). In the presence of ACV, however, the spatial distribution of D. erecta individuals was transformed, displaying a pronounced peak at 3 mm (Fig. 1k)—the interfly distance characteristic of courtship pursuit—along with a broad tail, reflecting the dynamic interactions of males as they indiscriminately advanced towards any individual who came into their field of view (FOV) (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d). The rare instances of D. erecta courtship on agar were transient, in contrast to the persistent pursuit observed in the presence of ACV (Fig. 1l,m). ACV thus seems to influence mating behaviours in D. erecta not simply by aggregating males and females but by restructuring their social dynamics.

Different strains of D. melanogaster vary markedly in their sensitivity to courtship cues28. Nevertheless, several strains, including a Cameroonian isolate collected within the overlapping geographic range of D. erecta, courted vigorously even in the absence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 2e), indicating that the lack of reliance on this environmental signal is a broadly shared trait in this species. Although the limited availability of D. erecta strains precluded a comparable analysis of intraspecific variation, these results indicate that the food volatiles of ACV in D. melanogaster and D. erecta cannot be readily explained by variation within species and instead point to species-level differences in the sensory control of courtship. We therefore extended our analyses to related Drosophila species with distinct host ecologies. Unlike D. erecta, its sister species Drosophila orena, which specializes on Syzygium waterberries18, the closely related generalist Drosophila yakuba16 and the more distantly related specialist Drosophila sechellia, which breeds on Morinda citrifolia17, all vigorously courted conspecifics in both the presence and absence of ACV (Fig. 1j). By contrast, ACV suppressed courtship in D. elegans, a specialist that reproduces on Ipomoea blossoms19, potentially reflecting the limited chemical overlap between ACV and the volatile bouquet of its floral host29. Thus, although the influence of the chemosensory environment on reproductive behaviours varies across species, D. erecta males appear to have evolved a unique dependence on food volatiles to promote their courtship.

How does the chemosensory environment transform the structure of the D. erecta social landscape? Because interactions between individuals were more frequent on ACV, we reasoned that food odours may heighten the salience of visual objects. To explore this possibility, we presented individual males with a stationary fly-sized target—a high-contrast hemispherical bead, 3 mm in diameter (Fig. 2a)—and assessed whether ACV altered their interactions with it. D. melanogaster males were largely indifferent to this visual target, independent of the presence of ACV, spending most of their time circling the perimeter of the arena. D. erecta males, by contrast, remained in close proximity to the bead, an effect that was enhanced by ACV (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Supplementary Video 3). Optogenetic activation of most olfactory sensory neurons using the Orco promoter (Fig. 2d), which replicates the attractive valence of ACV in D. melanogaster30, was sufficient to promote attraction to the bead in D. erecta males on agar, confirming that olfactory input underlies this shift in visual salience (Fig. 2e,f, Extended Data Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Video 4). Visual approach was not enhanced by the same optogenetic manipulation in D. melanogaster males, underscoring that in D. erecta, olfactory input exerts a species-specific influence on how males interact with their visual surroundings.

Despite the strong attraction of D. erecta males to the bead on ACV, they frequently walked away before returning to it, generating a distinctive radial pattern as males alternated between approach and retreat (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Video 3), suggesting that the olfactory environment may also promote visual exploration. To examine this, we placed five D. erecta males in a large arena (diameter 190 mm) decorated with a lattice of 13 beads arranged in a regular square array (Fig. 2g; distance along edge 30 mm). In the presence of ACV, males spent most of their time near one of the targets but also frequently traversed between them (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), often taking the shortest route (Fig. 2h–l and Supplementary Video 5). On agar, males restricted their exploration to a small fraction of the arena, remaining at their starting location or near the bead closest to it and rarely visiting any other visual targets (Fig. 2h–l, Extended Data Fig. 3h,i and Supplementary Video 5). Comparing the trajectories of solitary males showed that they display a similar shift in their behaviour in the presence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 3j), indicating that visual sampling is driven by the chemical, not social, context. Without the bead lattice, males on ACV showed no spatial bias and remained broadly distributed across the arena (Extended Data Fig. 3h). By contrast, the visual exploration of D. melanogaster males was unaffected by the chemosensory environment (Extended Data Fig. 3k–o). Olfactory cues thus selectively promote exploration in D. erecta males.

Beads, although attractive visual targets to males, rarely evoked courtship displays such as the wing extensions associated with song production, indicating they are not perceived as potential mates (Extended Data Fig. 3p). Indeed, replacing a single bead in the array with a decapitated female shifted the search dynamics of males: on encountering the female, males often terminated their exploration and maintained her at close range (Fig. 2m,n and Extended Data Fig. 3q,r). Males occasionally resumed exploration of nearby beads after encountering the female but now often sang as they approached (Fig. 2o), indicating that the distinct cuticular pheromones carried by D. erecta females altered the males’ interpretation of visual targets, triggering a shift from exploration to courtship. Males on agar failed to locate the female in the bead lattice (Fig. 2p), suggesting that their limited exploration in the absence of food volatiles hinders their ability to detect or pursue prospective female mates. Thus, ACV promotes locomotion in D. erecta males to drive more frequent sampling of visual objects in their environment, supporting a form of ‘social foraging’ in which they search for reproductive opportunities rather than food resources.

In D. melanogaster, courtship is triggered by recognition of an appropriate conspecific female, a behavioural switch mediated by a network of male-specific P1 neurons that integrate multisensory signals—including direct excitatory input from pheromone pathways—to gate entry into a persistent arousal state31,32,33,34. D. erecta females, like their D. melanogaster counterparts, produce sex- and species-specific cuticular hydrocarbons35 that robustly excite the P1 neurons of conspecific males36, indicating that they similarly serve as chemical determinants of mate recognition. Food volatiles could therefore facilitate D. erecta courtship simply by encouraging males to approach females and sample their pheromonal cues. Yet even in the rare instances when D. erecta males initiated courtship on agar, their pursuit was fleeting (Fig. 1l,m), pointing to the possibility that food volatiles are required not only to promote encounters with females but also to sustain male sexual arousal in this species.

Consistent with this, although optogenetic activation of P1 neurons in D. melanogaster is sufficient to evoke persistent courtship37,38, in D. erecta it triggered only transient courtship bouts towards an immobilized female in the absence of ACV, with males rapidly resuming indifference after the optogenetic stimulus (Fig. 3a,b). By contrast, in the presence of ACV, P1 neuron activation drove sustained courtship in D. erecta males, suggesting that although P1 neurons promote entry into a state of sexual arousal, olfactory cues are required for its perpetuation. This olfactory dependence extended to pursuit of a moving visual target. In the absence of ACV, P1 neuron activation evoked only brief bouts of courtship towards a fly-sized 3-mm projected dot rotating on the floor of the assay chamber, whereas in the presence of ACV, males pursued and sang to the target spontaneously, even without P1 activation (Fig. 3c–f and Supplementary Videos 6 and 7).

To determine whether continuous olfactory input is required to sustain a male’s arousal, we leveraged the fact that tethered males will spontaneously court a fly-sized visual target projected onto a panorama, faithfully tracking its motion while singing to it38 (Fig. 4a). D. erecta males were largely indifferent to this visual target alone but initiated robust pursuit upon presentation of ACV (Fig. 4b,c,e,f, Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 8). Notably, courtship tracking was transient, with males rapidly terminating their pursuit at the offset of the odour stimulus, reinforcing that ACV is required for the perpetuation of arousal (Fig. 4e,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). D. melanogaster males, by contrast, commenced courtship pursuit at the onset of the visual stimulus and persistently tracked it for the duration of the assay (Fig. 4c,e,f), consistent with evidence that visual cues are sufficient to arouse males of this species, even in the absence of further sensory feedback33,38 (Extended Data Fig. 5).
